title: Frome
subtitle: Discover the vibrant town of Frome! Known for its creative spirit, independent shops, artisan markets, and historic charm, Frome offers a unique blend of culture, community, and character.

title: Longrun Meadow & French Weir Park
subtitle: Longrun Meadow & the connecting French Weir Park are beautiful and tranquil green spaces for the people of Taunton to enjoy.
bodyContent: Longrun Meadow offers 24 hectares of open space crossed by a network of paths and trails for walkers and cyclists. There’s an orienteering course, facilities for canoeing and a chance to become involved in nature conservation, plus a spectacular green willow ‘cathedral’ and a magnificent open-sided barn that’s ideal for picnics. It also plays host to Taunton's Park Run. French Weir Park is a small community park, covering 2.4 hectares. It covers an area beside the River Tone. As a neighbourhood park it’s enjoyed by all ages and acts as an attractive through route between residential areas, shops, schools and colleges.

title: Cheddar Gorge & Caves
subtitle: Cheddar Gorge & Caves boasts extraordinary subterranean show caves, awe-inspiring cliffs and holds many fascinating secrets about our prehistoric ancestors.
bodyContent: Our Day Ticket gives access to six great attractions: Gough’s Cave: Prepare to be amazed by our stunning show cave featuring spectacular stalagmite and stalactite formations created over 500,000 years ago! See cheddar cheese maturing in the caves, view the site where Cheddar Man’s 10,000-year-old skeleton was discovered and learn about the extraordinary DNA discovery. A free audio guide is available in six languages, and there is also a special version for children. Cox’s Cave featuring Yeo’s Journey: The Power of Water. This spectacular immersive multimedia experience tells the captivating story of how our iconic caves were formed and evolved through the ‘Power of Water’. The story is brought to life using state-of-the-art animation, sound, lighting and colour. Beyond the View: Take a seat in front of our state of the art 270-degree screen. Discover historic tales, enjoy breathtaking aerial panoramic views, and learn about the special wildlife and plants that call the gorge home. Museum of Pre-History: Discover amazing artefacts unearthed in the Cheddar area that help tell the story of how people lived thousands of years ago. Jacob’s Ladder & The Lookout Tower: Venture up the 274 steps to the top of the gorge with rest stops along the route to admire the view. Marvel at the panoramic views and mosaic of landscapes across the Mendips and Somerset Levels. Cliff­ -Top Walk: Hike the 3-mile loop around the gorge. Look out for the wildlife and enjoy the stunning scenery. If you don’t have time to do the full circuit, you can go for a shorter walk up to the Pulpit Rock look out point, and head back down the ladder. Gough’s Café Sit back, relax, and take in the beauty of the gorge at Gough’s Cafe, close to the entrance of Gough's Cave. Enjoy a thirst-quenching chilled drink, warm yourself up with a hot beverage or choose from a selection of alcoholic drinks. Serving light lunches, delicious snacks, cream teas and delicious cake, to include vegetarian and vegan options. Enjoy the spectacular views from the comfort of our air-conditioned cafe or relax on the large patio where dogs are welcome. We even have a welcome bowl of water for our doggy friends. Our small play area for under 2-year-olds will keep the little ones entertained too! Accessibility Cheddar Gorge & Caves provides accessible toilets, free parking for blue badge holders and free admission for carers accompanied by a full paying visitor. The audio tour of Gough's cave is printed in braille. Assistance Dogs are permitted, and the museum is wheelchair accessible with lift. Those with severely restricted mobility or who are wheelchair dependent will find areas of Cheddar Gorge & Caves inaccessible. If you have any questions prior to your visit, please email Guest Services on info@cheddargorge.co.uk or call 01934 742343. Dog-Friendly Dogs are welcome in all attractions and water bowls are provided in the cave entrances, shop and café patio. Family and Children Cheddar Gorge & Cave is family friendly. We have baby changing facilities, buggy parking and are breast-feeding friendly. Gough’s café has a small play area for under two year olds, water refills and highchairs are available. Entry is free for children under the age of 5 years. Groups Cheddar Gorge & Caves has special group rates, coach parking and drop off points for group tours. We offer discounted exclusive group sessions for Rocksport adventure activities – adventure caving, rock climbing and freefall. Special Events We have a fantastic programme of events throughout the year to keep the whole family entertained, including the school holidays. Visit our What’s On page for more details. Thirst for adventure or a puzzle-solving mind? Rocksport: Imagine climbing the gorge rockface in the shadow of the 450ft cliffs, caving deep underground or taking part in our exhilarating Blackcat freefall in Gough’s Cave. Suitable for all abilities. Sessions available for adults and children aged 8 years and over. Escape Rooms : Up for a challenge? Our two Cheddar-themed rooms, Caved In and The Vault will test your brain power as you race against the clock to try to escape. Double the fun with our Ultimate Escape combo ticket at a discounted rate. Suitable for 12 years and over in groups of up to six people. Nature, wildlife, history, adventure - experience the wonder on an all-season day out in Somerset. For more information on how to plan your day at Cheddar Gorge & Caves and to book please visit www.cheddargorge.co.uk
tagline: Explore Britain’s biggest gorge, from the stunning stalactite caverns to the dramatic cliffs.

title: Bath's Historic Venues
subtitle: At the heart of the World Heritage City, Bath’s Historic Venues are beautiful buildings that were originally built for hospitality and entertainment.
bodyContent: Event Venue At the heart of the World Heritage City, Bath’s Historic Venues are beautiful buildings that were originally built for hospitality and entertainment. They offer delightful and unusual settings for weddings, parties, conferences and receptions. • Roman Baths and Pump Room – From the first century AD to the 21st century, people have been drawn to this place for entertainment and relaxation. Dating back nearly 2,000 years, the Roman Baths offer a unique and atmospheric setting for a memorable event. • The Pump Room – Built in 1795, the Pump Room is without doubt one of the most elegant venues in the country and it remains at the social heart of Bath. The Pump Room is a perfect choice for dinners, weddings, concerts and receptions. • Assembly Rooms –Designed by John Wood the Younger in 1769, this fine set of public rooms was purpose-built for a particular 18th-century form of entertainment: the assembly. The world-famous Fashion Museum is located on the lower ground floor. • The Guildhall – Built by Thomas Baldwin in 1775, the Guildhall has been at the centre of Bath's administrative life for over 350 years. As well as being a stunning location for all manner of corporate and private events, it continues to house the Register Office, Mayor's Parlour and city archives. • Victoria Art Gallery – This lovely Grade II listed building was named to celebrate Queen Victoria's 60 years on the throne. Centrally situated, it houses a fine collection of art. The building consists of a grand Upper Gallery and a more contemporary Lower Gallery, with an inviting marble entrance hall and staircase. Please visit the Bath’s Historic Venues website for more details, or contact our friendly team to discuss your event requirements.

title: ASK Italian
subtitle: ASK Italian restaurant offers the true taste of Italy in Taunton.
bodyContent: Our chefs work with the best ingredients, including many sourced directly from Italy, to put together some of the most delicious Italian dishes you’ll ever taste. Our menu is crammed with classic and contemporary cuisine and there’s enough choice to leave you wanting more. We’re based in the former Post Office building on Taunton’s main shopping street, close to Butlins family fun park. Perfect for popping in for coffee or lunch and nibbles while you’re wandering about the town centre. We’re also within easy walking distance of County Ground, the home of Somerset County Cricket Club, the charming Tudor church St Mary Magdalene, and some interesting venues, including the Brewhouse Theatre and Castle Hotel.

title: Somerset Churches Trust
subtitle: We are an independent, non-denominational trust raising money for the repair and improvement of churches and chapels open for Christian worship in the historic county of Somerset. The Trust, founded in 1996 exists to encourage interest and the involvement of all members of the community in the magnificent heritage of our fine religious buildings.
bodyContent: Discover Somerset's Heritage with Somerset Churches Trust.Once a month from March to October (excluding September when we hold a fundraising event) we arrange a visit to a number of churches. These church tours commonly known as 'Church Crawls" usually start at 2.00 pm and finish around 5.00 pm with tea. They are often lead by experts on church history and architecture such as the authors of the Pevsner The Buildings of England guides. All are welcome. We do not charge but we do ask for donations and also encourage those who attend to become members of the Trust. Individual membership is £20 per annum and family membership (two or more) is £30.00 a year. Full details of our annual programme and membership application is on our website.

title: Netherclay Community Woodland
subtitle: An area of improved pasture land on the banks of the River Tone planted with broadleaved trees north of Bishop's Hull great for riverside wildlife.
bodyContent: An area of improved pasture land on the banks of the River Tone planted with broadleaved trees north of Bishop's Hull great for riverside wildlife. OS Map Reference ST 207 252 Size 6 hectares Grazing animals No Walking trails The site is mostly level and laid to grass, with paths cut between the newly planted trees. Parts of the reserves can get very muddy during wet weather. Access Contact the Trust for access information. Dogs On a lead About the reserve This area of improved pasture land on the bank of the River Tone, north of Bishop’s Hull, has been planted with native broadleaved trees to create new woodland. The site is an extension of Somerset West and Taunton Council’s existing woodland plantation, created with the help of volunteers. The site was purchased with support from Viridor Credits Environmental Company and Bishop’s Hull Parish Council and is being developed in co-operation with Somerset West and Taunton Council, the parish and volunteers. The former line of the Grand Western Canal passes close to the northern margin and a public footpath roughly follows the route of the former towpath. Hedgerows lining the northern and western boundaries have sections dominated by English Elm. The northern hedge also features Hawthorn, Blackthorn, Field Maple, Elder, Common Dogwood, Pedunculate Oak and Ash. Good numbers of Brown Hairstreak butterflies can been seen along these hedges; also look out for Holly Blues and the Orange Tailed Clearwing Moth. The riverbank itself is mainly open but a number of mature standard trees occur, including several black poplars towards the western end. The river supports a diverse fauna including a range of less common species such as Otter, Water Shrew, Kingfisher and Dipper. Salmon and Brown Trout are known to migrate along this section of the river to spawn upstream. A pair of small ponds along the line of the northern boundary ditch provide a habitat for amphibians. Information boards are on site, together with some sculptures on Somerset West and Taunton Council’s area.
tagline: Improved pasture land on the banks of the River Tone

title: Mendip Spring
subtitle: Mendip Spring is one of the leading golf clubs in the South West of England & is situated in beautiful North Somerset countryside. Lying in Wrington Valley, overlooked by the Mendip Hills, it is within easy reach of Bristol, Weston super Mare and Bath, and the M4 and M5 motorways…
bodyContent: Mendip Spring is tucked away in the beautiful North Somerset countryside and is considered to be one of the South West’s leading Stay & Play venues. The Par 71 Brinsea Championship Course has water hazards, long Par 5’s, tricky par 3’s and an interesting mix of par 4’s, topped off with immaculately kept greens that are true all year round. This course is a delight to play and offers a thorough challenge of a golfer’s skill. The clubhouse at Mendip Spring is centred around an original 16th century farmhouse and has been tastefully refurbished to be warm welcoming and full of character, whilst still providing a comprehensive bar, restaurant and accommodation facilities. This venue is nestled away in one of the most beautiful parts of Somerset, just a stones throw away from the Mendip Hills an area of outstanding natural beauty and on a few miles away from Weston – Super – Mare and The City of Bristol. The venue is ideally located for a relaxing break away. Whether you are travelling for Business or Pleasure, the venues 19 attractive well-furnished rooms offer en-suite facilities with bath or shower. The accommodation is perfect for those wishing to stay overnight looking for a short break, visiting other areas of Somerset or golfers using the golf courses on site or other courses in the area. Mendip Spring is more than just a golf club and opens its doors everyone who is looking for a professional venue.

title: Blackdown Hills National Landscape
subtitle: The Blackdown Hills are a nationally important landscape in recognition of the special qualities of their natural and built environment. Being relatively unspoilt, the Hills offer a rare sense of timelessness.
bodyContent: Some of the most popular tourist destinations in the world are backwaters – places where little has changed or is likely to. Here we can take time to reflect on the relative constancy of the natural landscape. One such place is the area around the Blackdown Hills, in many ways archetypal English Countryside with hedgerows, copses, farmland and narrow lanes. The villages are distinctive thanks to the use of local stone, tiles and thatch and many of the hamlets date back to medieval days. Among the smallest of the UK’s protected landscapes, the Blackdown Hills have a remarkable variety of habitats from heath and grasslands to wet woodlands and bogs. The steep banks are a riot of wildflowers in Spring and the hedgerows and woods are still home to the nationally scarce hazel dormice. Standing guard on the northern ridge of the hills is the world’s only three-sided obelisk, a monument to the Duke of Wellington. A network of hedges, mature hedgerow trees and small copses link a rich mosaic of semi-natural habitats. The area is perfect for walks , cycling and horse riding where the quiet bridleways and byways offer many opportunities to explore and enjoy the locally distinctive buildings, archaeological remains and natural flora and fauna. The Hills have a variety of tourist accommodation providers ranging from bed & breakfast establishments, beautiful country houses, converted barns, farmhouses and cottages. There are a number of self-catering cottages and a small range of family run hotels and guesthouses. This area is renowned for its fantastic range of welcoming country inns, many of which offer terrific menus of home cooked food, sourced from local produce. The Blackdown Hills are perfect destination for short break holidays, where visitors can join in with organized activities such as guided walks, hedgerow skills workshops, fishing, arts and crafts, writing courses... the list is endless!

title: Further information about the new seafront play area planned for Burnham-on-Sea
subtitle: As reported on local media, some questions and comments have recently been raised with the town council about the new seafront play area.
bodyContent: As reported on local media, some questions and comments have recently been raised with the town council about the new seafront play area. Residents were welcomed to speak at a meeting of the Town Improvements Committee on 11th January 2021, where they pledged support for the play area but requested that it is not sited on the existing tarmac already used for improvised leisure, and instead sited on the grassed area, further south and out of sight of any residences. The committee chairman gave a full response, confirming information previously provided, and noting, “ the lawn areas are a designated green space and stand out against a large expanse of tarmac. ” He reiterated that the tarmac location in question had been publicly identified for improvement in 2018 and that the project was now at an advanced stage. The chairman agreed to ask the council to look at how the grassed lawns can be made more attractive. To assist those who might need more information on the project, reports of the questions asked by residents to date, along with answers provided by the council, have been published on the town council’s website. The installation of the new and inclusive play area is part of the ongoing Burnham Evolution business Plan, published in 2018, that aims to invest in the town to bring improvements and opportunity. The plan acknowledges that: We must recognise the need for residents’ quality of life to be balanced with the town’s retail and leisure offer. We must seek to offer a balance of uses for the community, business and visitors alike, along with an improved public realm.

title: Maunsel Lock
subtitle: Discover Maunsel Lock, a great place to start exploring the Bridgwater & Taunton Canal.
bodyContent: Maunsel Lock was once busy with boats plying their trade to and from Bridgwater Docks. Today, it’s a great place to start exploring the Bridgwater & Taunton Canal. A little bit of history Maunsel Lock, on the Bridgwater & Taunton Canal, is a picture of peace. During the Second World War however, it formed a line of defence known as the Wessex Stop (or Taunton) Line and all the swing bridges were removed. Many have now been reinstated as part of a programme of restoration. Download the Maunsel Lock map HERE Parking Toilets Café Picnic Boat trips Path Allow 1-2 hours for this visit * Don’t forget: Although the site is always open the facilities and boat trips may not be and some may be chargeable. Please check with local businesses before setting out. Five things to do at Maunsel Lock Look out for Second World War pillboxes where anti-tank equipment was stored. Maunsel Lock is on the edge of the Somerset Levels – a great place for wildlife. Look out for kingfishers, herons, dragonflies and damselflies. Enjoy a traditional cream tea in the Maunsel Lock Tea Rooms over looking the canal. Take a boat trip and discover more about the Bridgwater & Taunton Canal. Starting at Maunsel Higher Lock, explore the Somerset Space Walk. Scale models of the planets are positioned along the canal to represent the solar system. Did you know?... Our lock gates are handbuilt by skilled carpenters in our workshops in the West Midlands and Yorkshire, from FSC Green Oak. Each one is unique and can take up to a month to make. Once built they last for about 25 years. Go to canalriverexplorers.org.uk to discover lots of fun things to do with the family.
tagline: Discover Maunsel Lock - little adventures on your doorstep

title: Oh Take time out Walk Knoll...
subtitle: . we’ve left North Somerset. A steep and strenuous walk up Brent Knoll pays off with spectacular views of Somerset countryside and the Bristol Channel.
bodyContent: How to get there Start at map ref: ST336507 Car: The turning for Brent Knoll (Brent Street) is off the A38 near Sanders Garden Centre. Coming from the north you will need to go to the Edithmead roundabout and turn around. Then turn left into Brent Street. Church Lane is fourth on the right. Park on Church Lane and make your way up the road towards St Michael’s Church. As you round the corner, turn right on to the public footpath through the kissing gate. A gentle climb at first between woods and the churchyard boundary, pass through the second gate and turn right up the hill and the first steep section. The terrain can be uneven here and tricky if it’s been raining. A dry day is recommended. Take a breather, stop and enjoy the views as you ascend. Through the next gate and head straight on for a slightly gentler section. This time of year sheep are gamboling in neighbouring fields with their lambs. The path curves to the right, then to the left for the second and steepest section of the walk. There are steps near the top and a handy rail to hold on to, should you need it. Once you reach the gate you’re nearly there. Head through and climb the earth cut steps to the top. Enjoy the view, you’ve earned it. With Weston-super-Mare visible six miles to the north and Glastonbury Tor on the horizon to the south east, there’s an impressive vista to take in. Stroll around the top then head back the way you came. Watch your footing on some of the steeper steps near the top and enjoy the view as you descend.

title: Abbey Rise
subtitle: Abbey Rise is a large Victorian terraced townhouse offering panoramic city views and guaranteed off road private parking throughout your stay. It is just an 8-minute stroll from the train and bus station and hub of the city.
bodyContent: Abbey Rise is a large Victorian terraced townhouse offering panoramic city views and guaranteed off road private parking throughout your stay. It is just an 8-minute stroll from the train and bus station and hub of the city. Bath is Katherine’s home town and after travelling around the world working in large prestigious hotels she was drawn back to this cosmopolitan and beautiful UNESCO city, where she decided to open up her own bed and breakfast. Living and working as part of the Royal Household at Buckingham Palace has left its mark and Katherine continues to maintain those standards in her own home, where guests are treated to crisply ironed sheets, fluffy towels and wonderfully comfortable beds whilst enjoying a homely and welcoming atmosphere. Katherine has been running Abbey Rise for a number of years now and frequently welcomes returning guests who will always find some new and interesting change or addition-though Katherine’s famous homemade brownies and cakes are always on the menu!
tagline: Abbey Rise is a large Victorian terraced townhouse offering panoramic city views

The accommodation comprises of 11 tastefully decorated bedrooms,

title: Bloomfield House
subtitle: Bloomfield House, a Georgian detached Grade II listed building, has elegant and romantic rooms (four posters or half testers) fine art, antiques, splendid views all combined with environmental credentials and a friendly relaxed atmosphere.
bodyContent: The House Bloomfield House, a Georgian detached Grade II listed building, has elegant and romantic rooms (four posters or half testers) fine art, antiques, splendid views all combined with environmental credentials and a friendly relaxed atmosphere. The house is set well back from a quiet road. Well behaved children and pets are welcome. The Breakfast Our traditional full English breakfasts are freshly cooked to order and served from 7.30 am until 11 am. Ingredients are mostly organic, fair-traded and provided by local suppliers, including homemade preserves and artisan breads. Vegetarian, vegan and gluten-free options are always available. The Parking We have free off-street parking and an electric car charging point for our guests use. There is easy access to the city centre via a regular bus service which stops within a few feet of the entrance to our property. The walk into town is a downhill stroll of 20 mins, on the way back up – jump on the bus or grab a cab! . The Bedrooms All bedrooms have en-suite facilities and come with the usuals – TV, hospitality tray, toiletries, hair dryer. The guest bedrooms are situated on the second floor, we have no lift so are not suitable for those with mobility issues. We are, of course, happy to help you up the stairs with your luggage. On the upside this does mean each room has far reaching views. Please note, for those with allergies , that this is a family home and we have both cats and dogs on the premises. The cats do not have access to the guest bedrooms (nor do our dogs for that matter). DISCOUNTS Any mid-week stay (Sun-Thurs ) will attract a £10 discount. Please quote ‘Stay in Bath’ when booking (by phone) on 01225 420105. Any on-line booking – applicable discounts will be deducted upon check-out. (This sadly cannot be used in addition with other special offers.) We also offer discounts to those arriving in Bath by train or bus. Discounts do not apply to Bank Holidays or one night Saturday bookings which are, on occasions, available.
tagline: Bloomfield House, a Georgian detached Grade II listed building

title: 1 The Paragon City Centre Apartment
subtitle: Elegant first floor Georgian Apartment in Bath City centre with breath taking views across Bath and Beyond.
bodyContent: Elegant first floor Georgian Apartment built in 1790 in Bath Centre of the City with breath taking views across Bath the Apartment overlooks Walcot Street the Artisan quarter of the city with many vibrant shops and eclectic collection of characterful independent shops. The Apartment is spacious and light with many of its original features marble top fireplaces, high ceilings with cornice and sash windows.Wooden floor in the open plan living kitchen area . Spacious bedroom with super king or twin beds the view over looks Haymarket church and the beautiful Paragon full of tall Town houses dating back to the 1800s. Towels and bed linen robes and toiletries are provided. Free wifi connection. Whether it’s Shopping History or fine dining you are interested in you couldn’t get a better location then 1 The Paragon with the many famous attractions on your door step Thermae Bath Spa, Roman baths, Bath Abbey, Royal crescent, Assemble rooms, Pultney bridge, Milsom Street the hub of the city is just a short walk with many wonderful shops and restaurants. We are proud to say Jane Austen lived at 1 The Paragon just imagine staying here where Jane Austen resided!
tagline: Elegant first floor Georgian Apartment in Bath City centre.

title: South Western Railway
subtitle: With South Western Railway you can explore Somerset from anywhere in the country.
bodyContent: With South Western Railway you can explore Somerset from anywhere in the country. South Western Railway is a joint venture between FirstGroup and MTR Europe, two of the world’s leading train companies. The South Western franchise has over 235 million passenger journeys a year and covers routes between London Waterloo and south western England, including Exeter, Bristol and Portsmouth. They cover some of the busiest routes in the country, operating nearly 1,700 services each weekdays. You can visit southwesternrailway.com for live travel updates, train tickets, special offers and a full list of destinations, as well as top attractions in the area. You’ll also be able to keep up to date with all the rail improvements that are coming over the next few years. South Western Railway are also on Facebook and Twitter, so make sure you are following them to be the first to hear of special offers and events happening near you, as well as discounts, rail cards and more. There is also an app for those of you who want to plan your trip and get tickets on the go.
tagline: With South Western Railway you can explore Somerset from anywhere in the country.

title: Blagdon Lake
subtitle: Are there many anglers in the world who haven’t heard of Blagdon? The name stirs emotions for thousands of anglers as the home of still water trout fly fishing with catch records going back as far as the early 1900's.
bodyContent: The lake is relatively shallow, with an average depth of 14 feet and only 38 feet at its deepest point near the dam (west end of the lake). Travel along its narrow length to the east and you come to the shallowest area of the lake at Top End where the River Yeo enters. In between there are many superb fishing areas with proven track records of producing the goods – Bell’s Bush, Peg’s Point, Rainbow Point, Ash Trees, Rugmoor and Green Lawn, are all areas that successful anglers will quickly become accustomed to. All methods work on the lake but many locals and experts stick to small flies and nymphs fished slowly on or near the surface. Early season and in the dying days of the year lures and sinking lines can be effective, but it is the patterns that imitate the naturals which command most attention. Sitting at the foot of the Mendip Hills in an Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty (AONB), Blagdon Lake covers 440 acres and is classified as a SSSI by Natural England for its’ wildflower meadows and bird populations. The long, narrow shape makes it ideal for both boat and bank fishing. There are deep basins and long banks to drift over, plenty of points and promontories for access to deeper areas as well as shallow, sheltered bays of quieter water. Most of the seven-mile perimeter has easy bank access but to explore the more remote areas a boat is the answer. On the south shore of the Lake below Blagdon village is the Fishing Lodge. This beautiful, timber framed building epitomizes the old world charm of Blagdon Lake. There is an office and small tackle shop on site selling all the essential flies and accessories. The Lodge is manned during the mornings by friendly, knowledgeable staff who are there to help you enjoy your day by giving up to the minute information on how the water is fishing. Enjoy a complimentary cup of tea or coffee before fishing or during a leisurely lunch. We have a fleet of 20 boats for hire at Blagdon. Advance booking is essential as each boat is individually locked and when Blagdon Lodge is unstaffed anglers must report to Woodford Lodge, Chew Valley Lake, in order to sign in. For more info please click here

title: The Cheese and Grain
subtitle: The Cheese and Grain is a not-for-profit, member owned social enterprise and also a registered charity. Its main aim is to promote and boost Frome’s social, cultural and economic life.
bodyContent: The Cheese and Grain has an important role in Frome because we can host meetings, large (up to 500 people in the main hall) and small (up to about 30 people in our mezzanine). Every year we hold an annual member's meeting (the Annual General Meeting - the AGM). This is the meeting where the membership elects the Board of Trustees. There's plenty of time at the AGM to meet other members. Want to join now? Contact us and ask to be sent a membership form, or ask at the box office.
tagline: The Cheese and Grain is a not-for-profit, member owned social enterprise

title: Wraxall Vineyard
subtitle: The Grapes. The View. The Experience. The Memories.
bodyContent: Working in harmony with our surroundings, nurturing the vines and understanding the terroir is at the heart of the Vineyard; and the Vineyard is where great wine begins! Situated on a beautiful south-facing hill just south of the Mendips in Somerset, Wraxall Vineyard is surrounded by verdant countryside and breath-taking views. Blessed with a mild South West climate and rich fertile soils, our location is perfect for growing vines. Yet growing vines and producing wine is a slow process and a real labour of love. Owners David and Lexa took over Wraxall Vineyard as a family venture in 2021. Their aim and vision is to dedicate time and passion into producing truly great wines for all to share, celebrate and enjoy.

title: RHUBARB & CUSTARD NEGRONI
subtitle: Created in Italy 100 years ago, traditionally, a Negroni is stirred, not shaken, and is well known for its bitter flavour. There have been many variations of the classic Negroni cocktail over the years and here comes another one, but we can guarantee you’ve not tasted a Negroni like this before! Go on, give it a go, you know you want to...
bodyContent: METHOD • Add ice, gin, vermouth, rhubarb syrup to glass and stir well until glass is chilled. • Top with Brothers Rhubarb & Custard Cider and stir. • Squeeze and add a slice of lime to garnish. Head over to the Brothers Cider Website for the ingredients, measurements and more! https://brotherscider.co.uk/blogs/recipes/rhubarb-custard-negroni
tagline: Created in Italy 100 years ago, traditionally, a Negroni is stirred, not shaken.

subtitle: Home to the lords of the manor of Clevedon for centuries, the core of the house is a remarkable survival from the medieval period.
bodyContent: Clevedon Court in Clevedon, Somerset, National Trust property is an outstanding 14th-century manor house and 18th-century terraced garden Home to the lords of the manor of Clevedon for centuries, the core of the house is a remarkable survival from the medieval period. The house was purchased by Abraham Elton in 1709 and it is still the much-loved family home of his descendants today. Explore the striking display of Eltonware pottery and a fascinating collection of Nailsea glass.

title: Ferne Animal Sanctuary
subtitle: Ferne Animal Sanctuary is set within 72 acres of beautiful & protected countryside in the Blackdown Hills on the Devon/Somerset border. This charitable sanctuary takes in unwanted, abandoned and neglected animals and gives them a fantastic life either at the sanctuary or by finding them a special forever home.
bodyContent: Ferne Animal Sanctuary is set within 72 acres of beautiful & protected countryside in the Blackdown Hills on the Devon/Somerset border. This charitable sanctuary takes in unwanted, abandoned and neglected animals and gives them a fantastic life either at the sanctuary or by finding them a special forever home. Ferne Animal Sanctuary, located near Chard in Somerset, is a remarkable facility dedicated to the rehoming of dogs, cats, and horses. In addition to this, the sanctuary provides ongoing care and welfare for a wide variety of animals, including sheep, goats, cattle, pigs, geese, chickens, and an aviary housing birds from around the world. It is also home to smaller animals such as rabbits, guinea pigs, chinchillas and ferrets, ensuring they all receive the care and attention they need. Founded in 1939, at the onset of World War II, the charity was established to care for pets whose owners were going to war, or who had been displaced by the conflict. Over the years, it has forged strong connections with HM Armed Forces and the Royal Family. A typical visit to Ferne lasts between 90 to 150 minutes, during which visitors can enjoy observing the animals in their natural habitats. The experience includes a sensory garden designed to calm the senses with a variety of sounds, sights and smells. Visitors can explore the Willow Walk, which offers insights into animal care, as well as informative displays about our water voles, dragonflies, birds, and fungi. There's also a machinery wall showcasing equipment used throughout the years, along with a small play area for our younger visitors. Take the time to enjoy the stunning natural landscape of the Blackdown Hills from our viewing platform. Relax, gaze across the hills, and marvel at the beauty of nature at its finest. During the school holidays, Creative Corner offers a range of animal-themed activities and arts and crafts. We also host special events and workshops throughout the year, with full details available on our website. The Visitor Centre is open from 10 AM to 4 PM from Easter to October half term, though the shop and sanctuary are open every day, except Christmas Day, Boxing Day, and New Year's Day. Our well-stocked pet supplies and gift shop has everything you need for your animals, as well as delightful treats to tempt you. Dog friendly (dogs must be kept on leads) and accessible, Ferne has a good network of tarmac paths. However, due to the number of gates, we recommend that wheelchair users are accompanied. We have designated parking spaces for wheelchair users and visitors with special needs next to our Visitor Centre as well as in the main car park. All money raised goes to support our animal care and welfare. Unleash the Party Fun at Ferne Animal Sanctuary! title: Somerset Brick and Tile Museum
subtitle: The Museum tells the story of brick and tile making, one of the many labour-intensive industries once found in Somerset.
bodyContent: Somerset Brick and Tile Museum is open for general visits, guided tours, group visits and special events. The Museum tells the story of brick and tile making, one of the many labour-intensive industries once found in Somerset. At the heart of the Museum is one of the only traditional brick kilns to survive in southern England. It was one of six at the former Barham Brothers’ Yard in East Quay, Bridgwater, and was last fired in 1965. Bridgwater produced an impressive variety of bricks, tiles, terracotta plaques and other wares that created the look of many Somerset towns. The kiln is a Scheduled Ancient Monument and was saved from destruction in the 1990s. Somerset Brick and Tile Museum is part of the South West Heritage Trust, an independent charity committed to protecting and celebrating Somerset and Devon’s rich heritage.

title: Hestercombe House and Gardens
subtitle: Discover Somerset and lose yourself in fifty acres of lakes, temples, cascades, tranquil woodland walks, formal terraces, vivid colours and views that take your breath away…..
bodyContent: Discover Somerset and lose yourself in fifty acres of lakes, temples, cascades, tranquil woodland walks, formal terraces, vivid colours and views that take your breath away….. Hestercombe's famously restored gardens span three centuries of garden design and provide important examples of gardens in contrasting styles that continue to grow and develop. The restored 17th century watermill complex showcases historic uses of renewable energy alongside the original working mill machinery. The award-winning visitor facilities include the warm and welcoming Stables Restaurant with a bright, airy courtyard, gift shop and plant centre. Inside the historic Hestercombe House find Hestercombe Contemporary Art Gallery, gallery shop, second-hand bookshop and period rooms, providing lots more to see and do, whatever the weather.

title: Cleeve Abbey
subtitle: The Cistercian abbey of Cleeve offers a glimpse of daily life 800 years ago.
bodyContent: The Cistercian abbey of Cleeve is a haven of peace and tranquillity, offering a glimpse of daily life 800 years ago. It has some of the best-preserved monastic buildings in England, with many rooms retaining traces of their original decoration. The abbey is steeped in history, providing a fascinating day out for families and budding historians alike. Although the church was destroyed by Henry VIII during the dissolution of the monasteries, the cloister buildings (including the gatehouse, 15th century refectory with its glorious angel roof, and 13th century heraldic tiles) have survived remarkably intact. The great dormitory is one of the best examples in the country, and an exhibition and virtual tour tells the story of the abbey and daily life for the holy men that once inhabited it. Cleeve is one of the hidden gems of Somerset, located in a beautiful valley surrounded by countryside. It is ideal for walkers or visitors travelling on the West Somerset Railway. Click here to learn more about English Heritage sites in Somerset.
tagline: The Cistercian abbey of Cleeve offers a glimpse of daily life 800 years ago.

title: Cedars Hall, Wells
subtitle: Welcome to Cedars Hall Cedars Hall is a state-of-the-art performance venue providing a varied programme of top quality entertainment all year round. It is situated in the beautiful grounds of Wells Cathedral School in the heart of the City of Wells.
bodyContent: The hall hosts a number of professional (and amateur) productions throughout the year which include classical, jazz, folk and rock and pop and cabaret concerts, drama, talks and films. The main recital hall, Eavis Hall, has the capacity for audiences up to 350 and is a flexible and modern performance space. In addition to events in Eavis Hall, it serves as a hub for its significant community outreach, which provides music education (including workshops, concerts and masterclasses) for thousands of primary school children, elderly and disability groups in the South West each year. Cedars Hall is also available to hire for concerts and events - please enquire at boxoffice@cedarshallwells.co.uk Tickets for all events can be booked online or via our box office on 01749 834483 For more information visit: https://cedarshallwells.co.uk/

subtitle: The Grand Pier is open every day, except Christmas Day, so come hail, rain or shine, you’ll always get a warm welcome. Whatever the weather is doing outside, it’s still fun, fun, fun on the inside.
bodyContent: ⭐ Reward Card Discount Available The Grand Pier, Weston super Mare, Somerset is the ideal destination for non-stop indoor family theme park fun. This North Somerset pier, with its state-of-the-art Pavilion is a truly iconic destination for family days out, events, concerts, weddings, and corporate events. With rides, attractions and the latest arcade games a visit to the Pier is the perfect treat for kids of all ages. On weekends, bank holidays and North Somerset school holidays, Unlimited Ride Wristbands are available for both adults and children, explore here . Don't miss out on this fantastic deal for your fun-filled day! Come and discover everything the Grand Pier, Somerset has to offer, including: · The very latest amusements - including giant screen Space Invaders · Thrilling rides including: Sidewinder, Freefall and Robocoaster · An amazing two level 300 meter indoor Go-Kart track · Seaside favourites, including: dodgems, house of horrors and helter skelter · A three-level, dinosaur themed soft play area with dedicated adult seating · A choice of places to eat and drink - we even serve your favourite Costa coffee! With hundreds of amusements and games to play, a range of thrilling rides, and a choice of attractions for all ages everyone gets to have fun in the amazing Pavilion - it really is one big house of fun!!! When you’re ready for a bite to eat you’re spoilt for choice from traditional fish and chips to afternoon tea, and of course ice cream too! There’s even a pub for you to enjoy a relaxing drink as you take in the spectacular views. As a unique location our function rooms are always in demand, and we love creating the perfect setting for weddings and family celebrations. For businesses our dedicated events team is on hand for corporate events, ranging from team meetings and training sessions to large scale conferences.The fun continues into the night with a wide range of events from concerts to whodunnits. To make sure you don’t miss out visit and book your tickets online today.

title: Walton’s Guest House
subtitle: Walton’s Guest House, providing warm and friendly accommodation in central Bath for over 25 years.
bodyContent: Walton’s Guest House, an oasis in the centre of Bath catering for Business and Tourism. Centrally located in Bath, this Guest House offers great facilities and a short walk to the Royal Crescent, Bath City Centre & the Royal Bath Spa Complex. All rooms are luxury en- suite and our rates include a hearty full English breakfast cooked to order. A family business for over 40 years, we aim to make your stay enjoyable and trouble free and can offer helpful advice on what to do and see in the city and surrounding area including seasonal local events. Bath offers a wide variety of attractions throughout the year and Walton’s is within easy walking distance of the Music Festival venues, the Theatre Royal including The Egg and the Ustinov Studio, the Roman Baths and Thermae Spa complex, the Museum of Costume, Bath Rugby at the Recreation Ground, the Jane Austen Festival, the Christmas Markets in the Abbey Churchyard and all City Centre Shops. For those walking the Cotswold Way, Walton’s offers a convenient overnight stay on the western edge of the city centre. There is a bus stop outside the front door, should you wish to take a day trip to Bristol, during your stay There is free on-street parking between 6.00pm and 8.00am and a public car park immediately behind the hotel. I have a couple of Parking Permits, providing all day on- street parking. Call or email for group bookings and for seasonal and midweek offers. ​ Bedrooms: 7 Bathrooms: 7 Children: Most Welcome Pets: No Onsite Parking: No - On street parking permits available

title: Tucking Mill View, luxury self-catering cottage
subtitle: Tucking Mill View is a luxury self-catering cottage with outstanding views over the Midford/Tucking Mill valley, an Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty all on one level.
bodyContent: A real home from home, this self-catering cottage is ideal for those holidaymakers who wish to combine the country with the city… Newly renovated and maintained to the highest standard Tucking Mill View has been awarded the coveted 4 Star Gold Award for Exceptional Accommodation and Welcome by Visit England. TUCKING MILL VIEW ACCOMMODATION The single storey luxury self-catering cottage is 66 metres square…with a large open plan sitting room, with a 3 seater sofa and a snuggle sofa (which can double as a single sofa bed) and a modern fully equipped kitchen with washing machine and full size dishwasher. The calmly appointed bedroom in cream and turquoise has a luxury 1400 sprung king sized bed, with top quality Egyptian cotton bed linen. The only noise likely to waken you are the owls in the tree tops. For those balmy evenings, the private patio overlooking the valley is an ideal spot ..with a stone built barbecue and table and chairs you can enjoy every meal without being disturbed. Being so close to Bath, Tucking Mill View is the perfect balance for relaxing and unwinding as well as exploring the beauties of the Bath and wandering in the Somerset and Wiltshire countryside. As well as the gold Award for exceptional welcome, Visit England have also awarded the cottage the Cyclists’ and Walkers’ Welcome Awards and the cottage is an ideal centre for waling and cycling, particularly with he newly opened Two Tunnel Route into Bath..Sustrans 24 which passes by the cottage. AROUND AND ABOUT This secluded hamlet takes its name from the process of ‘tucking’ ,a process for cleansing wool, was undertaken. Being halfway between the historic villages of Midford and Monkton Combe, Tucking Mill benefits from access to two independent gastro pubs both within a 15 minute walk along the lanes, serving delicious home cooked food at evening and lunch times. The famous community pub, the Packhorse in South Stoke is a lovely 30 minute walk up the valley. MEDIA FACILITIES Facilities include free wifi , iPod docking station, flatscreen TV and DVD in the living room. Being so close to Bath, Tucking Mill View is the perfect balance for relaxing and unwinding as well as exploring the beauties of the Bath and wandering in the Somerset and Wiltshire countryside. PARKING Free private parking space for 2 cars is provided immediately outside the entrance to the cottage. REWARD CARD The benefits of the Reward Card with special discounts and extras like 3 hours for 2 in the Thermal span and 10% off entrance to the Roman Baths are available to all guests. Just look at the Reward website for more details. ABOUT TUCKING MILL SELFCATERING Tucking Mill view is one of the five 4 Star Luxury Gold properties int he Tucking Mill Self Catering portfolio owned by Michael and Ann. There are tow apartness in the city centre – the Old smithy Loft and No 2 Hedgemead court and a further two cottages in the vicinity of Tucking Mill, Midford….Brooks’ View and Fishermen’s Retreat, in an Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty. THOSE LOOKING AFTER YOU The property is managed by the Family Team ..with Ann who has a background in hospitality and done much travelling, Michael who built the barbecues and cares of the birds and the gardens and Head Housekeepr Nikki, the team will do its utmost to ensure you enjoy your stays. You will also likely meet Rob our invaluable man of all trades. We all hope you enjoy your stay.

title: Abbey Rise
subtitle: Abbey Rise is a large Victorian terraced townhouse offering panoramic city views and guaranteed off road private parking throughout your stay. It is just an 8-minute stroll from the train and bus station and hub of the city.
bodyContent: Abbey Rise is a large Victorian terraced townhouse offering panoramic city views and guaranteed off road private parking throughout your stay. It is just an 8-minute stroll from the train and bus station and hub of the city. Bath is Katherine’s home town and after travelling around the world working in large prestigious hotels she was drawn back to this cosmopolitan and beautiful UNESCO city, where she decided to open up her own bed and breakfast. Living and working as part of the Royal Household at Buckingham Palace has left its mark and Katherine continues to maintain those standards in her own home, where guests are treated to crisply ironed sheets, fluffy towels and wonderfully comfortable beds whilst enjoying a homely and welcoming atmosphere. Katherine has been running Abbey Rise for a number of years now and frequently welcomes returning guests who will always find some new and interesting change or addition-though Katherine’s famous homemade brownies and cakes are always on the menu!
tagline: Abbey Rise is a large Victorian terraced townhouse offering panoramic city views

Georgian elegance with 21st century comfort! 3 Herschel Place has been designed and furnished to be a luxurious “home from home” in the heart of Bath. Luxury accommodation, superb location The apartment is within easy walking distance of all Bath’s famous sights and shops, so you can leave your car parked in the private space outside. Built in 2008 to continue the original Georgian Terrace, Number 3 Herschel Place combines the elegance of Georgian style on the outside with the benefits of modern building techniques inside. Home comforts A small gated patio area and your own front door lead to warmth and comfort, new furniture and modern appliances, streamlined new bathrooms and a well equipped, modern fitted kitchen – the ideal base for enjoying the pleasures of our beautiful city! The same luxurious comfort as our other apartment, 4 St George’s House .

title: Brooks’ View
subtitle: Brooks’ View is the epitome of the favoured cottage for those seeking a special place to stay.
bodyContent: Unashamedly a luxury romantic self-catering cottage 12 minutes from Bath city centre, the cottage is ideal for weekends away, mini moons, honey moons or just a few days’ escape in the delightful countryside. Many walks for walkers and splendid for cyclists being on Sustrans Two Tunnels Route 24. Sleeping 2 in the master bedroom, recently converted Brooks’ View not only has a luxury 1400 pocket sprung bed but also a decadent bathroom with a large walk in shower and a Victorian roll top claw bath. The cosy living room has a comfortable sofa and a snuggle sofabed for that extra guest. In the winter the traditional wood burning stove provides a lovely focal point and also extra heat. There is a small dining area with a traditional pine table and 4 chairs. The kitchen is fully equipped and has both a dishwasher and a clothes washer. On those halcyon days you can easily breakfast on the patio just outside the cottage. Built in the early 1800s, Brooks’ View is one of 4 artisan cottages built for the Somerset Coal Canal workers in the tiny hamlet of Tucking Mill, in the Midford Valley, an Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty. An area of total peace and calm yet so close to the City. An ornithologist’s delight too..with the bird feeders attracting gold finches, coal finches, blue tits, herons and nuthatches to mention a few. Down by the brooks there is a summerhouse with a patio and a lovely stone barbecue. Ideal for enjoying that glass of cool crisp wine. Flyfishing can be arranged if you fancy a breakfast trout. AROUND AND ABOUT Lying in the historic hamlet of Tucking Mill there is plenty to interest our guests. The wildlife lovers will adore the birds and the geologists the delights of exploring the basis of the structure of the UK. this is the home of William Smith and many of his original surveys were done around this area. Bath is the most obvious attraction with the historic Abbey where Edgar the first King of England was crowned, the Roman Baths and the Thermae Spa together with the most wonderful Georgian architecture much loved by Jane Austen and her fans today. At only 20 minutes distance there is Longleat, the Saxon town of Bradford on Avon, the National Trust village of Lacock used in Jane Austen and Harry Potter films and 45 minutes drive takes you to . And there are many more…Cheddar Gorge, Wookey Hole, Bristol with the Science Museum and famous zoo. MEDIA FACILITIES There is free Wifi throughout the cottage and there is a small TV in the bedroom as well as a larger flat screen in the sitting room. An iPod Docking station is also provided. There is a selection of DVDs, a variety of books as well as some board games. PARKING Free private parking space for one car is provided and a second by arrangement REWARD CARD The benefits of the Reward Card with special discounts and extras like 3 hours for 2 in the Thermae Spa are available in this cottage. Full details in the cottage and on this website. ABOUT TUCKING MILL SELF CATERING Brooks’ View is one of the five 4 Star Luxury Gold properties in Tucking Mill Self Catering owned by Michael and Ann. There are two apartments in the city centre, The Old Smithy Loft and No 2 Hedgemead Court, and three cottages just 12 minutes drive away at Tucking Mill, Midford, a historic hamlet just outside the city boundaries in an Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty. THOSE LOOKING AFTER YOU The property is managed by the Family Team..With Ann who has a background in hospitality and much travelling, Michael who built the barbecues and is in charge of the logs,birdfeeding and Head Housekeeper Nikki the team will do its utmost to ensure you enjoy your stay. You will also probably see Rob our invaluable man of all trades around… Short and long breaks available
tagline: Brooks’ View is the epitome of the favoured cottage for those seeking a special place to stay.

title: 4 St George’s House
subtitle: Lovely new first floor apartment with private parking, 5 minutes level walk from the centre of Bath.
bodyContent: Newly built and opened in December 2014, St George’s House is a contemporary Bath stone building in a quiet location off a Georgian crescent, just 5 minutes level walk from the town centre and less than 10 minutes from Bath’s most famous crescent, The Royal Crescent. Our two bedroom apartment sleeps 4 in comfort. Soft leather and oak furniture, really comfortable beds, a sleek modern kitchen and two contemporary bathrooms, excellent modern heating and insulation all make for a relaxing and luxurious home for enjoying the pleasures of Bath. All of Bath’s famous sights and shops are within an easy walk – you won’t need your car while you are here and can leave it in our allocated private secure parking space. The same luxurious comfort as our other apartment, 3 Herschel Place.
tagline: Lovely new first floor apartment with private parking.

title: Target Sports at Mendip Activity Centre
subtitle: Target Sport activities for the whole family at Mendip Activity Centre.
bodyContent: Mendip Activity Centre offer Target Sports for public booking at their activity centre on the Mendip Hills. Perched in the heart of Somerset’s wild and beautiful countryside, this is your chance to channel your inner Robin Hood. Whether you're a beginner or a secret pro, these adventures are a blast. Activities available include Archery, Air Rifle and Axe Throwing whilst Nerf & Gel Battles and ArcheryActive are available as private group sessions. From calm precision to full-blown foam fun, there’s something for every level of energy and age group age 6+. All sessions are led by friendly, experienced instructors who’ll guide you safely and confidently every step of the way. Sessions run in all weathers thanks to undercover ranges, and you can book for individuals, families, birthday parties or just because you fancy something adventurous to do this week!
tagline: Targetsport activities for the whole family at Mendip Activity Centre.

title: Tobogganing at Mendip Activity Centre
subtitle: Blast down the floodlit toboggan slope on colorful Zibob toboggans! Tobogganing at Mendip Activity Centre is available for either individual spaces or exclusive hire of half or the whole slope! Keep an eye out for the extremely popular seasonal sessions at Easter, Halloween and Christmas!
bodyContent: Mendip Activity Centre offer Tobogganing sessions on their purpose-built slope in the Mendip Hills. It’s their most popular activity for a reason. Fast, fun and full of laughter, it’s a brilliant introduction to the thrills of the slope with no snow required and no experience needed. Tobogganing at Mendip is perfect for all ages, from adventurous kids to nostalgic grown-ups. Individual spaces are available for ages 4 to 12 whilst everyone can take part if you book it privately. And keep an eye out for their themed tobogganing sessions across the year, like Twilight Tobogganing, spooky Halloween specials and Easter adventures.

title: The Land Girls
subtitle: Locations: Dulverton, Crowcombe Heathfield, Bampton. Release date: September 1998.
bodyContent: Parts of Exmoor were became a perfect recreation of wartime Britain for the evocative melodrama, The Land Girls. Although set in Dorset, David Leland’s adaptation of Angela’s Huth’s 1995 novel was filmed in the National Park, notably in the picturesque market town of Dulverton. Starring Anna Friel, Rachel Weisz, Catherine McCormack, the film follows three young women who arrive on a remote farm in 1941 as members of The Women’s Land Army and form close friendships against the backdrop of the war and rural life. The production shot for around month on a farm in Bampton just over the border in Devon, followed by a week or so in Dulverton. Dulverton Town Hall features particularly prominently and much of the town centre was transformed for one of the film’s most memorable scenes - a parade scene that included a flyover from a real Spitfire. As well as dressing many of the shop fronts, the shoot involved 200 extra, many of them local residents, dressed as soldiers, airmen, and air raid wardens. The film also shot at Bossington Beach and Crowcombe Heathfield station on the West Somerset Railway , which doubled as the station in the fictional village of Bamford. Dulverton Heritage Centre · Visit Dulverton · Visit Exmoor · Exmoor National Park · West Somerset Railway :
tagline: Locations: Dulverton, Crowcombe Heathfield, Bampton. Release date: September 1998.

title: The Somerset Cricket Museum
subtitle: Tucked away just a stone’s throw from the Cooper Associates County Ground, the Somerset Cricket Museum is one of Taunton’s most unique cultural treasures. Whether you're a lifelong cricket fan or simply curious about Somerset’s heritage, this museum blends sporting history with centuries‑old architecture in a way that’s truly special.
bodyContent: The Somerset Cricket Museum is housed in the Old Priory Barn, a remarkable Grade II* listed building. It’s the only surviving structure of the Augustinian Taunton Priory, originally founded around 1115—giving the museum an atmospheric backdrop steeped in nearly a millennium of history. The museum itself officially opened to the public in April 1989, created by the Somerset Cricket Club and the Somerset Cricket Society to preserve and celebrate the county’s cricketing heritage. a { text-decoration: none; color: #464feb; } tr th, tr td { border: 1px solid #e6e6e6; } tr th { background-color: #f5f5f5; } Step through the doors and you’re greeted with a treasure trove of cricketing memorabilia: Exhibits on Cricket Legends The museum showcases players who have left their mark on the game, including Ian Botham and Marcus Trescothick. These exhibits offer an intimate look at the careers, achievements, and influence of Somerset’s finest. Historic Collections From early cricket equipment to iconic matchday artefacts, the displays trace the evolution of the sport in Somerset. Some star pieces even include rare items tied to the wider cricketing world, reflecting Somerset's place in cricket history. Archives & Records The museum is also home to extensive records, memorabilia, and cricketing literature, shedding light on the Somerset County Cricket Club’s milestones and the sport’s deep cultural impact across the region. Part of what makes the Somerset Cricket Museum special is its connection to the wider cricket community. It sits within the Somerset County Cricket Club family and contributes to making the Taunton ground one of the most welcoming cricket venues in England. The Somerset Cricket Museum is a wonderful blend of local history, sporting heritage, and architectural beauty. Whether you're visiting Taunton for a match, exploring the town’s historical sites, or looking for a family-friendly outing, this small but fascinating museum is well worth your time.
tagline: Discovering Somerset Cricket Museum in Taunton: A Hidden Gem for Cricket Lovers

title: Swan Hotel Wells
subtitle: The Swan combines the beauty of a historic building with all the advantages of a modern hotel. The hotel is a striking, idyllic 15th-century coaching inn set in the timeless city of Wells, opposite the famous Wells Cathedral. The city itself is full of culture and reminders of older times, a beautiful location to visit.
bodyContent: This hotel has a fantastic location in the city of Wells, being right in the centre with plenty of shops and places to visit. For 600 years they have had many guests enjoy this wonderful inn, with a few famous faces too. The Cathedral is directly opposite the hotel and you can admire its magnificence from our outside seating area, directly leading into the Cathedral gardens. For film buffs, this hotel also had various scenes filmed here for the well known Simon Pegg film ‘Hot Fuzz’ The bedrooms at The Swan are traditional, stylish and comfortable but still offer all the modern amenities you need to enjoy a relaxing stay in Wells. title: Crofton Beam Engines and their 200 Year Old Technology – a Talk by Jon Willis
subtitle: This talk is part of the autumn programme of the Somerset Industrial Archaeology Society.
bodyContent: a { text-decoration: none; color: #464feb; } tr th, tr td { border: 1px solid #e6e6e6; } tr th { background-color: #f5f5f5; } a { text-decoration: none; color: #464feb; } tr th, tr td { border: 1px solid #e6e6e6; } tr th { background-color: #f5f5f5; } a { text-decoration: none; color: #464feb; } tr th, tr td { border: 1px solid #e6e6e6; } tr th { background-color: #f5f5f5; } a { text-decoration: none; color: #464feb; } tr th, tr td { border: 1px solid #e6e6e6; } tr th { background-color: #f5f5f5; } a { text-decoration: none; color: #464feb; } tr th, tr td { border: 1px solid #e6e6e6; } tr th { background-color: #f5f5f5; } a { text-decoration: none; color: #464feb; } tr th, tr td { border: 1px solid #e6e6e6; } tr th { background-color: #f5f5f5; } a { text-decoration: none; color: #464feb; } tr th, tr td { border: 1px solid #e6e6e6; } tr th { background-color: #f5f5f5; } Jon Willis of the Kennet and Avon Canal Trust tells the story of the two historic beam engines still housed within their Grade I listed pumping station. One of the engines dates from 1812 and is recognised as the oldest working beam engine in the world. Both engines are still capable of carrying out their original purpose, pumping water to the summit level of the Kennet and Avon Canal. This illustrated talk explores the history, engineering and continuing operation of these remarkable examples of early industrial technology. For details about how to take part in this online meeting, please visit: www.sias.me.uk
tagline: This talk is part of the autumn programme of the Somerset Industrial Archaeology Society.

title: Axbridge
subtitle: Axbridge is a charming market town at the foot of the beautiful Mendip Hills, near to Cheddar, with a character all of its own. Once part of a Saxon defence system against the Viking invaders, its history goes back to King Alfred's time.
bodyContent: Things to do in Axbridge, Somerset Half-timbered buildings lean towards each other across a narrow street leading from the medieval square in the centre of this picturesque town. Once a river port and valued for its wool production, Axbridge is on the edge of the Mendips ; overlooking the Levels and Bristol Water’s Reservoir. The town supports a number of independent shops and places to eat and drink. Pride of place in the square goes to King John’s Hunting Lodge which is a National Trust property housing a Museum of local history run by Axbridge and District Museum Trust. Despite its name, the building is actually early Tudor with wonderful uneven floors! It contains the village stocks among other curiosities. In fact Axbridge can trace its history even further back - to the time of King Alfred - when it was one of 30 places fortified to defend Wessex against the Vikings. It was close to the Royal Hunting Forest of Mendip and was granted a Royal Charter by King John in 1202 allowing it to hold markets among other privileges. Its prosperous past is reflected in the quality of the buildings in Axbridge, particularly the fine 13th century St John’s Church which is the oldest to survive, dating back to 1245. Not all residents were well off as the Axbridge Union Workhouse behind West Street testifies. Well into the 19th century it was customary once a year for a bull to be chased out of The Square and butchered to feed the poor. The Cheddar Valley Railway Line, which became known as ‘The Strawberry Line’ for taking the local fruit to London, is now a foot and cycle path linking Yatton and Cheddar with plans for it to continue to Shepton Mallet . Nearby is Axbridges' lavender fields Lavender & Co.

title: Cleeve Abbey
subtitle: In Washford lies one of the undiscovered jewels of Somerset, providing an interesting day out for families and budding historians alike. The Cistercian abbey of Cleeve is a haven of peace and tranquillity, said to contain the finest cloister buildings in England.
bodyContent: In Washford lies one of the undiscovered jewels of Somerset, providing an interesting day out for families and budding historians alike. The Cistercian abbey of Cleeve is a haven of peace and tranquillity, said to contain the finest cloister buildings in England. Visitors today can catch a glimpse of monastic life 800 years ago; although the abbey church was destroyed by Henry VIII during the dissolution in 1536, the cloister buildings including the gatehouse, 15th century refectory with its glorious angel roof and 13th century heraldic tiles have survived remarkably intact. The great dormitory is one of the best examples in the country, and an exhibition and virtual tour tells the story of the abbey and daily life for the holy men that once inhabited it. You can find out more about the conservation project to protect the medieval tiled pavement for the future. Access to the 13th century tiled pavement will be reinstated from 25 March 2016. The abbey is located in a beautiful valley surrounded by countryside so is ideal for walkers or visitors travelling on the West Somerset Railway, which stops at Washford station. It is just a ten minute walk to Cleeve Abbey from the station and with your train ticket you can get a discount on your entry ticket. Whatever the weather, there is plenty to explore at the Abbey and if sunny, there is lots of space for a picnic in the peaceful grounds with a stream running through them. Don't Miss: Serene Sounds - experience the serene sounds of recorded monastic music in the atmospheric Cloister (each weekend throughout July and August, 11am - 4pm)The monks' dormitory, one of the finest examples left in BritainThe magnificent architecture, carved angels and heraldic tiled floorsOur story bag, 'Brother Cedric and the missing sheep', a fun way for families to explore the abbey togetherThe 'Green Man' - ask the staff where he can be found!
tagline: In Washford lies one of the undiscovered jewels of Somerset.

title: Somerset County Cricket Club
subtitle: Situated in the historical town of Taunton, Somerset’s county capital, the County Ground cricket club makes for the perfect day out.
bodyContent: The Cooper Associates County Ground in Taunton is the home of Somerset County Cricket Club who have played there since 1882. It is overlooked by the towers of three churches and is renowned for its quintessentially English character and history. The pitch is surrounded by a number of stands and pavilions such as the Marcus Trescothick Pavilion, Lord Ian Botham Stand and the James Hildreth Stand. It currently has a capacity of 8,500 but can be increased to 12,500 for internationals. The County Ground hosted International World Cup games in 1983, 1999, 2017 and 2019. It has also played host to sell-out concerts from artists including Elton John, Rod Stewart and Lionel Richie. The Somerset Cricket Museum is located at the CACG and houses displays that highlight the rich and successful history of the club. Also on site are the SCCC Shop, the official merchandise store of Somerset County Cricket Club, as well as accessible spaces that can be used for conferences, events, dinners and a variety of other functions.
tagline: Situated in the historical town of Taunton, Somerset’s county capital.

title: Mendip Hills National Landscape
subtitle: The Mendip Hills are one of England’s most attractive National Landscapes. The distinctive limestone ridge rises from the flat Somerset Levels and Chew Valley just south of Bristol. The windswept plateau is punctuated by spectacular dry valleys and gorges, and impressive rocky outcrops.
bodyContent: Rising from the Somerset Levels are the distinctive Mendip Hills, that with the lakes of Chew Valley and Blagdon, form the 198sq kms that is the Mendip Hills National Landscape. The magnificent Mendip Ridge stretches all the way from Brean Down in the west towards Frome in the east. The western half is designated as an area of outstanding natural beauty due to the astonishing array of landscape features; the gorges, caves, valleys, lakes, woodlands and grasslands. The Mendip Plateau is 325 metres above sea level at its highest point and there are many fantastic viewpoints along the warm southern slopes to explore, taking in the Somerset Levels all the way to the Quantock Hills Natural Landscape . The steep north slopes overlook the patchwork farmland of the Chew Valley and Yeo Valley, and their beautiful lakes, with views across the Severn Estuary to Wales. These impressive hills demonstrate geology ranging from Devonian to Jurassic and exposed rock outcrops are common. Across the top of the Mendip Plateau you will see dry stone walls criss-crossing the landscape, marking out the farmland and providing a home for wildlife, while making use of the surface rock in the area. The iconic Cheddar Gorge is situated along the edge of the National Landscape and is known as the highest inland vertical cliff in the country, but there are many other fascinating geological features to be discovered. The Mendip National Nature Reserve, part of the King’s series of NNRs , follows the southern border of the Mendip Hills and many of the network of site are within the boundary of the National Landscape. There are also many Sites of Special Scientific Interest (SSSI). Wildlife makes its home in many and varied features of this incredible landscape; adders love the dry stone walls, greater horseshoe bats hibernate in the caves and the Cheddar Pink flourishes on the cliffs above the village. Dormice love the hedgerows, and the flower-rich grasslands are home to butterflies, beetles and skylarks. The elusive water vole makes its home, or burrow, close to the beautiful lakes of the area. In fact, Chew Valley Lake has been designated a Special Protection Area for bird species due to its international importance. The features of the area have provided inspiration for people throughout history; Aveline’s Hole is the oldest cemetery site in Britain, ancient burial mounds are dotted across the landscape, and the abundance of lead around Charterhouse meant the site became a strategically important for the Romans, who set up mines in the area shortly after their arrival. These days the main activity is farming, both dairy and sheep farming. Many of the farms and surrounding areas also rely on tourism and many host their own festivals and events, with vibrant communities supporting them. The tough landscape, and the challenges it offers, inspires sporting events throughout the year. There are many hiking, cycling and running events, as well as more specialist activities like climbing, caving, horse riding and gliding. The lakes host activities too; sailing, fishing and bird watching to name a few. The Mendip Hills have been providing food and shelter for people since the earliest days of settlement in this country and are still, slowly, giving up their secrets. Scientists recently reconstructed the head of a man who lived here some 10,000 years ago and whose remains were found in a cave at Cheddar . Cheddar Man is the oldest almost complete skeleton of our species, Homo sapiens , ever found in Britain. You can let your imagination run free in these hills with their stories graphically written in stone. There is the stone witch of Wookey Hole , the hymn-inspiring ‘Rock of Ages’ at Burrington Combe and the wonderful dry stone walls that decorate the wind swept hills. From Britain’s highest inland limestone cliffs that form the world famous Cheddar Gorge, you can look down on the Vale of Avalon with its tales of Arthur and to the coast visited, so legend has it, by Joseph of Arimathea. Joseph was a metal merchant and the hills were mined for lead until the last century. They are still a quarried for stone and have more than 200 scheduled ancient monuments including prehistoric barrows and remnants of WW2. On the hilltops there are hundreds of ancient monuments, while on the steeper slopes flower rich grasslands and wooded combes offer a variety of habitats for wildlife. The hill tops also provide spectacular views across to Wales, the Quantocks and Glastonbury Tor . Hidden beneath the hills are the famous Mendip caves - Cheddar and Wookey cave attractions , but the many less accessible caves make this a popular area for caving. The area also offers sailing and fishing on the reservoirs, cycling , horse riding , walking and host of other activities . Plenty of outdoor activity businesses are here for you to try out something new. Our Greentraveller On-line Guide to the Mendip Hills Natural Landscape will allow you to discover the best of the region whilst minimising your impact on the landscape. From eco-minded B&Bs to farm shops offering fresh, local produce, to activity centres, we have uncovered the greenest businesses in the area.
