title: Crowcombe Court
subtitle: Crowcombe Court is a licensed wedding venue able to host civil ceremonies and wedding receptions where you are offered an exclusive, bespoke day to remember.
bodyContent: Weddings http://www.crowcombecourt.co.uk/weddings/ Grade 1 Listed Crowcombe Court is West Somerset’s premier wedding and events venue. It offers couples the chance to celebrate in an exclusive and luxurious environment. Crowcombe Court is a licensed wedding venue able to host civil ceremonies and wedding receptions where you are offered an exclusive, bespoke day to remember. With eight magnificent en-suite guest rooms, the splendour of the Great Hall and reception rooms and the intimate club atmosphere of the vaulted undercroft cellars, Crowcombe Court is unique and exceptional. The excellence of the dining at Crowcombe Court has gained an enviable reputation. All catering requirements are delivered by our superb ‘in house’ Chefs where the couples and their guests can enjoy some of West Somerset's finest food beautifully prepared and served. The house is heated throughout and has ample free parking. Corporate Crowcombe Court offers an idyllic venue for corporate events such as seminars, presentations, team development through facilitated experiential learning, mindfulness and wellbeing in the workplace, product launches, press days and more. The wide range of magnificent rooms of varying sizes, including a vaulted undercroft and bar, can be combined to provide an event which includes reception, dining and lecture spaces. The gardens, which include a small lake, walled garden and private copse, lend themselves to experiential learning events providing a platform for varied and diverse programmes. Multiple activities can be undertaken concurrently which can maximise the delivery of seminar, team development and training content. Group sizes can be as small as 8 and as large as 100. You are guaranteed exclusively and confidentiality, there is no public access. The house is heated throughout and has ample free parking. Helicopter landing areas are available nearby. Shooting A magnificent Grade 1 listed mansion which offers hospitality to sporting guests with exclusivity and traditionality. A shoot lodge in the old style Crowcombe Court provides you and your team with a shoot lodge run by people who shoot, stalk and fish themselves and understand just what you need, when you need it. Crowcombe Court may be booked by teams of guns and their companions, and can accommodate a maximum of 18 guests across 9 King size rooms. A typical stay will include dinner bed and breakfast either for the evening prior to shooting or the evening of the shoot. Dinner consists of three courses followed by local cheeses and wine selected from our standard wine list. (A fine wine list is available). Pre dinner drinks are included as is a decanter of malt whisky. The dinner menu must be chosen in advance. Post-shoot deep and remedial massage from "Bodyfix" available (prior booking required) Ample car parking is available. A drying room is available. Helicopter landing areas are available nearby.
tagline: Grade 1 Listed Crowcombe Court is West Somerset’s premier wedding and events venue.

title: Bridgwater
subtitle: A rich legacy as a port and commercial centre is joined by Europe’s largest illuminated carnival, which lights up the streets every November.
bodyContent: Historic market town Bridgwater is home to the most illustrious of Somerset’s famous street carnivals A rich legacy as a port and commercial centre is joined by Europe’s largest illuminated carnival, which lights up the streets every November. What to do in Bridgwater A lively town with a rich history, Bridgwater Carnival best symbolises the town’s festive spirit. Residents near and far come together each November to witness the largest illuminated procession in Europe. To get in on the action, check the official Bridgwater Carnival Website for this year’s date, travel advice and accommodation information. Learn about the history of Bridgwater at the Blake Museum, where you’ll discover its past as a port and centre of commerce. The centre of Bridgwater is small enough to explore on foot, so head out to find examples of the fine architecture built during its commercial heydey - check out Cornhill, Castle Street and King Square for some key construction landmarks. Absorb some local culture at the Bridgwater Arts Centre - one of the first in the country - as well as Somerset Brick and Tile Museum, and the Bridgwater and Taunton Canal and Docks. Head to the town centre to find a combination of well-known and independent shops, plus lots of options for dining.

title: Thurlbear Wood
subtitle: Thurlbear Wood is an ancient woodland just a few miles to the south-east of Taunton with many open glades and rides allowing the woodland flora to flourish. The reserve has good all year round interest.
bodyContent: Thurlbear Wood is an ancient woodland just a few miles to the south-east of Taunton with many open glades and rides allowing the woodland flora to flourish. The reserve has good all year round interest. OS Map Reference ST 274 213 Size 16 hectares Grazing animals No Walking trails Visitors are advised to keep to marked tracks and to not enter into fenced area. Please be aware of the derelict lime kiln in the reserve - do not enter fenced area. Access Access from three main access points: a minor road off the A358 to the north of the reserve; from Church Farm in Thurlbear village via the bridleway over the small stream; along the public footpath from Slough Green. Footpaths around the reserve. Dogs On a lead About the reserve The reserve lies on mildly calcareous mudstones and a narrow band of Blue Lias limestone which suites a wide range of wildflowers. The woodland is dominated by Pedunculate Oak with a some Ash, Field Maple and lots of Hazel. Scattered throughout the woodland are a range of trees and plants that are very much indicators that this is an ancient woodland. They include the Wild Service tree, Small-leaved Lime, Wych Elm, Bird’s Nest orchid, Wood Anemone and Sweet Woodruff. If you come in spring look out for Early Purple Orchids and Goldilocks Buttercup. As summer comes the open glades and rides are the places to look for flowers such as Yellow-Wort, Carline Thistle, Wild Thyme and Bee Orchid. The numerous old trees throughout the wood provide lots of hole nesting sites for Great and Blue Tits to flourish, and also nesting in holes in trees here are Greater Spotted and Green Woodpecker, and Nuthatches. Woodcock are occasionally seen here in winter. In summer Speckled Wood butterflies are common throughout and the Silver-washed Fritillary also occurs. A range of other butterflies have been recorded in grassy areas including Grizzled Skipper, Dingy Skipper, Brown Argus and Duke of Burgundy. This is a good place to look out for bats in the evening and Pipistrelle, Soprano Pipistrelle, Serotine, Bechstein's, Natterer's and Brown Long-eared amongst others have been seen. Dormice are also present as are Badgers. Roe Deer are relatively common. During summer Adders and Slow Worms might be spotted in sunny glades and rides. Did you know Two hundred and thirty seven species of fungi have been recorded at the reserve including the Dotted Fanvault, Butter Waxcap and the Snowy Waxcap? Reserve conservation management - The management aims to maintain the variety of habitats and species present within the wood. Some areas are coppiced in the traditional way; different blocks (coupes) are done on different length rotations. These coupes provide different age coppice which benefit different bird, plant and animal species. Some areas are managed much less intensively in an attempt to create original woodland conditions, in order to achieve this a proportion of the larger trees are occasionally felled and left to rot on the woodland floor. The glades and rides are mown, and the cuttings removed, annually in the late summer or early autumn. This maintains the limestone grassland plants and associated butterflies. Thurlbear Wood is also close to Blackdown Hills AONB and NT Wellington Monument.
tagline: Ancient woodland just a few miles to the south-east of Taunton

title: Mendip Hills National Landscape
subtitle: The Mendip Hills are one of England’s most attractive National Landscapes. The distinctive limestone ridge rises from the flat Somerset Levels and Chew Valley just south of Bristol. The windswept plateau is punctuated by spectacular dry valleys and gorges, and impressive rocky outcrops.
bodyContent: Rising from the Somerset Levels are the distinctive Mendip Hills, that with the lakes of Chew Valley and Blagdon, form the 198sq kms that is the Mendip Hills National Landscape. The magnificent Mendip Ridge stretches all the way from Brean Down in the west towards Frome in the east. The western half is designated as an area of outstanding natural beauty due to the astonishing array of landscape features; the gorges, caves, valleys, lakes, woodlands and grasslands. The Mendip Plateau is 325 metres above sea level at its highest point and there are many fantastic viewpoints along the warm southern slopes to explore, taking in the Somerset Levels all the way to the Quantock Hills Natural Landscape . The steep north slopes overlook the patchwork farmland of the Chew Valley and Yeo Valley, and their beautiful lakes, with views across the Severn Estuary to Wales. These impressive hills demonstrate geology ranging from Devonian to Jurassic and exposed rock outcrops are common. Across the top of the Mendip Plateau you will see dry stone walls criss-crossing the landscape, marking out the farmland and providing a home for wildlife, while making use of the surface rock in the area. The iconic Cheddar Gorge is situated along the edge of the National Landscape and is known as the highest inland vertical cliff in the country, but there are many other fascinating geological features to be discovered. The Mendip National Nature Reserve, part of the King’s series of NNRs , follows the southern border of the Mendip Hills and many of the network of site are within the boundary of the National Landscape. There are also many Sites of Special Scientific Interest (SSSI). Wildlife makes its home in many and varied features of this incredible landscape; adders love the dry stone walls, greater horseshoe bats hibernate in the caves and the Cheddar Pink flourishes on the cliffs above the village. Dormice love the hedgerows, and the flower-rich grasslands are home to butterflies, beetles and skylarks. The elusive water vole makes its home, or burrow, close to the beautiful lakes of the area. In fact, Chew Valley Lake has been designated a Special Protection Area for bird species due to its international importance. The features of the area have provided inspiration for people throughout history; Aveline’s Hole is the oldest cemetery site in Britain, ancient burial mounds are dotted across the landscape, and the abundance of lead around Charterhouse meant the site became a strategically important for the Romans, who set up mines in the area shortly after their arrival. These days the main activity is farming, both dairy and sheep farming. Many of the farms and surrounding areas also rely on tourism and many host their own festivals and events, with vibrant communities supporting them. The tough landscape, and the challenges it offers, inspires sporting events throughout the year. There are many hiking, cycling and running events, as well as more specialist activities like climbing, caving, horse riding and gliding. The lakes host activities too; sailing, fishing and bird watching to name a few. The Mendip Hills have been providing food and shelter for people since the earliest days of settlement in this country and are still, slowly, giving up their secrets. Scientists recently reconstructed the head of a man who lived here some 10,000 years ago and whose remains were found in a cave at Cheddar . Cheddar Man is the oldest almost complete skeleton of our species, Homo sapiens , ever found in Britain. You can let your imagination run free in these hills with their stories graphically written in stone. There is the stone witch of Wookey Hole , the hymn-inspiring ‘Rock of Ages’ at Burrington Combe and the wonderful dry stone walls that decorate the wind swept hills. From Britain’s highest inland limestone cliffs that form the world famous Cheddar Gorge, you can look down on the Vale of Avalon with its tales of Arthur and to the coast visited, so legend has it, by Joseph of Arimathea. Joseph was a metal merchant and the hills were mined for lead until the last century. They are still a quarried for stone and have more than 200 scheduled ancient monuments including prehistoric barrows and remnants of WW2. On the hilltops there are hundreds of ancient monuments, while on the steeper slopes flower rich grasslands and wooded combes offer a variety of habitats for wildlife. The hill tops also provide spectacular views across to Wales, the Quantocks and Glastonbury Tor . Hidden beneath the hills are the famous Mendip caves - Cheddar and Wookey cave attractions , but the many less accessible caves make this a popular area for caving. The area also offers sailing and fishing on the reservoirs, cycling , horse riding , walking and host of other activities . Plenty of outdoor activity businesses are here for you to try out something new. Our Greentraveller On-line Guide to the Mendip Hills Natural Landscape will allow you to discover the best of the region whilst minimising your impact on the landscape. From eco-minded B&Bs to farm shops offering fresh, local produce, to activity centres, we have uncovered the greenest businesses in the area.

title: Pathways through Summer Walk Puxton Moor
subtitle: Restored footbridges and pedestrian gates have opened up the moor between Congresbury and Puxton to walkers for the first time in years.
bodyContent: How to get there Start at map ref: ST 437638 Car: Congresbury is on the A370. Free parking is available at the Bristol Road car park. Turn into Kent Road, which is near the junction, then Gooseham Mead. Bus: The X1 and W1 run along the A370. From August, a council supported 88 service will also run Start the walk from the Bristol Road and High Street junction. Head into Broad Street, passing the Grade II-listed village cross, and turn right into Paul’s Causeway. Go over the cobbled steps, past the pretty Court House, and the footpath is in front of you, behind a fence. This leads to the graveyard of the 13th century St Andrew’s Church. Keep to the left, then exit over a stile on your left. Cross the field, veering to your right, towards another stile. Go over the bridge and walk alongside the rhyne. Follow the path round and you come out onto the Strawberry Line walk and cycle path. Cross straight over, between the hedge and rhyne, and through a gate. Continue ahead. You are walking alongside Littlewall Rhyne, which is on your righthand side. Watch out for stinging nettles and thorns here, but you might also see some dragonflies. Go over the stile and continue on, alongside the rhyne. At the gate, cross the rhyne and enter the field, keeping to the left-hand side. About half way along is another gate and a footbridge over the rhyne. Cross here, then head diagonally right across the next field, towards the farm buildings. Exit through the kissing gate and turn left onto Dolemoor Lane Click HERE f or full details and FREE PDF copy

title: Cedars Hall, Wells
subtitle: Welcome to Cedars Hall Cedars Hall is a state-of-the-art performance venue providing a varied programme of top quality entertainment all year round. It is situated in the beautiful grounds of Wells Cathedral School in the heart of the City of Wells.
bodyContent: The hall hosts a number of professional (and amateur) productions throughout the year which include classical, jazz, folk and rock and pop and cabaret concerts, drama, talks and films. The main recital hall, Eavis Hall, has the capacity for audiences up to 350 and is a flexible and modern performance space. In addition to events in Eavis Hall, it serves as a hub for its significant community outreach, which provides music education (including workshops, concerts and masterclasses) for thousands of primary school children, elderly and disability groups in the South West each year. title: Wells Cathedral
subtitle: Built between 1175 and 1490 Wells Cathedral in Somerset has been described as “the most poetic of the English Cathedrals”.
bodyContent: ⭐ Reward Card Discount Available Built between 1175 and 1490 Wells Cathedral has been described as “the most poetic of the English Cathedrals”. Set in the medieval heart of England’s smallest city, and an easy drive from Bristol, Bath and Cardiff, Wells is the earliest English Cathedral to be built in the Gothic style. The current building is a significant landmark in the South West of England, has an international reputation and is TripAdvisor ranked number one for things to do in Wells and in Somerset. Wells Cathedral has unique features that separate it from other English cathedrals including its iconic West Front and the beautiful ‘scissor arches’ supporting the central tower, as well as one of the largest collections of historic stained glass in the country. The Cathedral also boasts the famous Wells Clock (which is considered to be the second oldest clock mechanism in Great Britain), the fascinating octagonal Chapter House and one of only four chained libraries in the UK. Wells Cathedral welcomes thousands of visitors each year who join in with regular daily services and events or who come simply to enjoy the calm and hospitality of this wonderful and holy place. Stay, if you can, for Evensong with the Cathedral’s world renowned choir (term times); a peaceful and moving end to your day. Tours: Discover hidden spaces and chambers, explore the south transept roof space and marvel at the nave from a very different perspective via the Cathedral's popular and longer High Parts tours which can be pre-booked via the website at www.wellscathedral.org.uk/visit/tours . The Cathedral runs complimentary ground floor tours daily (Monday-Saturday) and tickets include access to an audio tour. Guided tours for group visits can also be pre-booked via the Visits team at visits@wellscathedral.org.uk Families When term breaks up the Cathedral offers creative workshops for children accompanied by their parents or guardians. We also provide free children explorer backpacks which are available free of charge on arrival and which help children to learn about the main highlights and history of the Cathedral. Group Visits: The group rate (+10) for pre booked self guided visits is £10 and £12 to include a highlights tour. Unreserved groups are charged the standard on the door price of £14. For more information, and to book, please email visits@wellscathedral.org.uk Vicars’ Close: Adjoining the Cathedral is Vicars’ Close, believed to be the only complete medieval street left in England. Vicars’ Close was designed to provide accommodation for the Vicars Choral, who sing the daily services, and this is still the case today. This centuries-old tradition is unique and a much valued part of the continuing life of Wells Cathedral. The medieval windows of the houses and the garden archways seem to have survived more or less intact until the early nineteenth century, and even now a few still exist. Make a Day of It A warm welcome awaits you at our Cathedral shop which stocks a wide range of unique mementoes and gifts. The Loft at Wells Cathedral café is also open daily for coffee, delicious home-made lunches and afternoon teas http://www.wellscathedral.org.uk
tagline: Wells Cathedral in Somerset has been described as “the most poetic of the English Cathedrals".

title: 2 Hedgemead Court
subtitle: Hedgemead Court is our luxury, family-owned 2 bedroom apartment in Bath city centre.
bodyContent: Hedgemead Court is Ann and Michael ‘s newly-renovated Bath city centre apartment. You can visit Bath’s best attractions within a few minutes’ walk as the apartment is just a stone’s throw from Walcot Street artisan quarter and the Bath Abbey. Furthermore, from the ground floor balcony you have views across the adjacent 5-acre Hedgemead Park and down Walcot Street. Inside the apartment the interior is light, spacious and modern. 2 Hedgemead Court is easy to reach with on-site private parking directly outside; a rarity in Bath city centre! You’ll stay at the top of Walcot Street’s artisan quarter, which is full of vibrant independent shops, only a stroll from Bath Abbey and numerous restaurants. Most of all our holiday let is a great alternative to hotels for those wanting a space of their own, on business or for pleasure.

subtitle: Keynsham railway station is on the Great Western Main Line in South West England, serving the town of Keynsham, Somerset. It is 113 miles 63 chains (183.1 km) down the line from London Paddington and is situated between Oldfield Park and Bristol Temple Meads stations.

title: Somerset Food Trail
subtitle: A year round map and annual festival helping consumers discover the best of Somerset’s sustainable farms and artisan food producers. The Somerset Food Trail and annual July festival is an 'open farm’ and farm-to-fork showcase that puts the spotlight on Somerset's smaller-scale, nature-friendly farmers and artisan producers, giving visitors a better understanding of where food comes from and the many benefits of buying local.
bodyContent: This Somerset festival celebrates regenerative farming and sustainable food through farm visits, cultural events and feasts using ingredients sourced within a 30-mile radius. Highlights include foraging, community growing and affordable good food, championing nature-friendly farming and reconnecting people with where their food truly comes from.

title: Dunster Castle
subtitle: Fortified home of the Luttrells for 600 years, remodelled 100 years ago. Fine 17thC staircase and plaster ceilings. Terrace garden of rare shrubs.
bodyContent: During the winter months, the castle, watermill, and grounds are open at weekends and closed during the week. The Watermill Tearoom, Stables Shop and Parkland are open daily from 10am until 4pm. The car park is also open daily from 10am until 5pm. From 5 April 2025, the whole site is open daily. A fortress that became a family home for the Luttrells, who lived at Dunster for 600 years, the castle was extensively remodelled in the 1870s to create a Victorian country house. The castle boasts breath-taking views over Exmoor, Somerset, and the Bristol Channel as well as holding fine interior features such as a fine 17 th century carved staircase, ornate plaster ceilings, and rare leather wall hangings. Discover how Dunster Castle was used in its heyday and how the family hosted grand occasions from society balls to polo matches with the brilliant ‘Chapters’ guide as well as ‘Castle Explorers, available for children. You can then enjoy a leisurely stroll through beautiful terraced gardens with a collection of palms, sub-tropical plants, and the Dunster Lemon tree. Sited on the River Avill, Dunster Castle is also home to a working watermill that sits within the river gardens. Visit the mill to see the waterwheels in action and even purchase some of the freshly-milled flour. Refreshments are available in the newly-refurbished Watermill Tearoom and also outside the castle in the Tenants’ Hall Café. Accessibility Overview here. Facilities in addition to those listed below: Baby changing facilities Children's trails Courtesy vehicle Stair Climber Trampers available to book
tagline: Dramatically sited on a wooded hill and the fortified home of the Luttrells for 600 years.

title: MARSHMALLOW CIDER & BUTTERNUT SQUASH SOUP
subtitle: Now, this is a Brothers recipe if ever we did see one. You’re probably thinking how on earth have they combined Marshmallow cider and butternut squash into a great-tasting soup. But trust us – they did! Sweet, spicy, and warming from the inside out this is a must-try for the adventurous cooks out there. The Marshmallow cider and butternut squash create a moreish sweetness to the soup with the chilli knocking it back and bringing some heat. Grab a spoon and tuck in!
bodyContent: METHOD: • In a large skillet, heat oil over medium heat. • Brown chicken thighs on both sides; sprinkle with salt and pepper. • Remove from pan. • Add onion to same skillet; cook and stir over medium heat 2-3 minutes or until softened. • Stir in barbecue sauce, honey and Toffee Apple; increase heat to medium-high. • Cook 1 minute, stirring to loosen browned bits from pan. • Add chicken and apples to slow cooker, pour over Toffee Apple mixture. • Cover and cook on low 3.5 hours until chicken is tender. • Serve with steamed veg. Head over to the Brothers Cider Website for the ingredients list and more! https://brotherscider.co.uk/blogs/recipes/marshmallow-cider-butternut-squash-soup
tagline: Now, this is a Brothers recipe if ever we did see one.

title: County Classics Motor Museum
subtitle: Britain’s newest Motor Museum!
bodyContent: Located in the centre of Taunton, County Classics Motor Museum launched on 20th November 2023. With a focus on cars and motorcycles from our youth – from the 1950s to the 1990s – though exhibits range from 1915 to the early 2000s. With carefully-selected motoring memorabilia, and every one of the up to 100 cars and 80 motorcycles individually captioned and explained The museum grew from the personal dream of a very ‘driven’ schoolboy: Pat Hawkins bought and sold his first car at the age of 11 and as he grew his businesses from nothing he built up a fine collection of cars and motorcycles alongside them. With a cafe and gift shop.

title: Somerset Cricket Museum
subtitle: The aim of the Somerset Cricket Museum is to advance the education of the public in the history and development of cricket by maintaining a museum for the permanent exhibition and preservation of items of educational and historic value particularly, but not exclusively, of Somerset County Cricket Club.
bodyContent: The charity owns two buildings and the land on which they stand and the Museum itself is housed in a 15th century stone barn, the last remaining building of Taunton Priory, which was founded about the year 1120 and dissolved by Henry VIII in 1539. The museum building has had a variety of uses and modifications over the centuries, the most recent being as a store in a builder’s yard and before that as a farm barn. Almost derelict in the 1980s, it was classified as an ancient monument. The newly established Somerset Cricket Museum bought it in the 1980s and set about major reconstruction works to make it safe and to replace the roof. It is now Grade II* listed. Following the receipt of a major legacy in 2010 the building has been completely renovated and brought up to modern safety and efficiency standards. The Museum has exhibits related to: · Women’s and Girls Cricket · Cricket clothing and equipment from the last 100 years · A picture gallery of all the Somerset captains since 1875, teams and the famous players who have played for Somerset including Harold Gimblett, Ian Botham, Viv Richards and Joel Garner. · Old ground and club equipment such as a printing press, horse shoes etc · Historic documents and scorebooks The majority of the above, plus other features Including audio facilities for our visually Impaired visitors, children’s activity sheets and a histories of local cricket clubs are all available on the website. subtitle: Outdoors & Active is an award winning outdoor and travel store, having been voted Britain’s best independent outdoor store and also appearing in the final of Britain’s best small shop. bodyContent: Over the years they have extended their range of products to include being the local Scout shop supplying uniform for Squirrels, Beavers, Cubs, Scouts, Explorers and adult leaders, they also stock cadet and airsoft clothing and equipment. They have customers travelling all over the world all year round and are also specialists for the Duke of Edinburgh award and Ten Tors expeditions. They also believe in good old customer service, where possible and will always aim to be as helpful and informative as possible. title: Montacute House, National Trust
subtitle: Montacute House is a masterpiece of Elizabethan Renaissance architecture and design
bodyContent: Montacute House, Somerset is a masterpiece of Elizabethan Renaissance architecture and design. With its towering walls of glass, glow of ham stone and its surrounding gardens, it is a place of beauty and wonder. Sir Edward Phelips was the visionary force and money behind this masterpiece, which was completed in 1601. Built by skilled craftsman using local ham stone under the instruction of William Arnold, master mason, the house was a statement of wealth, ambition and showmanship. Come face to face with the past in the Long Gallery; measuring over 52 metres, it is the longest of its kind in England. The Gallery houses over 60 Tudor and Elizabethan portraits on loan from the National Portrait Gallery. Beautiful gardens surround Montacute, constantly changing, filling the house with scent in summer and providing an atmospheric backdrop for a winter walk. Whether you just want to let the children run and explore, or be inspired by the collections housed within the walls of Montacute, you will leave with lasting memories and a desire to soon return. You may even recognise some of the sights, as Montacute House featured in the BBC’s highly acclaimed production of Hilary Mantel’s Wolf Hall. Within 20 minutes’ drive you will find four fascinating smaller properties, each with a unique character, history and story to tell. Their combined age of 2,300 years spans from the medieval period to the early 19th century. Explore Stoke Priory, a fine collection of medieval farm buildings; Treasurer's House, with its great hall and unusual wall painting; Stembridge Tower Mill, the last remaining thatched windmill in England; and the Priest’s House, a medieval home of great character not to be missed. While you’re in the area, why not also visit Lytes Cary Manor and Tintinhull Garden (see the National Trust website for more details).
tagline: Montacute House in Somerset is a masterpiece of Elizabethan Renaissance architecture and design

title: Ferne Animal Sanctuary
subtitle: Ferne Animal Sanctuary is set within 72 acres of beautiful & protected countryside in the Blackdown Hills on the Devon/Somerset border. This charitable sanctuary takes in unwanted, abandoned and neglected animals and gives them a fantastic life either at the sanctuary or by finding them a special forever home.
bodyContent: Ferne Animal Sanctuary is set within 72 acres of beautiful & protected countryside in the Blackdown Hills on the Devon/Somerset border. This charitable sanctuary takes in unwanted, abandoned and neglected animals and gives them a fantastic life either at the sanctuary or by finding them a special forever home. Ferne Animal Sanctuary, located near Chard in Somerset, is a remarkable facility dedicated to the rehoming of dogs, cats, and horses. In addition to this, the sanctuary provides ongoing care and welfare for a wide variety of animals, including sheep, goats, cattle, pigs, geese, chickens, and an aviary housing birds from around the world. It is also home to smaller animals such as rabbits, guinea pigs, chinchillas and ferrets, ensuring they all receive the care and attention they need. Founded in 1939, at the onset of World War II, the charity was established to care for pets whose owners were going to war, or who had been displaced by the conflict. Over the years, it has forged strong connections with HM Armed Forces and the Royal Family. A typical visit to Ferne lasts between 90 to 150 minutes, during which visitors can enjoy observing the animals in their natural habitats. The experience includes a sensory garden designed to calm the senses with a variety of sounds, sights and smells. Visitors can explore the Willow Walk, which offers insights into animal care, as well as informative displays about our water voles, dragonflies, birds, and fungi. There's also a machinery wall showcasing equipment used throughout the years, along with a small play area for our younger visitors. Take the time to enjoy the stunning natural landscape of the Blackdown Hills from our viewing platform. Relax, gaze across the hills, and marvel at the beauty of nature at its finest. During the school holidays, Creative Corner offers a range of animal-themed activities and arts and crafts. We also host special events and workshops throughout the year, with full details available on our website. The Visitor Centre is open from 10 AM to 4 PM from Easter to October half term, though the shop and sanctuary are open every day, except Christmas Day, Boxing Day, and New Year's Day. Our well-stocked pet supplies and gift shop has everything you need for your animals, as well as delightful treats to tempt you. Dog friendly (dogs must be kept on leads) and accessible, Ferne has a good network of tarmac paths. However, due to the number of gates, we recommend that wheelchair users are accompanied. We have designated parking spaces for wheelchair users and visitors with special needs next to our Visitor Centre as well as in the main car park. All money raised goes to support our animal care and welfare. Unleash the Party Fun at Ferne Animal Sanctuary! title: Longleat
subtitle: Explore a world of adventure at Longleat. From a Drive Through Safari expedition, to discovering inside our iconic Elizabethan mansion, there’s plenty to entertain you.
bodyContent: Explore a world of adventure at Longleat. From a Drive Through Safari expedition, to discovering inside our iconic Elizabethan mansion, there’s plenty to entertain you. Travel the globe within this Wiltshire estate – stop off at African Village for a chance to see our new pack of African painted dogs, herd of Grants zebras and leap with lemurs. Say hi to our cheeky monkeys and bring your pack to meet our pack of wolves! Listen out for the Longleat lions’ roars as you explore. Continue your adventure on foot and walk with mischievous meerkats in Jungle Kingdom, feed rainbow lorikeets and watch our playful giant otters. Don’t forget to visit Koala Creek to see England’s only resident koalas, watch our sleepy sloths climb around or check in with our native red squirrels. Hop on board the Boat Safari and explore Half Mile Pond. Home to our family of noisy Californian sea lions, views of Gorilla Colony and Colobus monkeys will make quite a splash. Why not feed the sea lions to add to your unique day out? All aboard Longleat Railway! Enjoy a delightful ride around the lake and keep an eye on the action from our miniature railway. Or discover more about our history by adding a guided house tour to your itinerary. If your little cubs are looking to play, be sure to visit Little Explorer’s Garden and the Adventure Castle for plenty of room to let their imaginations run wild. Why not challenge yourself to our Hedge Maze and see if you can find your way through the winding passages? And no day is complete without a ride on Rockin’ Rhino! Book your tickets for a day out like no other or make your visit extra special with a VIP experience!
tagline: Longleat, nestled within 900 acres of ‘Capability’ Brown landscaped grounds.

title: Clarks Village
subtitle: If you haven't experienced the magic of Clarks Village yet, you've been missing out! Nestled amidst the stunning Somerset countryside, our shopping centre offers a serene and breathtaking environment like no other.
bodyContent: Admire the majestic trees, some of which have stood for over a century, and enjoy our abundance of green spaces and landscaped gardens. Take a moment to relax amidst nature, savouring the horticulture, insects, and birds that inhabit our surroundings. We are also proud to be a dog-friendly outlet, where well-behaved four-legged companions are even allowed in most stores. At Clarks Village, we invite you to embark on a retail adventure and explore the remarkable experiences waiting to be discovered in our surrounding area. Come and discover the endless possibilities that await you! Time to shop! With over 75 stores and 90 renowned brands to explore, Clarks Village provides a shopping experience like no other. Enjoy up to 60% off the recommended retail prices every day, allowing you to shop to your heart's content. Take your time; there's no need to rush. As you peruse the stores, make sure to pause and treat yourself to a coffee, or perhaps a refreshing cup of tea—hot, iced, or even bubble tea. And when hunger strikes, indulge in a delightful assortment of snacks, including pasties, of course (because you are in the Westcountry!), cakes, waffles, sandwiches, and so much more. The options are endless. Accessible and Inclusive Clarks Village warmly welcomes all guests. With all stores located on ground level, easy access is provided for those with mobility challenges. Our Guest Services team is dedicated to supporting individuals with hidden disabilities, ensuring a comfortable experience for everyone. For more information, check out our accessibility information page .
tagline: If you haven't experienced the magic of Clarks Village yet, you've been missing out!

title: At the Manor
subtitle: Manor Farm House self catering accommodation is spacious, comfortable and tastefully decorated and can accommodate large groups of 10-15 guests.
bodyContent: We are a 15 minute drive from the beautiful city of Bath and a perfect location for family celebrations, birthdays and anniversaries, wedding groups, girlie gatherings and business meetings. The country house has a calming, relaxing atmosphere. We also provide bed and breakfast accommodation. This gorgeous country Manor near Bath in the heart of Somerset was once a Grange and run by Monks from a nearby monastery in Tudor times. We are tucked away down a quiet country lane in the heart of the conservation village of Norton St Philip. The central village location allows our guests a leisurely stroll to the local pubs including the famous George Inn. Discover stunning countryside walks and a meander around the historic conservation village of Norton St Philip. There are many cycle routes in this area too including the renovated old train tunnel into Bath. We are also close to Bradford on Avon for canal walks, boating and cycling, Wells – the film Hot Fuzz was filmed here, Longleat Safari Park, Glastonbury – climb the ancient Tor, Stonehenge, Frome – the best market ever is held the first Sunday of each month and Salisbury.
tagline: Manor Farm House self catering accommodation is spacious, comfortable and tastefully decorated

title: Toghill House Farm
subtitle: Toghill House stands on the very edge of the Cotswolds. Within a stone’s throw of the site of the battle of Lansdown and with the Cotswold Way and the old east to west Roman road running through the grounds, Toghill is steeped in history.
bodyContent: Toghill House stands on the very edge of the Cotswolds. Within a stone’s throw of the site of the battle of Lansdown and with the Cotswold Way and the old east to west Roman road running through the grounds, Toghill is steeped in history. Located on a working farm only 4 miles north of Bath, with spectacular views over the Welsh mountains, Mendips, Cotswolds and Historic Bath. We have 9 rooms, some of which are in the 17th century farmhouse and others in the pretty Cotswold stone converted barns and stables in a delightful courtyard setting.
tagline: Toghill House stands on the very edge of the Cotswolds.

title: The Rising Sun Inn
subtitle: Book direct to get the best price at our hotel in Bath city centre.
bodyContent: Book direct to get the best price at our hotel in Bath city centre, a traditional English pub, dating from the 1700s. We’ve brought it bang up to date with a clean, fresh decor; subtle, modern lighting; and a warm, friendly atmosphere. We’re Just off the famous Pulteney bridge, right in the heart of historic Bath and we’re less than two minutes walk from the shops, restaurants, and attractions. Come and discover why customers love our dog friendly pub, excellent food, and bed & breakfast.
tagline: Book direct to get the best price at our hotel in Bath city centre.

title: Whitley Coach House
subtitle: Whitley Coach House is a truly luxurious self-contained 1804 Georgian built.
bodyContent: Recently modernised stone coach house providing self-catering accommodation for long, short or one night stays. Whitley Coach House is an ideal base from which to visit Bath, Lacock, Longleat, Bowood House, Stonehenge, National Trust properties and many other local attractions. Only 20 minutes from Bath and 5 Minutes from Lacock – 10-minute walk to a great Pub/Resturant and local shop/cafe, free fast Wi-Fi, 40″ smart TV with Netflix and free private parking. Private garden with teak furniture on wooden decking. With luxurious bedding including a handmade king size Lit Bateau bed with a Vi-Spring luxuriously comfortable handmade mattress. Immediate and live AVAILABILITY. Accepting: American Express plus most credit and debit cards. Whitley Coach House self-catering accommodation has a large bedroom with a super king-size (5ft 6ins x 6ft 6ins) Lit Bateau oak bed designed and handmade with a supremely comfortable Vi-Spring handmade pocket sprung mattress. The living room has high ceilings with exposed beams and includes two three-seater sofas one with a large double pull-out bed. In addition, there is a luxurious deep sprung folding bed for use in the bedroom or entrance hall. ONLINE BOOKING or do look at our Website: www.whitleycoachhouse.co.uk The Space Whitley Coach House is a detached former coach house to a Georgian house, renovated four years ago and just redecorated, providing spacious self-catering accommodation. Whitley Coach House has a large bedroom with an individually designed and handmade kingsize bateau bed designed and handmade in oak, with a supremely comfortable Vi-Spring pocket sprung mattress. The living room has high ceilings with exposed beams and a solid oak floor and includes two three-seater sofas one with a large super king size pull-out bed. The living room has views of the private garden, teak furniture and decked veranda. The kitchen table seats up to six people. This self-catering accommodation has fast broadband, a 40 inch smart TV with Freeview channels and the ability to watch other online services like Netflix. Guest Access The back has a private wooden decked terrace for use in dry weather and garden beyond. There is plenty of private parking. A barbeque can be provided if asked for at an extra charge. Whitley Coach House self-catering accommodation is not adapted for wheelchair users but has a step up into the property on entry. Once inside there are no steps, it is a converted coach house on one level. Interaction with Guests Your host will normally hand you the keys and discuss Whitley Coach House and the surrounding area with you on arrival. Unless you need help or are staying over a week, you will be left alone to enjoy your stay.
tagline: Whitley Coach House is a truly luxurious self-contained 1804 Georgian built.

bodyContent: This detached barn is 3/4 of a mile from Church Farm along a country lane. It has its own landscaped garden and private driveway with plenty of parking. Use of the Indoor Heated Swimming Pool and Games Room 3/4 of a mile away at Church Farm – Sleep up to 12 – 6 miles from Bath – Rural Retreat

title: Abbey Rise
subtitle: Abbey Rise is a large Victorian terraced townhouse offering panoramic city views and guaranteed off road private parking throughout your stay. It is just an 8-minute stroll from the train and bus station and hub of the city.
bodyContent: Abbey Rise is a large Victorian terraced townhouse offering panoramic city views and guaranteed off road private parking throughout your stay. It is just an 8-minute stroll from the train and bus station and hub of the city. Bath is Katherine’s home town and after travelling around the world working in large prestigious hotels she was drawn back to this cosmopolitan and beautiful UNESCO city, where she decided to open up her own bed and breakfast. Living and working as part of the Royal Household at Buckingham Palace has left its mark and Katherine continues to maintain those standards in her own home, where guests are treated to crisply ironed sheets, fluffy towels and wonderfully comfortable beds whilst enjoying a homely and welcoming atmosphere. Katherine has been running Abbey Rise for a number of years now and frequently welcomes returning guests who will always find some new and interesting change or addition-though Katherine’s famous homemade brownies and cakes are always on the menu!
tagline: Abbey Rise is a large Victorian terraced townhouse offering panoramic city views

title: 4 St George’s House
subtitle: Lovely new first floor apartment with private parking, 5 minutes level walk from the centre of Bath.
bodyContent: Newly built and opened in December 2014, St George’s House is a contemporary Bath stone building in a quiet location off a Georgian crescent, just 5 minutes level walk from the town centre and less than 10 minutes from Bath’s most famous crescent, The Royal Crescent. Our two bedroom apartment sleeps 4 in comfort. Soft leather and oak furniture, really comfortable beds, a sleek modern kitchen and two contemporary bathrooms, excellent modern heating and insulation all make for a relaxing and luxurious home for enjoying the pleasures of Bath. All of Bath’s famous sights and shops are within an easy walk – you won’t need your car while you are here and can leave it in our allocated private secure parking space. The same luxurious comfort as our other apartment, 3 Herschel Place.
tagline: Lovely new first floor apartment with private parking.

title: Burys Cottage
subtitle: Burys Cottage has a cosy and romantic feel to it being tucked away in the furthest corner of the row of cottages.
bodyContent: Burys Cottage has everything you should need for a romantic getaway. The cottage has a double bedroom with ensuite bathroom. It is ideally located between Bath (5 miles) and Bradford on Avon (2 miles). The popular ‘Longleat House and Safari Drive -Through’ is 12 miles (30% off gate price tickets available for our guests when purchased online – if booked at least one week in advance). Church Farm is a working sheep farm in an Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty. There is a luxurious indoor heated indoor pool (12m x 5m) onsite, perfect for guests whatever the weather. Burys Cottage has its own individual patio area with table, chairs and sun parasol. Farm shop and country pub/s within walking distance. Kennet and Avon Canal nearby for boating, cycling and walking. The cottage features a country feel with vaulted ceilings and exposed beams with soft furnishings to compliment. Enjoy admiring the sheep in the fields surrounding the farm. Welcome cream tea on arrival. Free Wifi.
tagline: Burys Cottage has a cosy and romantic feel to it

title: The Queensberry Hotel
subtitle: Independently owned by Helen & Laurence Beere The Queensberry Hotel occupies four individual town houses in the centre of Georgian Bath.
bodyContent: Independently owned by Helen & Laurence Beere The Queensberry Hotel occupies four individual town houses in the centre of Georgian Bath. This relaxed contemporary 4 stars boutique hotel has 29 individually designed bedrooms, combining comfort with the building’s original architectural features. Guests can enjoy a host of complimentary services such as Wifi, shoe shine, evening turn-down and tea and coffee served in the Drawing Room. The Olive Tree Restaurant has been awarded with 3 AA Rosettes and serves the finest modern British cuisine in a relaxed environment.
tagline: Independently owned by Helen & Laurence Beere

title: Abbey Mews – sleeps up to 10
subtitle: Luxury 4 bedroom Georgian town house along a medieval cobbled street in the historic heart of Bath.
bodyContent: Located just a short stroll from Bath Abbey and the Roman Baths and a two to three minute walk from the Bath Spa railway station, Abbey Mews provides the perfect self-catering accommodation for your special stay in Bath. Newly available for exclusive use holiday rental after extensive renovations, Abbey Mews combines Georgian elegance with modern luxury. Ideal for families, friends and small groups, 6 Pierrepont Place sleeps from 8 to 10 persons and promises you privacy, exclusivity and independence during your stay in this World Heritage City.
tagline: Luxury 4 bedroom Georgian town house.

title: Bill’s Clarks Village
subtitle: After a day of retail therapy, unwind at our newly opened Bill’s Restaurant, just steps away from the outlet stores.

title: Snowsports at Mendip Activity Centre
subtitle: Experience Mendip Activity Centre's floodlit 165-meter snowsport slope nestled in ancient woodland, offering year-round thrills for all skill levels. Perfect for both beginners and experienced snowsport fanatics. Learn to ski or snowboard where legends like skier Dave Ryding and snowboarder Jenny Jones began.
bodyContent: Mendip Activity Centre offer Skiing and Snowboarding sessions on their 165-metre dry slope. It’s the only slope of its kind in Somerset and the perfect place to learn or practise, with views over the hills and the thrill of the mountains without leaving the West Country. Whether you're a total beginner or brushing up before a trip, their friendly instructors have you covered. Lessons run all year for children and adults. You can also book private lessons or ski or snowboard by yourself (as long as you are at the right recreational standard). Your adventure awaits!

title: A Good Girl's Guide
subtitle: Location: Axbridge Release date: Series One, July 2024
bodyContent: Image credits: © BBC and Moonage Pictures The Medieval town of Axbridge provides a key setting for BBC TV’s A Good Girl’s Guide to Murder, standing in for the fictional town of Little Kilton in the screen adaptation of Holly Jackson’s hugely successful books. A Good Girl’s Guide follows student Pippa Fitz-Amobi, played by Emma Meyers, as she investigates the murder or Andie Bell, a schoolmate supposedly killed by her boyfriend, Sal Singh five years ago. Filming for Series One took place in the spring/summer of 2024 and picturesque Town Square and surrounding roads and alleyways featuring in many key scenes. Axbridge’s narrow streets and half-timbered buildings, which include King John’s Hunting Lodge, can be seen throughout the series, notably in stunning aerial sequences. Overlooking the square is St John’s the Baptist’s Church, which also appears in key scenes. A space in front of the church was used for the memorial mural which is central to the mystery – a prop created for the show and removed after filming. The Axbridge Drug Stores, just outside the square on High Street, was used for some of the interiors of Pip’s family home, including the kitchen and Pip’s bedroom. Other locations in Series One include Redcliffe Caves, Redland and Westbury-on-Trym. Axbridge also hosted filming for Series Two in early summer, 2025. Release details are to be confirmed.
tagline: Location: Axbridge Release date: Series One, July 2024

It doesn't matter if you have never played before its about fun and enjoyment. Taunton Trailblazers is a team for people with neurological conditions it is open to anyone over the age of 40 and is a mixed team. It doesn't matter if you have never palyed befor come along snd give it a go!.

subtitle: This talk is part of the autumn programme of the Somerset Industrial Archaeology Society.
bodyContent: a { text-decoration: none; color: #464feb; } tr th, tr td { border: 1px solid #e6e6e6; } tr th { background-color: #f5f5f5; } a { text-decoration: none; color: #464feb; } tr th, tr td { border: 1px solid #e6e6e6; } tr th { background-color: #f5f5f5; } a { text-decoration: none; color: #464feb; } tr th, tr td { border: 1px solid #e6e6e6; } tr th { background-color: #f5f5f5; } a { text-decoration: none; color: #464feb; } tr th, tr td { border: 1px solid #e6e6e6; } tr th { background-color: #f5f5f5; } a { text-decoration: none; color: #464feb; } tr th, tr td { border: 1px solid #e6e6e6; } tr th { background-color: #f5f5f5; } a { text-decoration: none; color: #464feb; } tr th, tr td { border: 1px solid #e6e6e6; } tr th { background-color: #f5f5f5; } Paul Upton recalls how brothers William and Thomas Stoate established a flour milling business in Watchet in 1832. The business later introduced steam power, helping to modernise production, but suffered a major fire in 1911. The mill was subsequently used by the Exmoor Paper Bag Company, whose turbine is now preserved and on display outside the building. Tickets available on the door

title: What is Wassailing and possibly the most iconic drink brand in the world originating from Somerset!
subtitle: Somerset Fascinating Facts It’s one of the big three Somerset comestibles — Cheddar cheese, strawberries and cider.
customFields:
[{"key":"NewsID","value":"244"},{"key":"NewsBody","value":"

Every farm used to make its own cider, and many farmers used to pay their workers in cider.

The traditional cider-producing year — gathering the harvest in autumn, pressing the apples, fermenting the cider, ‘wassailing’ the apple trees with shotguns each January to drive away evil spirits and ensure a healthy harvest the next year — still lives on. (An orchard wassail refers to the ancient custom of visiting the trees, singing to them, reciting traditional incantations and dancing, in order to encourage them to produce an excellent harvest.). 

These days there are at least 30 working cider producers within Somerset. You can visit them, see the work going on, and buy Somerset cider within sight of the orchards where it was produced. It’s delicious, it’s cloudy — and it’s stronger than you think!

Our World famous Cider Brands based here is Somerset

title: Highbridge
subtitle: The ‘bridge’ in the name of this town gives a clue to its influence in the days when transport by water and rail was more common than today when the motorway takes most of the traffic. Highbridge, as a market town, grew up around the bridge over the Brue and served numerous communities including those on the nearby peat moors.
bodyContent: One of the markets’ best sellers was Caerphilly cheese which in fact originated from farms in this area and gained its name because so much of it went across to Wales where it was popular with the miners as a cheap, salty source of nourishment. In Highbridge it was made at the West of England Creamery. There was also a large bacon curing business in the town established in the late 19th century. With its position, in former times, on the main route from Bristol to the South West, Highbridge once had its own wharf, canal and railway line. The canal linked the town with Glastonbury but was bought by its rival Somerset Central Railway Company and ceased being used. On the new railway’s board were two brothers – James and Cyrus Clark – who founded the famous Somerset shoe company. Today Highbridge is a known as the birthplace of Frank Foley who saved thousands of Jews during the last war. A statue of him is on the town green. Highbridge has a 42-acre leisure and nature park, Apex Park with lakes, walks and picnic areas.

title: Vivary Park
subtitle: Vivary Park is Taunton’s premium park, located just minutes away from the town centre. At 7.5 hectares, Vivary Park is the perfect place to go for a picnic, a stroll or to spend the day.
bodyContent: Linking the end of the pedestrianised High Street with the lower slopes of the Blackdown Hills is the award-winning Vivary Park, a member of the European Garden Heritage Network and laid out on the site of the vivarium fish lake which, in mediaeval times supplied the castle and the priory. Vivary Park is an important part of Taunton’s history. The Taunton Flower Show has occupied the park for the first weekend in August since at least 1851. Previously a medieval vivarium for the priory and castle, the park was officially laid out in 1895 as a public space for recreation and organised events. The iconic front gates and bandstand still stand today. In 1902, an Oak tree was planted close to the bandstand to mark the coronation of Edward VII and the fountain was unveiled in 1907 as a memorial to the late Queen Victoria. Today its 7.5 hectares are home to tennis courts, a large children’s play area, pay-and-play golf course, a tree trail and the Vivary Adventure and High Ropes Centre. Download a map of the park here
tagline: One of the top attractions in the town

title: Blackdown Hills National Landscape
subtitle: The Blackdown Hills are a nationally important landscape in recognition of the special qualities of their natural and built environment. Being relatively unspoilt, the Hills offer a rare sense of timelessness.
bodyContent: Some of the most popular tourist destinations in the world are backwaters – places where little has changed or is likely to. Here we can take time to reflect on the relative constancy of the natural landscape. One such place is the area around the Blackdown Hills, in many ways archetypal English Countryside with hedgerows, copses, farmland and narrow lanes. The villages are distinctive thanks to the use of local stone, tiles and thatch and many of the hamlets date back to medieval days. Among the smallest of the UK’s protected landscapes, the Blackdown Hills have a remarkable variety of habitats from heath and grasslands to wet woodlands and bogs. The steep banks are a riot of wildflowers in Spring and the hedgerows and woods are still home to the nationally scarce hazel dormice. Standing guard on the northern ridge of the hills is the world’s only three-sided obelisk, a monument to the Duke of Wellington. A network of hedges, mature hedgerow trees and small copses link a rich mosaic of semi-natural habitats. The area is perfect for walks , cycling and horse riding where the quiet bridleways and byways offer many opportunities to explore and enjoy the locally distinctive buildings, archaeological remains and natural flora and fauna. The Hills have a variety of tourist accommodation providers ranging from bed & breakfast establishments, beautiful country houses, converted barns, farmhouses and cottages. There are a number of self-catering cottages and a small range of family run hotels and guesthouses. This area is renowned for its fantastic range of welcoming country inns, many of which offer terrific menus of home cooked food, sourced from local produce. The Blackdown Hills are perfect destination for short break holidays, where visitors can join in with organized activities such as guided walks, hedgerow skills workshops, fishing, arts and crafts, writing courses... the list is endless!

title: Taunton Minster Church of St Mary Magdalene
subtitle: Taunton Minster Church of St Mary Magdalene is church of England parish church in Taunton and has the tallest tower in Somerset.
bodyContent: The foundations of St Mary Magdalene church were probably laid in the early eighth century when Ina, king of the West Saxons established Christianity in Taunton. St Mary’s was made into the Parish Church of Taunton by the Bishop of Winchester in 1308, with the structure itself being completed in 1508. The church is mainly built of sandstone and has a painted interior, except for the ‘forest’ of pillars which line the four aisles – a rare feature in a parish church. Most of the statues and stained glass date from a restoration project during the Victorian era. In 2008 glass 'Angel Doors' were installed at the entrance to the church to celebrate the 700th anniversary of St Mary's becoming the Parish Church. The tower was built in the 15th and 16th centuries. It was rebuilt in 1858-62 (in replica) under the guidance of the architect Sir Giles Gilbert Scott and is considered to be one of the best examples of a Somerset tower. At 163 feet (50m) tall it stands as the tallest church in Somerset. On completion of the re-build, the donkey which had hauled all the stone up the tower was himself hoisted to the top from whence to survey his handiwork! Taunton's first known fire engine was housed in the tower in 1734 and today it is home to a pair of nesting peregrine falcons. The Father Willis Organ was opened at a ceremony in 1882 and was built by a firm that was the 'Rolls Royce' brand of its time. The quality of Willis’ work is especially evident in the harmonically rich and assertive main principal chorus, the blending reeds, the solo Corno di bassetto on the Choir manual, the sweet and fulsome Harmonic flute, and the rasp of the pedal Ophicleide. Sunday and weekday services welcome locals and those from further afield. The Coffee Shop and The Book & Gift Shop provide a place to stay and relax whilst enjoying a cup of tea with friends or browsing the shelves. Both are non-profit making, with any money made going back into supporting the work of the church. St Mary's also hosts a wealth of concerts and events throughout the year from the Mayor's Charity Concert and the Chamber Philharmonia Cologne to Tower Open Days.
tagline: The tallest church tower in Somerset

title: Bishops Lydeard
subtitle: Nestled at the foot of the Quantock Hills, Bishops Lydeard is a vibrant village with an wonderful mixture of local attractions and ammenties.
bodyContent: The thriving village of Bishops Lydeard is located 6 miles north west of Taunton and is nestled at the foot of the Quantock Hills, an AONB. A short drive from the village takes you up to Cothelstone from where the Quantocks can be explored and the breathtaking views admired. And just along from Cothelstone is Fyne Court , a National Trust nature reserve and visitor centre which the Trust itself calls a 'hidden gem'. The Church of St Mary the Virgin is located in the heart of the village and is built of red sandstone, with a tall, typically Somerset tower embellished with facings of creamy Ham Hill stone. With sections dating from the end of the thirteenth century, the church is notable in particular for its interior furnishings which feature a medieval rood screen, a Jacobean pulpit and diverse pew carvings. Visitors to the village can also explore the Bishops Lydeard Mill , a working mill with a restored watermill, and experience the thrills of West Somerset Railway's steam locomotives at the Bishops Lydeard terminus. The village is also home to the CAMRA-accredited microbrewery Quantock Brewery .
tagline: Bishops Lydeard is a vibrant village with an wonderful mixture of attractions and ammenties.

title: Porlock
subtitle: Porlock is a place for everyone and all seasons. Porlock is a special and unique village. It has retained much of its medieval charm including the 13th Century church of St Dubricius with its famous truncated spire and many attractive and historic buildings.
bodyContent: Porlock is a special and unique village. It has retained much of its medieval charm including the 13th Century church of St Dubricius with its famous truncated spire and many attractive and historic buildings. Porlock sits in a splendid position surrounded on three sides by the wooded and heather clad hills of Exmoor and by the Bristol Channel to the North. Although it only has a population of 1300 it is a lively, living village with a vibrant calendar of activities and an amazing variety of shops, restaurants and accommodation. Exmoor is a dark skies reserve and Porlock is the ideal base for star gazers of all ages. It also offers an excellent base for walking or cycling. With activities such as horse riding and outdoor adventures available there is something for everyone.

title: Blakehay Theatre
subtitle: Leading the way in this zeitgeist for Weston-super-Mare the Blakehay Theatre create Theatre for the whole community, bringing national popular shows and treading subject matters onto the stage. A creative hub for artists and performers in the local area and a cultural home for fans of the arts.
bodyContent: The theatre’s uniquely diverse program of locally produced and touring work is curated especially for you. We are striving to create an inclusive creative community to make the most of a beautiful venue by using all of its spaces for artistic endorsers, and we are delighted you want to be a part of it. With an intimate 200 seat main house, 100 seat Studio Theatre and a warm and welcoming theatre bar, the Blakehay Theatre is able to present a variety of shows and events in these spaces. With community classes taking place in our beautiful studios, there is something for everyone at the Blakehay Theatre. We may be little, but we have big ideas! The vision is to build a ‘big-city’ creative culture into the heart of the Victorian seaside resort of Weston-super-Mare. We need continued public support to help sustain and grow this vision through ticket sales, personal donations, sponsorship and help spreading the word! We are constantly working and adapting our programme each season to bring new and exclusive works to Weston-super-Mare, but we can’t do that without your support, so please spread the word and support our little theatre with big ideas!
tagline: Leading the way in this zeitgeist for Weston-super-Mare the Blakehay Theatre

title: Exciting opportunity to run our Café Bar in The Princess Theatre - Burnham on Sea
subtitle: Burnham-on-Sea & Highbridge Town Council invites tenders to lease The Princess Theatre and Arts Centre Café Bar.
bodyContent: Exciting opportunity to run our Café Bar 26th Jan 2021 Burnham-on-Sea & Highbridge Town Council invites tenders to lease The Princess Theatre and Arts Centre Café Bar. With Covid restrictions ongoing, The Princess is taking new approaches to the services it offers for when it reopens. For the last 10 years we have enjoyed a fruitful and rewarding relationship as a volunteer operated café and bar. In those 10 years much has changed, not only on the stage of our unique theatre, but also with theatre-going audiences and significantly in the eating and drinking sector. The Town Council is inviting any interested parties to explore new ideas for the future of food and drink at the theatre and to make proposals to them for the next three years. The successful party will have the opportunity to re-work the existing bar and café menu to maximise service for daytime visitors and enhance the overall theatre experience for audiences. In normal times we are a vibrant theatre and arts centre offering culture and entertainment in Burnham-on-Sea and Highbridge welcoming more than 7000 audience members a year and many more in terms of daytime visitors. Beccy Armory, our Business Development Officer says “this is a very real chance for an entrepreneur or an established business to work alongside The Princess and re-imagine its eating and drinking experience. Right now our reopening pathway is unclear and as with other businesses The Princess has had to be innovative in how we deliver for our audiences taking our work online. We have an incredible kitchen space with professional equipment so even now whilst caterers cannot operate in their normal way there is still much opportunity.” Cllr Louise Parkin said “This is a really exciting opportunity to provide the catering at a high-profile visitor attraction and the Council is looking for suitably qualified, innovative caterers and experienced companies who will develop the business in synergy with The Princess.” The deadline for tender applications is 12 noon 2nd March 2021. To request a detailed tender document containing full information about the theatre, catering requirements and the tender process please contact: info@burnham-highbridge-tc.gov.uk with the subject line Princess Café Lease.

title: Exploring the tidal trail around Uphill
subtitle: Take a tour through salt-marshes and open grasslands just south of Uphill to see some award-wining nature reserves.
bodyContent: The walk starts in Uphill boat yard, a tranquil spot alongside Uphill quarry. Wharf Side Tea Room is now open if you need some refreshments before you head off. Continue past the preserved lime kiln, which was built between 1780 and 1850 to provide lime, through the kissing gate into Uphill Nature Reserve. The reserve has recently been awarded another Green Flag. Uphill Quarry was used from the 1800s to 1940s and in 1826 three caves were discovered that had been used by Neanderthal people during the Ice Age. Tools and bones were discovered, including those from a woolly mammoth and cave lion. Follow the path through the reserve, past the 19th century explosives store, which was used for blasting the quarry stone. Dogs need to be kept under close control as cattle graze in the fields. Go through the wooden gate and follow the path up the hill. Look behind you for wide-ranging views of Brean Down, Uphill, and across the Severn estuary. title: West Somerset Railway
subtitle: West Somerset Railway, Somerset, is a heritage steam railway operating between Minehead and Bishop's Lydeard, near Taunton. It is the longest independent railway in Britain, (20 miles).
bodyContent: West Somerset Railway, Somerset is the longest Heritage line in the United Kingdom. Time Table can be seen HERE for 2024 The line is situated in Somerset, four miles outside the County town of Taunton , starting at Bishops Lydeard and finishing at Minehead . The line meanders through the Quantock Hills , an area of outstanding natural beauty and along the Bristol Channel Coast. We have 10 stations along the line each having something different to offer. There are various historic sites that may be of interest to visitors to the area, for example Crowcombe Heathfield station was the location for the filming of the Beatles’ “A Hard Days Night” and scenes from “The Land Girls” were also shot here. The historic town of Watchet dates back to Saxon times, and boasts narrow streets, local shops, museums and lots of places to eat and drink. Washford is a great place to alight, just a short walk from the station we have Cleeve Abbey and the Torre Cider Farm, which are both well worth a visit. Fancy something a little different then why not visit Dunster Castle which is nestled in the medieval village of Dunster ? Dunster also has a working Watermill , the Old Yarn Market building and the Dolls Museum or continue on to Minehead home of our final station. Minehead is situated at the foot of North Hill where the beach is literally right across the road, we have cafes, shops and plenty of arcades along the seafront, making this a go to location. The West Somerset Railway also have combined tickets on selected dates throughout the year. These include, Cream Tea and Cheese and cider specials and linked trips with Hestercombe Gardens and Dunster Castle. We organise Steam Galas in the Spring and Autumn, and we are host to a Diesel Gala too. In the latter part of the year we have our popular Christmas services, we have Santa services running out of Minehead and Bishops Lydeard from the end of November until Christmas Eve, we also have our Sherry and Mince pie specials for you to enjoy.
tagline: Heritage steam railway operating between Minehead and Bishop's Lydeard, near Taunton.

title: Apsley House
subtitle: Located about 30 minutes walk from the City Centre, the Apsley House in Bath was built as a country home by The Duke of Wellington.
bodyContent: Located about 30 minutes walk from the City Centre, the Apsley House in Bath was built as a country home by The Duke of Wellington, after his momentous victory against Napoleon in the Battle of Waterloo. The rumour is that it was built as a place where he could keep his mistress of that time, as he was estranged from his wife years earlier. The hotel has been refurbished in great style and every care has been taken to preserve the natural elegance of the house, but still provide modern comforts. The magnificently proportioned reception rooms offer both style and comfort, with many period features complimented by the house being furnished with fine antiques and original oil paintings. Owned by Nick and Claire Potts ‘Apsley House Hotel’ is one of Bath’s finest small hotels. Resident Managers, Kate and Miro, offer guests a very warm welcome and personal care with the atmosphere more in keeping to that of a Private House than that of a hotel. Reception is always available if you require information on how best to spend your time in and around the beautiful city of Bath. Our Reservations department is open from 10am – 9pm daily. The Hotel has 12 delightfully appointed en-suite rooms across three floors (no lift access). Some rooms feature air-conditioners. Free Wireless internet access is available throughout. A freshly cooked feast of a breakfast with daily specials, is served in our elegant dining room. A lovely south facing garden is ideal for the summer evening aperitif. Complimntary parking is also available.
tagline: Located about 30 minutes walk from the City Centre, the Apsley House in Bath

title: The Royal Hotel
subtitle: A great tradition providing hospitality for over 150 years, within walking distance of all of Bath’s leading attractions.
bodyContent: The Royal first opened as a hotel in 1846 and has been owned by the present owners since 1995. title: Taunton School
subtitle: Taunton School is a co-educational independent school serving pupils aged 13 to 18. The campus also includes Taunton School International and Taunton School International Middle School for overseas students; Taunton Preparatory School (aged 7 to 13); Taunton Pre-Prep School (aged 4 to 7); and Taunton Nursery (aged 0 to 4).
bodyContent: Set in a beautiful 56-acre site, Taunton School is a lively community, which aims to challenge, nurture and inspire young people to succeed in a global community. Taunton School consists of a caring Nursery and Pre-Preparatory School, inspiring Preparatory School and an innovative Senior School and International School. The campus includes a brand new £3.6 million Dining Hall, extensive sports fields, two swimming pools, specific music, art and D&T departments and a 19 th century Grade II listed Chapel. A new sixth form centre and library will be completed this year and plans are underway for a £20million state-of-the-art international school and enhanced sports facilities. The school offers a supportive boarding environment for children from 7 to 18 years. With close friends at hand, boarders have the opportunity to develop life skills within a relaxed but controlled atmosphere. As a non-selective school, Taunton School has achieved consistently excellent GCSE results and some of the most exceptional A-level and International Baccalaureate results in South West England. Approximately 96% of all sixth form leavers take up university or college places and approximately three or four students are accepted into Oxbridge each year. Taunton School is one of the only schools in the UK to offer four unique Sixth Form pathways: the popular IB Diploma, A-levels, Level 3 BTEC Diploma in Business and in Sport & Exercise Science, as well as Pre-foundation and Foundation courses in Business.

title: Alfred Gillett Trust
subtitle: Explore our magnificent collection based on the Clark family and their 200-year-old global shoemaking business. With over 100,000 objects, we are open to the public for research, enquiries, tours, and events. We are building a museum that will inspire the world with the family and community stories behind Clarks shoes, opening by 2025.
bodyContent: With objects and archives spanning six generations of a family firm, we tell the story of the development of Street as a company village, 200 years of shoemaking heritage, the Clark family and their economic, social and political concerns based around their Quaker beliefs, and local history, including our popular collection of fossilised marine reptiles – the ichthyosaurs that swam in these waters under our feet 200 million years ago, found right here in Street. Community and family are rooted at the heart of Clarks history. Iconic material from marketing design, commissioned from the best artists and photographers of the day, can be found alongside examples of shoes from across the globe, collected to energise and inform creative design. Day-to-day records of running a company over two hundred years sit alongside stories of innovation and experimentation with fascinating stories of factory working life. With aspirations to build a museum and to expand the archive we are poised and ready to convert the site to a fully open public offer in time for the 200-year anniversary of the founding of the company in 2025 including a number of galleries, newly landscaped grounds, a café and a shop, welcoming visitors from near and afar. We operate a research and enquiry service by appointment, conduct tours and talks for interested groups, and have an annual programme of events such as outdoor theatre and cinema in the grounds of the Grange.

title: Barrington Court, National Trust
subtitle: Barrington Court, located in the stunning south Somerset countryside, is a charming Tudor manor house complimented beautifully with Gertrude Jekyll-inspired gardens, apple orchards and a working kitchen garden.
bodyContent: Barrington Court Somerset National Trust - Discover the haunting echoes of the past at Barrington Court, a Tudor manor house free from collections and furniture. Explore using your imagination and your senses to discover a house full of memories, where light fills the rooms and you feel you can almost touch the past. The property was saved from ruin and restored by the Lyle family in 1920s, when the Court House resembled a barn rather than the proud manor house that it is. Close your eyes and you’ll almost be able to hear the sounds and see the sights of the glamorous parties held in the great hall during Barrington’s heyday. On the first floor listen out for the voices resonating from the past, of the young evacuees who called Barrington home during the Second World War. Stroll through the Gertrude Jekyll inspired gardens, which with their focus on plant varieties and colours are a delight for all the senses. Be spurred on in your own garden or allotment by the stone-walled kitchen garden that produces a variety of delicious fruit and vegetables. Don’t just take our word for it, why not stop off in the Strode House Restaurant to taste these home-grown delights. Barrington Court predominantly featured in BBC’s highly acclaimed recent production of Hilary Mantel’s Wolf Hall.
tagline: Barrington Court, located in the stunning south Somerset countryside.
