title: Somerset Craft Distillery Ltd
subtitle: Our award winning Spirit of Glastonbury ® hand crafted small batch dry gin is the very essence of Somerset. Distilled using water drawn from deep beneath the mystical Glastonbury Tor and containing nine botanicals including apples from Somersets traditional orchards, each bottle is wax sealed and handwritten with its own batch number. Conceived, developed, distilled and bottled in Somerset. Voted– Best Classic Gin in England at the World Gin Awards 2022.
bodyContent: Here at Somerset Craft Distillery we believe in quality. Our award winning gin is distilled in our own copper still named Guinevere . We use nine carefully chosen botanicals including juniper berries grown on English farms and apples from Somersets traditional orchards along with cinnamon, liquorice, orris. correander, angelica, almonds and lemon. Distilled using water drawn from deep beneath the 158m high Glastonbury Tor to an alcoholic strength of 42%. Tasting Notes: ‘On the nose - unmissable Juniper – but with Spirit of Glastonbury ® the distillers have turned up the volume – you know its gin before the first sip. The mouthfeel is very smooth and confident’ ( Hand Crafted Drinks Magazine); ‘ Rich sweet caramel and toffee on the nose. Some notes of vanilla. Dense and round and a little different while still retaining its classic character’ (World Gin Awards 2022). Tell us what you think? Navy Strength. Navy Strength gin is traditionally stronger and at 57% ABV our Navy Strength Spirit of Glastonbury ® certainly fits the bill. The higher ABV really allows those botanicals to shine through. Try it as a sipping gin – or with your favourite tonic. Silver Medal winner at the 2022 London Spirits Competition.
tagline: Our award winning Spirit of Glastonbury ® hand crafted

title: Gin and Haze Cocktail
subtitle: 275ml Thatchers Haze cider 25ml shot of premium quality gin such as Thatchers Orchard Cut Gin Mint Cucumber, lime and red apple to garnish
bodyContent: 275ml Thatchers Haze cider 25ml shot of premium quality gin such as Thatchers Orchard Cut Gin Mint Cucumber, lime and red apple to garnish Fill the glass with ice, add the gin and Thatchers Haze. Stir to mix. Top with mint, cucumber, lime and of course a slice of red apple. Quick to prepare, serve in a balloon glass for a classic gin cocktail, or for something more informal, why not use a handled jar. A Thatchers family favourite going back over generations, Thatchers has brought gin and cider right up to date with its refreshing cloudy cider, Thatchers Haze. Add to the apple experience by using Thatchers Orchard Cut Gin, which is crafted with cider from Thatchers’ Katy apples and fresh apple for characteristic flavour. Botanicals including juniper, local Somerset lavender, coriander, macadamia nut, buttercup, Seville orange, lemon and lime have been chosen to work alongside the apple flavours, providing a beautifully balanced drink with floral and fruity notes.
tagline: 275ml Thatchers Haze cider 25ml shot of premium quality gin such as Thatchers Orchard Cut Gin Mint

title: Cheddar Gorge & Caves
subtitle: Cheddar Gorge & Caves boasts extraordinary subterranean show caves, awe-inspiring cliffs and holds many fascinating secrets about our prehistoric ancestors.
bodyContent: Our Day Ticket gives access to six great attractions: Gough’s Cave: Prepare to be amazed by our stunning show cave featuring spectacular stalagmite and stalactite formations created over 500,000 years ago! See cheddar cheese maturing in the caves, view the site where Cheddar Man’s 10,000-year-old skeleton was discovered and learn about the extraordinary DNA discovery. A free audio guide is available in six languages, and there is also a special version for children. Cox’s Cave featuring Yeo’s Journey: The Power of Water. This spectacular immersive multimedia experience tells the captivating story of how our iconic caves were formed and evolved through the ‘Power of Water’. The story is brought to life using state-of-the-art animation, sound, lighting and colour. Beyond the View: Take a seat in front of our state of the art 270-degree screen. Discover historic tales, enjoy breathtaking aerial panoramic views, and learn about the special wildlife and plants that call the gorge home. Museum of Pre-History: Discover amazing artefacts unearthed in the Cheddar area that help tell the story of how people lived thousands of years ago. Jacob’s Ladder & The Lookout Tower: Venture up the 274 steps to the top of the gorge with rest stops along the route to admire the view. Marvel at the panoramic views and mosaic of landscapes across the Mendips and Somerset Levels. Cliff­ -Top Walk: Hike the 3-mile loop around the gorge. Look out for the wildlife and enjoy the stunning scenery. If you don’t have time to do the full circuit, you can go for a shorter walk up to the Pulpit Rock look out point, and head back down the ladder. Gough’s Café Sit back, relax, and take in the beauty of the gorge at Gough’s Cafe, close to the entrance of Gough's Cave. Enjoy a thirst-quenching chilled drink, warm yourself up with a hot beverage or choose from a selection of alcoholic drinks. Serving light lunches, delicious snacks, cream teas and delicious cake, to include vegetarian and vegan options. Enjoy the spectacular views from the comfort of our air-conditioned cafe or relax on the large patio where dogs are welcome. We even have a welcome bowl of water for our doggy friends. Our small play area for under 2-year-olds will keep the little ones entertained too! Accessibility Cheddar Gorge & Caves provides accessible toilets, free parking for blue badge holders and free admission for carers accompanied by a full paying visitor. The audio tour of Gough's cave is printed in braille. Assistance Dogs are permitted, and the museum is wheelchair accessible with lift. Those with severely restricted mobility or who are wheelchair dependent will find areas of Cheddar Gorge & Caves inaccessible. If you have any questions prior to your visit, please email Guest Services on info@cheddargorge.co.uk or call 01934 742343. Dog-Friendly Dogs are welcome in all attractions and water bowls are provided in the cave entrances, shop and café patio. Family and Children Cheddar Gorge & Cave is family friendly. We have baby changing facilities, buggy parking and are breast-feeding friendly. Gough’s café has a small play area for under two year olds, water refills and highchairs are available. Entry is free for children under the age of 5 years. Groups Cheddar Gorge & Caves has special group rates, coach parking and drop off points for group tours. We offer discounted exclusive group sessions for Rocksport adventure activities – adventure caving, rock climbing and freefall. Special Events We have a fantastic programme of events throughout the year to keep the whole family entertained, including the school holidays. Visit our What’s On page for more details. Thirst for adventure or a puzzle-solving mind? Rocksport: Imagine climbing the gorge rockface in the shadow of the 450ft cliffs, caving deep underground or taking part in our exhilarating Blackcat freefall in Gough’s Cave. Suitable for all abilities. Sessions available for adults and children aged 8 years and over. Escape Rooms : Up for a challenge? Our two Cheddar-themed rooms, Caved In and The Vault will test your brain power as you race against the clock to try to escape. Double the fun with our Ultimate Escape combo ticket at a discounted rate. Suitable for 12 years and over in groups of up to six people. Nature, wildlife, history, adventure - experience the wonder on an all-season day out in Somerset. For more information on how to plan your day at Cheddar Gorge & Caves and to book please visit www.cheddargorge.co.uk

title: Porlock
subtitle: Porlock is a place for everyone and all seasons. Porlock is a special and unique village. It has retained much of its medieval charm including the 13th Century church of St Dubricius with its famous truncated spire and many attractive and historic buildings.
bodyContent: Porlock is a special and unique village. It has retained much of its medieval charm including the 13th Century church of St Dubricius with its famous truncated spire and many attractive and historic buildings. Porlock sits in a splendid position surrounded on three sides by the wooded and heather clad hills of Exmoor and by the Bristol Channel to the North. Although it only has a population of 1300 it is a lively, living village with a vibrant calendar of activities and an amazing variety of shops, restaurants and accommodation. Exmoor is a dark skies reserve and Porlock is the ideal base for star gazers of all ages. It also offers an excellent base for walking or cycling. With activities such as horse riding and outdoor adventures available there is something for everyone.

title: The Compass
subtitle: A beautiful classic pub, just off Junction 24 on the M5 and near Bridgewater, with a large beer garden and onsite parking, serving up a wide selection of favourite pub dishes and beverages.
bodyContent: The Compass is a classic English pub - the perfect place for enjoying some delicious food or a refreshing cold beverage with friends and loved ones. Recently refurbished, we invite you to check out our extensive food menu, with a range of vegan and vegetarian recipes to tempt any tastebud - from traditional Sunday roasts with all the trimmings to Afternoon Tea and food deals throughout the week, as well as a range of cask ales, gins, wines, and cocktails, and a menu of low or non-alcoholic options, you will be spoilt for choice. Seating indoors and a lovely beer garden to the rear – we have plenty of space to enjoy our comfortable surroundings all year round. Well behaved dogs are welcome too . We look forward to welcoming you at The Compass, North Petherton soon.

title: Peter Hayes Sculpture
subtitle: I have always been interested in the history of ceramics – why and how ‘things’ are made of clay. This interest was extended after I spent several years travelling through Africa working with various tribes and village potters and being intrigued how, with limited technology and basic tools, they were able to get such exquisite, beautiful surfaces. I found the same inherent skills in India, Nepal Japan and New Mexico. I tried to adopt the ideas picked up from my travels in my own work. By buildi
bodyContent: About Peter Hayes II have been working on large scale ceramic forms which I have placed in the landscape. My main aim is that the work should not compete with the landscape, but evolve within the environment. With this in mind I have introduced other minerals into the Raku ceramic surface such as iron and copper. With the elements of time and erosion, the individual piece takes on its own developing surface. Recently, one of these large commissions has taken me again to India. My Client suggested I make it on site. Now I have discovered Udaipur in Rajasthan where I come for inspiration, when my studio in Bath in England gets cold in the winter months. This has introduced me to other artists and craftsmen enabling me to work with a range of different materials, such as glass, marble, stone and Damascus steel. In practice I go by the seat of my pants. I have always worked this way, not going by any particular rules or methods. I find it joyful to work with many different materials. Each has its own character, its own limits, its own tolerance – some materials fight back, some play the game. Finally I think it’s the material that is in charge and it will only let you make what it wants. It is my job to push it to its limits and somehow an equilibrium is made between maker and material.
tagline: I have always been interested in the history of ceramics – why and how ‘things’ are made of clay.

title: Ferne Animal Sanctuary
subtitle: Ferne Animal Sanctuary is set within 72 acres of beautiful & protected countryside in the Blackdown Hills on the Devon/Somerset border. This charitable sanctuary takes in unwanted, abandoned and neglected animals and gives them a fantastic life either at the sanctuary or by finding them a special forever home.
bodyContent: Ferne Animal Sanctuary is set within 72 acres of beautiful & protected countryside in the Blackdown Hills on the Devon/Somerset border. This charitable sanctuary takes in unwanted, abandoned and neglected animals and gives them a fantastic life either at the sanctuary or by finding them a special forever home. Ferne Animal Sanctuary, located near Chard in Somerset, is a remarkable facility dedicated to the rehoming of dogs, cats, and horses. In addition to this, the sanctuary provides ongoing care and welfare for a wide variety of animals, including sheep, goats, cattle, pigs, geese, chickens, and an aviary housing birds from around the world. It is also home to smaller animals such as rabbits, guinea pigs, chinchillas and ferrets, ensuring they all receive the care and attention they need. Founded in 1939, at the onset of World War II, the charity was established to care for pets whose owners were going to war, or who had been displaced by the conflict. Over the years, it has forged strong connections with HM Armed Forces and the Royal Family. A typical visit to Ferne lasts between 90 to 150 minutes, during which visitors can enjoy observing the animals in their natural habitats. The experience includes a sensory garden designed to calm the senses with a variety of sounds, sights and smells. Visitors can explore the Willow Walk, which offers insights into animal care, as well as informative displays about our water voles, dragonflies, birds, and fungi. There's also a machinery wall showcasing equipment used throughout the years, along with a small play area for our younger visitors. Take the time to enjoy the stunning natural landscape of the Blackdown Hills from our viewing platform. Relax, gaze across the hills, and marvel at the beauty of nature at its finest. During the school holidays, Creative Corner offers a range of animal-themed activities and arts and crafts. We also host special events and workshops throughout the year, with full details available on our website. The Visitor Centre is open from 10 AM to 4 PM from Easter to October half term, though the shop and sanctuary are open every day, except Christmas Day, Boxing Day, and New Year's Day. Our well-stocked pet supplies and gift shop has everything you need for your animals, as well as delightful treats to tempt you. Dog friendly (dogs must be kept on leads) and accessible, Ferne has a good network of tarmac paths. However, due to the number of gates, we recommend that wheelchair users are accompanied. We have designated parking spaces for wheelchair users and visitors with special needs next to our Visitor Centre as well as in the main car park. All money raised goes to support our animal care and welfare. Unleash the Party Fun at Ferne Animal Sanctuary! title: Clifton Suspension Bridge Trust
subtitle: Clifton Suspension Bridge Visitor Centre tells the story of the 'ornament of Bristol' and the people who built, maintain and treasure it. Explore the turbulent history of the ‘first love’ of famous British engineer Isambard Kingdom Brunel through an award winning exhibition packed with family activities and staffed by knowledgeable volunteers.
bodyContent: Visitor Centre Clifton Suspension Bridge Visitor Centre tells the story of the 'ornament of Bristol' and the people who built, maintain and treasure it. Explore the turbulent history of the ‘first love’ of famous British engineer Isambard Kingdom Brunel through an award winning exhibition packed with family activities and staffed by knowledgeable volunteers. The Visitor Centre is open between Friday and Monday throughout the winter and may be found in Leigh Woods on the North Somerset side of the bridge, a short walk from Clifton Village where you’ll find bus stops, pay and display parking, boutique shopping, cafes and coffee shops. Under the current Covid-19 guidance, pre-booking of tickets is strongly recommended. ( www.cliftonbridge.org.uk/visitor-centre ) Bridge Once the far-fetched dream of local wine merchant William Vick, the bridge was the first solo project of the famous British engineer Isambard Kingdom Brunel who came up with ambitious plans to build the highest and longest bridge in the world. Sadly, Brunel did not live to see his ‘first love’ completed. The bridge took 33 years to build and opened as a monument to his achievements after his death. The Bridge is open 24 hours a day 7 days a week, 365 days a year and can be crossed on foot or by bicycle free of charge, although vehicles must pay a £1 toll towards the maintenance and upkeep of this Grade I listed structure. Groups may book private tours at any time, with a coach drop-off point available on Observatory Road, BS8 4AW (there is a weight limit of 4 tons so coaches may not cross the bridge). A programme of events runs throughout the year for families and adult learners. The bridge spans the spectacular Avon Gorge and is illuminated each evening, lighting up half an hour before sunset. Photographers may like to visit the viewpoints on Sion Hill or at the Cumberland Basin.
tagline: The Bridge is open 24 hours a day 7 days a week, 365 days.

title: Cleeve Abbey
subtitle: The Cistercian abbey of Cleeve offers a glimpse of daily life 800 years ago.
bodyContent: The Cistercian abbey of Cleeve is a haven of peace and tranquillity, offering a glimpse of daily life 800 years ago. It has some of the best-preserved monastic buildings in England, with many rooms retaining traces of their original decoration. The abbey is steeped in history, providing a fascinating day out for families and budding historians alike. Although the church was destroyed by Henry VIII during the dissolution of the monasteries, the cloister buildings (including the gatehouse, 15th century refectory with its glorious angel roof, and 13th century heraldic tiles) have survived remarkably intact. The great dormitory is one of the best examples in the country, and an exhibition and virtual tour tells the story of the abbey and daily life for the holy men that once inhabited it. Cleeve is one of the hidden gems of Somerset, located in a beautiful valley surrounded by countryside. It is ideal for walkers or visitors travelling on the West Somerset Railway. Click here to learn more about English Heritage sites in Somerset.
tagline: The Cistercian abbey of Cleeve offers a glimpse of daily life 800 years ago.

title: Da Costa
subtitle: Enjoy legendary Italian bonhomie at Da Costa, through dishes rooted in traditions, care and imagination. Our tables are for food. And for family stories.
bodyContent: Da Costa has been named for and inspired by Artfarm co-founder Iwan Wirth’s maternal grandfather, who originated from the small mountainous village of Rivamonte Agordino in the Veneto region of Northern Italy. He emigrated to Switzerland in the early 20th century and opened a restaurant much loved for its simple, honest fare. A century later, and some 800 miles from that first restaurant, Da Costa continues this glorious culinary adventure. The menu is an exploration of traditional northern Italian recipes featuring an array of antipasti, homemade pastas and risottos and daily specials cooked over fire. Using freshly grown seasonal ingredients from our walled garden and surrounding area, our dishes blend the best of both words – quintessential Englishness with Italian culinary flair. Our wine list includes a global selection of 100 bins with a collection of Italian and British wines from small domain producer including wines from Durslade Farm’s own vineyards.

title: The Kennard
subtitle: The Kennard gives you the chance to discover and enjoy a stay in a true Georgian Town House.
bodyContent: The Kennard gives you the chance to discover and enjoy a stay in a true Georgian Town House, now restored to a boutique guesthouse. Built as a lodging house in 1794, The Kennard, today, offers twelve recently refurbished and individually decorated bedrooms, furnished for your every comfort, over five floors with a fine selection of superior doubles, standard doubles, snug doubles, two singles with shared bathroom, a twin and a triple room. Our rooms offer either a view over our garden and the city, or look out onto the street. We also have a small sitting area and an honesty bar located on the landings. Quietly situated only 5 minutes from the Abbey, the Roman Baths, the Thermae Spa and the railway station and some of the best restaurants and shopping venues our beautiful city has to offer. We hope you will stay with us and enjoy the experience of staying in one of Bath’s original Georgian townhouses with service and accommodation that truly reflects this beautiful city’s social history and culture.
tagline: The Kennard gives you the chance to discover and enjoy a stay in a true Georgian Town House.

title: Stable Cottage: 6 bed country cottage
subtitle: Stable cottage is created from a stone built-stable block dating from the 1840’s.
bodyContent: It is located in the beautiful Georgian village of Freshford which lies at the junction of the Frome and Avon valleys in the southern Cotswolds. There are some wonderful walks to local pubs following the riverside and canals. All just 15 minutes from Bath by car but the secret of this location is the 9 minute train journey to Bath from the village station, just a short stroll from the cottages. The cottage : Stable cottage is a newly renovated, limestone floored, 3 bedroom, two bathroom (one is en-suite) cottage. It has large windows to the front of the house filling the bedrooms and downstairs with light on a sunny day. It has an open plan living/dining area with free view TV/DVD and two large suedette couches and comfortable chairs. For dining there is a blond Oak dining table and chairs to seat 6 . The Stables can accommodate 6 people in three bedrooms (two king size and one double) . The kitchen is fully equipped with cookware,dishwasher and washing machine . The house also offers Iron/Ironing board, Hairdryers All bed linen and towels . There is a Welcome pack of tea, coffee, sugar, milk, bread, butter, eggs and bacon. Free WiFi. There are also books and board-games in the house for the use of guests. If you have any questions on Bath and the local area before or during your stay please let us know. We would be delighted to help. Neighbourhood overview : Freshford is a beautiful ancient village with a wonderful pub just a few minutes walk from the cottage( The Inn at Freshford) that serves restaurant quality food and all the local beers and ciders.They have an excellent fully stocked( from wine to organic humus!)community shop that also has a good quality cafe that serves lunch. There is also a local doctors surgery. The village is nestled at the junction of the Frome and Avon valleys . The Kennet and Avon canal is a 15 minute walk from the cottage. Getting around : You don’t need a car to stay in the cottage. The village station is a few minutes walk away. Trains hourly off peak and thrice hourly at peak times. Bath 9 mins, Bristol 22mins. London Padington to Bath Spa 1.5 hours Bath Spa to Freshford 9 minutes Bath Spa to Freshford “ https://www.thetrainline.com/train-times/bath-spa-to-freshford ” Freshford to Bath Spa “ https://www.thetrainline.com/train-times/freshford-to-bath-spa ” There is also a local bus service to all the adjacent villages and Bath. The cottage has two parking spaces suitable for one medium and one small car or a single large SUV.the surrounding towns you might want to visit. Other things to note If you are a runner or keep fit enthusiast the owner is a qualified Personal Trainer (Bath Uni) with much Marathon and half marathon experience. She specialises in Ladies training. Please let us know if you would like guided running or some Personal Fitness training.
tagline: Stable cottage is created from a stone built-stable block dating from the 1840’s.

title: The Old Smithy Loft
subtitle: Our luxury 4 Star Gold self-catering apartment was once the workplace (smithy) of local blacksmiths.
bodyContent: Just two minutes walk from the Kennet and Avon Canal (good spot for cycle rental) which runs through Bath city centre and 10 minutes from Bath Abbey. THE OLD SMITHY LOFT This elegant first floor apartment is decorated in duck egg blue and cream throughout and is particularly relaxing as the Old Smithy is down a cul de sac, away from the hustle and bustle of Bath.Situated just off Bathwick Hill, your stroll in to town in Jane Austen’s footsteps takes you along iconic Pulteney Street, past Laura Square, along Pulteney Bridge, the only bridge with shops on in the UK and admire the weir. You will find yourself just beside the Abbey and the Guild Hall. Of course, you don’t need to go even that far to enjoy the historic features of Bath..the Holburne Museum, home of many Gainsboroughs and a lovely cafe and Sydney Gardens one of the Uk’s original pleasure Gardens are within 10 minutes walk. Newly converted, the large open plan fully equipped kitchen, dining and sitting area with ample room for 4 is ideal for relaxing after a day in Bath. The apartment sleeps up to 4 in 2 bedrooms with the option of kingsize double and single beds and a flat screen TV in each. All our beds gave luxury 1200 pocket sprung mattress and Egyptian cotton bed linen to ensure you have a very comfortable sleep. The bathroom has a full sized bath and a drench shower. PARKING This is free and immediately outside the door and is 3 metres (the standard car park size) wide. The neighbouring property has no rights over the car park area. MEDIA The Old Smithy Loft, 4 Star Gold luxury self catering also benefits from free Wifi, iPod docking staton, flat screen TV, games and books apart from the TVs in both bedrooms and in the sitting room. REWARD CARD In the apartment you will find full details of the Reward Card which entitles you to discounts at many restaurants, shops and attractions such as 3 hours for 2 at the Thermae Spa. THOSE LOOKING AFTER YOU Owned and managed by the Family Team…with a background in hospitality and having travelled all over, Ann, Nikki and Michael will all do their best to use their experience to make your stay enjoyable.

title: Target Sports at Mendip Activity Centre
subtitle: Target Sport activities for the whole family at Mendip Activity Centre.
bodyContent: Mendip Activity Centre offer Target Sports for public booking at their activity centre on the Mendip Hills. Perched in the heart of Somerset’s wild and beautiful countryside, this is your chance to channel your inner Robin Hood. Whether you're a beginner or a secret pro, these adventures are a blast. Activities available include Archery, Air Rifle and Axe Throwing whilst Nerf & Gel Battles and ArcheryActive are available as private group sessions. From calm precision to full-blown foam fun, there’s something for every level of energy and age group age 6+. All sessions are led by friendly, experienced instructors who’ll guide you safely and confidently every step of the way. Sessions run in all weathers thanks to undercover ranges, and you can book for individuals, families, birthday parties or just because you fancy something adventurous to do this week!
tagline: Targetsport activities for the whole family at Mendip Activity Centre.

title: 28 Years Later
subtitle: Location: Cheddar Gorge Release date: June 2025
bodyContent: The third instalment of the ‘28’ horror franchise, ‘28 Years Later’ filmed pivotal scenes in Cheddar Gorge in July 2024. The scenes, which come at the end of the film, were shot over five days just to the north and south of Arch Rock, one of the most striking sections of the gorge, and see Spike (12-year-old Alfie Williams) fending off an attack from a horde of the ‘infected’, driven to homicidal madness by the ‘Rage Virus’. Oscar winning Director, Danny Boyle described the gorge as “Extraordinary… amazing… one of the most unique pieces of British landscape”. For the scene, his crew of around 100 installed a fake rock slide across the width of the gorge - a wood and fibreglass structure prepared off-site and slotted into place, piece-by-piece, and dressed by the ‘greens team’ to be a convincing pile of Cheddar limestone. The road itself was dressed with fake rocks and flora to give the dystopian feel. Written by Alex Garland, the film’s cast includes Jodie Comer, Aaron Taylor-Johnson and Ralph Fiennes. Cheddar Gorges and Caves is one of the county’s premier tourist attractions, seeing around half a million visitors each year. title: Dolebury Hill Fort
subtitle: Somerset Fascinating Facts - Do Fairies really live on top of the hill and what are they hiding?
customFields:
[{"key":"NewsID","value":"240"},{"key":"NewsBody","value":"

Fairies called Redshanks purportedly live on Dolebury Hill, protecting a hidden cache of treasure.

DOLEBURY HILL FORT THE MENDIPS SOMERSET,  WITH COMMANDING VIEWS OVER THE SURROUNDING COUNTRYSIDE, it’s no wonder the hill called Dolebury Warren (or Camp) became a fort during the Iron Age, remaining in use until Roman times. A number of archaeological finds indicate this long period of occupation, with Palaeolithic flint work, Bronze Age pottery and Roman coins and pottery all being unearthed. In the post-medieval period, the site became a large burrow for the breeding of rabbits, the resulting meat and fur trade providing employment for a number of people. It was in this period that the name ‘Warren’ was added. Remains of the ancient fort are still visible today, with the hill becoming a haven for a large number of wildflowers and rare butterflies. If you are lucky enough to visit in spring, the woods below the hilltop come alive with swathes of bluebells.


For more on Somerset's incredible history and heritage go to our interactive E Book.

title: Wiveliscombe
subtitle: Situated at the foot of the Brendon Hills at the gateway to Exmoor, 'Wivey' is a thriving local centre surrounded by attractive countryside that is never far away.
bodyContent: Situated at the foot of the Brendon Hills at the gateway to Exmoor , 'Wivey' is a thriving local centre surrounded by attractive countryside that is never far away. It contains numerous shops, many still with their Victorian frontages, whilst the pubs stock ales from the town's two breweries. Follow the Historic Town Trail - unlock the town's history and discover why Wiveliscombe was directly involved in the London Blitz. There's an impressive wealth of creativity to be discovered in the surrounding parishes, with artists, potters, sculptors and photographers taking part in the 10 Parishes Festival which takes place in and around Wiveliscombe. Local artist, Michael Fairfax recently unveiled a public art sculpture to be used as a tourist information point in the town's square representing local history and features. title: Wellington
subtitle: Wellington gave its name to the famous ‘Iron Duke’, victor at the Battle of Waterloo, and the 175ft monument built on the Blackdowns was erected in his honour.
bodyContent: The town’s growth and prosperity date back to the 18th century when the Fox family started to build their integrated woollen mill. Today visitors can visit the Wellington Museum to discover more about the historic town. Wellington Park is an important example of late Victorian design and has been awarded Green Heritage status. The town’s Wellesley Cinema also reflects the past, having been designed in the 1930s. Wellington is also well known for its food with various events and initiatives to celebrate the best in local food and drink. Wellington is an excellent self-contained local shopping centre with a fine choice of independent retailers.
tagline: Wellington gave its name to the famous ‘Iron Duke’, victor at the Battle of Waterloo.

title: West Somerset Railway
subtitle: West Somerset Railway, a true country branch line of the old Great Western Railway is full of fascination whether you are looking for a nostalgic ride back in time through lovely countryside or to study the railway and industrial heritage which our line preserves..
bodyContent: The historic steam locomotives, coaches and wagons, and the buildings of our ten unique stations linked by a twenty mile scenic journey will repay hours of exploration. The surrounding countryside is as varied as it is beautiful. The gently rolling Quantock Hills and distant Exmoor, unspoilt villages and farms nestling in leafy lanes, the cliffs and coast of the Bristol Channel with views of distant South-Wales, confident Church Towers, Dunster's imposing Castle and Minehead's seaside charm are all waiting to be discovered.
tagline: The longest heritage railway in England

title: ⭐East Lambrook Manor Gardens
subtitle: The quintessential English cottage garden created by the celebrated 20th-century plantswoman and gardening writer Margery Fish and made famous through her many books. It is a unique garden of great beauty and charm with noted collections of snowdrops, hellebores and geraniums and an excellent specialist plant nursery and tea room.
bodyContent: ⭐ Reward Card Discount Available The garden may have changed ownership but the quintessential English cottage garden created by the celebrated 20th-century plantswoman and gardening writer Margery Fish is still open. The garden was made famous through her many books, and it retains a unique beauty and charm, with noted collections of snowdrops, hellebores and geraniums and an excellent specialist plant nursery, and Tea Room. East Lambrook Manor Gardens in South Somerset is a hidden gem, yet it is easily accessible from the A303 at South Petherton, near Yeovil. The home from 1938 to 1969 of the doyenne of cottage gardening Margery Fish, it was here that she developed her own unselfconscious style, combining plants in a relaxed and informal manner to create a garden of great beauty and charm that has encouraged generations of budding gardeners. Open Tuesday to Saturday 10 am to 5 pm, the internationally famous garden was given Grade-1 status by English Heritage in 1992 and is recognised as the premier example of the English cottage garden style. Winding paths between abundantly planted beds and borders, often edged with the local hamstone, typify the garden which is divided into different areas such as the Terrace Garden, Silver Garden, the newly restored Green Garden and The Ditch. The latter, along with the Woodland Garden, contain most of the garden’s extensive collection of snowdrops and hellebores. The 17 th century Malthouse is home to the Tea Rooms serving coffee, tea, cakes and cold drinks. The Margery Fish Plant Nursery specialises in cottage garden plants and interesting perennials. Accessibility: Limited disabled access due to some narrow paths and steps. Dogs on leads permitted. Disabled toilets.

title: Victoria Art Gallery
subtitle: Opened in 1900, the Victoria Art Gallery boasts an outstanding collection of paintings, sculptures and decorative arts. The gallery is located in the centre of Bath, near the famous Pulteney Bridge. Entry to the permanent exhibitions is free.
bodyContent: Opened in 1900, the Victoria Art Gallery boasts an outstanding collection of paintings, sculptures and decorative arts. The gallery is located in the centre of Bath , near the famous Pulteney Bridge. Entry to the permanent exhibitions is free. You’ll see more than 1,500 artworks, including many by artists who have lived and worked in the Bath area, such as Thomas Gainsborough and Walter Sickert. The work on show spans the 15th century to the present day. In the 18th century Bath was an important centre for portrait painting, and in the 20th century it again became famous thanks to the innovative works being produced by artists at the renowned Bath Academy of Art at Corsham Court. Alongside the permanent collections, the Victoria Art Gallery also hosts an exciting programme of temporary exhibitions and events throughout the year. Please check the Victoria Art Gallery website for the latest information.
tagline: Opened in 1900, the Victoria Art Gallery boasts an outstanding collection.

title: Brothers Cider
subtitle: Brothers Drinks Co was established in 1992 by four brothers from the Showering family, who have been making cider in Somerset since 1658.
bodyContent: Brothers Drinks Co was established in 1992 by four brothers from the Showering family, who have been making cider in Somerset since 1658. We first started selling our Pear Cider at the Glastonbury Festival in 1995 near what was then called the Jazz World Stage. These days it is called The West Holts Stage. Over the years, festival goers kept asking us if it was possible to get our drink when the festival was over and so we decided to market it to pubs and supermarkets. Now you can get it all over the country and at many festivals. We are independent, British and are passionate about what we do. Our free-spirited essence is upheld by approaching things with a unique perspective. Here at Brothers, we take our values and commitment to sustainability very seriously, but it’s something we haven’t really shouted about until now. We have zero to landfill, all our waste is segregated to optimise the opportunity of being recycled or reused. A massive solar panel system is now installed here at the cider mill, where it will directly supply the presses with clean energy and lastly, all our left-over fruit pomace is turned into energy which helps to heat the local swimming pool!
tagline: Brothers Drinks Co was established in 1992 by four brothers from the Showering family.

title: Nature Reserves in Somerset
subtitle: As a county rich in wildlife, Somerset unsurprisingly has a huge number of nature reserves. These are great places to visit. Most are open all year and many allow dogs. With such a diverse landscape, Somerset’s reserves encompass meadows, cliffs, hills, downs, woods, waterways and wetlands. Somerset Wildlife Trust looks after 70 of the County’s reserves and they are listed on its website: www.somersetwildlife.org along with a range of events throughout year organised by the Trust.
bodyContent: As a county rich in wildlife, Somerset unsurprisingly has a huge number of nature reserves. These are great places to visit. Most are open all year and many allow dogs. With such a diverse landscape, Somerset’s reserves encompass meadows, cliffs, hills, downs, woods, waterways and wetlands. Somerset Wildlife Trust looks after 70 of the County’s reserves and they are listed on its website: www.somersetwildlife.org along with a range of events throughout year organised by the Trust. Among the top places for birdwatching in Britain are The Avalon Marshes. Its reed beds attract summer visitors, are home to booming Bitterns and host the amazing starling roosts in the winter. The marshes are not just water and reeds. There are wonderful meadows and small woodlands, most of which enjoy special protection. They offer opportunities to see some of the UK’s rarest creatures. More information about this area can be found on the website: www.avalonmarshes.org Giving nature a home in Somerset, the Royal Society for the Protection of Birds (RSPB), has four reserves. They are: Swell Wood, an ancient woodland on the edge of the Blackdown Hills; West Sedgemoor and Greylake on the Levels and Moors and Ham Wall at Avalon Marshes. Directions to them can be found on the website: www.rspb.org.uk Natural England has several National Nature Reserves in Somerset, including Shapwick Heath on the Avalon Marshes and Bridgwater Bay, an internationally important roosting site for waterfowl and wading birds, with around 190 species of bird. Find out more from www.naturalengland.org.uk Of The Hawk and Owl Trust’s three reserves in the UK, one is in Somerset. At Shapwick it is creating permanent wet grassland and fen to support owls and other birds of prey. A guide to the reserve can be found at: www.hawkandowl.org A new salt marsh being created on the Steart Peninsula along the Bristol Channel is the largest wetland habitat creation scheme in England. It is expected to boost many species of birds as well as benefit fish. Over time it will become a fully-vegetated Atlantic salt marsh. Owned by the Environment Agency, it is managed by the Wildfowl and Wetlands Trust (WWT). Open all year, there is access for people with disabilities, horse riders, cyclists and walkers. New panoramic viewpoints, wildlife observation hides, information points and sign posts have all been installed.
tagline: As a county rich in wildlife, Somerset unsurprisingly has a huge number of nature reserves.

title: Foxglove Cycle Trail
subtitle: The Foxglove Cycle Trail was designed by the Taunton Area Cycling Campaign to explore a town of attractive green spaces and watercourses, some off the beaten track.
bodyContent: The 11 mile mainly flat Foxglove Cycle Trail follows some of the town’s traffic free paths and mainly quiet roads. It is suitable for all ages, particularly families. You can join it at any point along the Foxglove Cycle Trail, to come back to the same point. There are attractive green areas to pause in and sections along some of Taunton’s many streams and the Taunton-Bridgwater Canal and River Tone. There are wildlife havens along the Foxglove Cycle Trail. Download the leaflet with the route and information on places of interest and refreshment stops here or pick up your free copy at the Taunton Visitor Centre. Local bike hire available at Somerset Bike Hire
tagline: An 11 mile mainly flat, circular cycle trail around Taunton

title: Connect to a Care Home and fight loneliness this Christmas
subtitle: Somerset County Council and the NHS are encouraging organisations across Somerset to connect to their local care home with a new digital campaign, #ConnectACareHome.
bodyContent: Somerset County Council and the NHS are encouraging organisations across Somerset to connect to their local care home with a new digital campaign, #ConnectACareHome. Organisations are being asked to send video messages to their local care homes, to help combat the loneliness and isolation experienced by residents and staff who may have been unable to see their loved ones due to Covid restrictions. The idea for the campaign came from a small group of NHS and SCC colleagues working together on digital projects. Sarah Moore, Service Manager for the council’s ICT and Tech Transformation team, said: “A lot of time in my job is spent looking at how we can use digital technologies to improve lives for people across Somerset. Working with colleagues in NHS and Adult Social Care alerted me to just how hard this year has been for staff and residents in our care homes, and we were all really keen to do something to create some smiles. “I contacted my daughters’ schools to suggest we send a video of the children’s Christmas carols and performances to our local care home. Working with colleagues, we thought why not see if we can connect all our care homes in Somerset this Christmas? It’s never been so important to let them know we care.” Mel Lock, Somerset County Council’s Director for Adult Social Care, said: “We’ve already sent a message out to schools asking them to take part in this fantastic campaign, sharing videos of their Christmas nativity, special messages from the children, and even Christmas songs. But we’re keen to encourage a wide range of organisations to take part – from local businesses, community groups, charities and more. We don’t want any care homes to be left behind this year, so please help us spread the word.” David Huxtable, Somerset County Council’s Cabinet Member for Adult Social Care said: “It’s been an incredibly difficult year for our care homes this year, and so important that we reach out - we have the technology to connect like never before, so there really is no reason for anyone to be suffering in loneliness and isolation. The #ConnectACareHome campaign is a great way to lift spirits and make a difference this Christmas – let’s get it trending!” How to take part: • Find your nearest care home Visit: CQC - Find a care home and pop in your organisation’s postcode • Get in touch to say hello and introduce yourself You should be able to find their contact details on Google • Get consent Make sure the person in the video knows they are being recorded and knows where the video will be shown. Children will need signed consent from parents. • Record your video This can be done on a phone, or using a camera if you have one. Here are some great tips for filming on your phone. • Edit your video If recording on a phone, there are free editing apps such as Kinemaster or Inshot which you can use to create your video. You can also use programs such as iMovie for Macs, or Movie Maker if you use Windows. OpenShot works on both Mac and Windows, and is also free. • Upload your video to Youtube Don’t forget to make it an unlisted video. • Share your video Email a link of your unlisted Youtube video to your local care home • Delete the video Have they seen it? Delete the video later if you need to. • Tell us about it! We’re really keen to hear about all your great videos and messages, so please let us know what you’re doing by emailing CommunicationsTeam@somerset.gov.uk - or tag us on Twitter @SomersetCouncil or on Facebook @SomersetCountyCouncil . Let’s spread some festive cheer and get the hashtag #ConnectACareHome trending this Christmas! Support is available to anyone who needs it via the Somerset Coronavirus Support Helpline on 0300 790 6275 . The helpline is open seven days a week from 8am to 6pm and offers a range of support – from help accessing food or medicines, to emotional and financial support, and employment, skills and business advice. Ends For further information, please contact the Press Office on 01823 355020 or email pressoffice@somerset.gov.uk For the latest updates on coronavirus, and to sign up to our newsletter, visit: https://www.somerset.gov.uk/coronavirus/ For more information, please contact the Press Office on 01823 355020 or email pressoffice@somerset.gov.uk . To view all our news releases, please visit www.somersetnewsroom.com The SCC Communications Team are also on social media: www.twitter.com/somersetcouncil www.facebook.com/somersetcountycouncil www.flickr.com/somersetcountycouncil www.youtube.com/yoursomerset To find out who the elected Somerset County Councillor is for a particular area, simply visit www.somerset.gov.uk/councillors-and-democracy/councillors/somerset-county-councillors/ Somerset County Council County Hall, Taunton, Somerset, TA1 4DY If you no longer wish to receive emails from the Somerset County Council Communications Team, please email communications@somerset.gov.uk and tell us and we will remove you from our media contacts distributio n list.

title: The Helicopter Museum
subtitle: The Helicopter Museum is the largest dedicated Helicopter Collection in the World with over 100 helicopters on display in an all weather undercover hangar. Exhibits include two of the Queen's Royal Flight helicopters, the current world speed record holder G-LYNX, a Vietnam Veteran Huey and a Russian Hind Gun Ship.
bodyContent: In addition to over 100 helicopters, the Helicopter Museum includes other breathtaking attractions like its WWII Pilots’ Block, Weston Aviation Exhibition and Blood Hound Missile. This all contributes to a fun day-out for all the family with plenty of opportunity to learn about these marvellous machines and their huge impact on Somerset’s history. The museum hosts various special events throughout the year. These include various car shows, hair-rasing Halloween hilarity and festive Christmas events. The most popular of these special events are the World At War Weekend and Balloons, Birds & Bubbles . At these events, the museum is completely transformed to provide visitors the opportunity to enjoy authentic military vehicles or hold a live owl! Those who haven’t had their fill of aviation history can also attend one of the museum’s open cockpit days. Here visitors can climb into the pilot’s seat of a genuine helicopter and be taken through the controls by an experienced volunteer, many of whom have spent their careers flying such aircraft. Those who really want to feel the thrill of soaring high up in the clouds can even book their seat on one of the many helicopter experience flights the museum offers throughout the year. After all that excitement, visitors can refuel in the museum’s new café which was opened as part of a new visitor service building in July 2020. It offers drinks, snacks and tasty lunches. A particular highlight is the pilots’ all-day breakfast that is big enough to satisfy even the hungriest aviation superfan!
tagline: The Helicopter Museum is the largest dedicated Helicopter Collection in the World

title: Hit the Streets of Clevedon for a healthy walk
subtitle: Walking groups are helping people across North Somerset stretch their legs, make new friends and feel healthier. Organised walks usually last about an hour but a new group has launched in Clevedon to offer residents a slightly more vigorous, 90-minute route. Life joined them to take in the sights around the town…
bodyContent: How to get there Start at map ref: ST 408710 Car: Parking is available at the former Morrisons supermarket, off Great Western Road - Route information Distance: just over 3 miles Difficulty: easy – a fairly flat route around the town Duration: allow up to 90 minutes Map: OS Explorer 153 Walking groups are helping people across North Somerset stretch their legs, make new friends and feel healthier. Organised walks usually last about an hour but a new group has launched in Clevedon to offer residents a slightly more vigorous, 90-minute route. Life joined them to take in the sights around the town… Start the walk in Queen’s Square, then turn left onto Old Church Road. Turn right onto Queen’s Road and continue uphill towards the crossroads at the end. Cross the road and turn left into Sunnyside Road. At the next crossroads turn right, which is still Sunnyside Road. From here you can go through a gate into Sunhill Park. Follow the path to your right, through the trees, and then head towards Sunhill House. This is now Clevedon Community Centre after being bought by the people of the town in 1949. Go around the side of the building and exit through the car park onto Princes Road. Turn right onto this road, cross over, and then at the junction turn left into Linden Road, then right into Herbert Road. Go through a wooden gate into Herbert Gardens, which was donated to the people of Clevedon by the Elton family in 1865. Follow the path and you will pass a ruined stone structure, which formed part of Wycliffe Girls School. Click HERE for full details and FREE PDF copy

title: Do you Fondue? Marston Park's traditional Fondue recipe
subtitle: We're launching our delicious Fondue recipe with you, because, quite frankly, we've become rather obsessed with perfecting this mouthwatering cheesy delight!
bodyContent: Traditional Fondue recipe Serves : 4 Preparation time : 1 hour Required : Fondue set Notes : This recipe works equally well with vegan cheeses and alcohol free wine. For a gluten free alternative just use gluten free bread or cooked vegetables. Ingredients : 1 garlic clove, halved 200g Comte cheese 200g Gruyère cheese 200g Emmental cheese 500ml of French Sauvignon Blanc white wine 1 tablespoon cornstarch 1 teaspoon fresh lemon juice 1 1/2 tablespoons Kirsch Freshly ground pepper Freshly grated nutmeg Fresh crusty bread cut into cubes Cornichons Pickled onions Optional sides of roast potatoes, lightly boiled broccoli and cauliflower, charcuterie. Optional Kirsch for dipping bread before it goes in the fondue. Step 1 Prepare and plate up the cornichons, pickled onions and any additional cold sides before you start cooking. This will mean you can give the fondue your full focus, serve it fresh, and have time to keep stirring. Step 2 Rub the garlic around the inside of the fondue pot and then discard. Place the pot on a low heat. Step 3 Add the white wine, lemon juice and Kirsch to the pot. Grate the nutmeg over the pot and add some ground black pepper. Step 4 Grate the Comte, Gruyère and Emmental cheese onto a large plate or chopping board. Step 5 Sieve the cornflour and shake over the grated cheese. This will help ensure there are no lumps and the fondue binds well. Step 6 Keep stirring the liquid in the pot with a wooden spoon and slowly add the grated cheese a small handful at a time. Step 7 Ensure you have a smooth and gooey consistency that is stringy when you raise the spoon. When you feel it’s ready, light a tea light on the table under the pot and serve with your sides.
tagline: We're launching our delicious Fondue recipe with you

title: Chapter 22 – the roots and records store in Bath
subtitle: Your eyes will arrive at Bath’s independent record and houseplant store, Chapter 22, long before you do, when they become transfixed on the stunning display of houseplants that come flowing out of its front door. The colourful cacti and beautiful button ferns brighten up the entirety of Broad Street and entice even the least curious of souls to poke their nose in.
bodyContent: Past the welcoming flora entrance, you will find the local owners, Dean Brown and Nicola Taylor, have a created a spectacle for the senses. Customers are not only treated to the sight of more luscious houseplants but also the crisp sounds of a classic LP playing in the background, and the aromatic smell of fresh coffee too. The unique store is only small but manages to artfully combine both of Dean and Nicolas’ life passions for music and floristry, all whist having room for people to sit down and enjoy a cup of coffee at the back. Dean has run the record label Chapter 22 Records since the 80’s and has helped develop bands like Balaam and the Angel, The Mission, Pop Will Eat Itself, Neds Atomic Dustbin and Dawn After Dark. Meanwhile, Nicola has been a florist for 30 years and her experience certainly shows by her ability to wonderfully arrange the rare and exotic houseplants around the shop. The two opened the store in September of this year after settling on the idea during the lockdown and say they have been overwhelmed with the city’s response. “We’ve only been open 9 weeks, but we’ve been really busy with local people and tourists.” Dean said, when we visited Chapter 22 at the beginning of November. “At a weekend, we have people here at 8.30pm grabbing a drink and listening to some music in the listening booths. It’s really become what we wanted it to be.” The store can be easily found on the left side of Broad Street, if you are walking up the hill, and it’s a great spot for getting someone a special gift, or to simply chill out. There’s full range of house plants on offer from Red Anthuriums to Big Band Zebra Cacti and Senecio ‘String of Pearls’ succulents. The variety of vinyl in Chapter 22 is equally as diverse with Ed Sheeran’s latest album ‘Equals’ being played next Abba’s Gold and the Sex Pistols’ Same Old Ten Inch Bollocks, all of which are available to purchase. Dean said his favourite thing about his shop was the amazing mix of people that come in but for us it had to be the awesome listening booths at the back, where you can set up for some work and listen to anything from Dean’s collection by yourself, using the booth’s personal record player and headphones. It’s a truly masterful use of space and has such a palpable connection to Dean and Nicolas’ wonderful personalities that you’d be foolish not to pop in on your next visit to Bath. You can check out Chapter 22’s website here and follow their social media here .

title: The Old Pound Inn
subtitle: The Old Pound Inn is a traditional village pub in Langport with a reputation for good honest food, drinks and rooms. We offer a family-friendly and dog-friendly service with regular events (quizzes, bingo, markets, live music nights) and special offers. Check out the website for the latest news.
bodyContent: The Old Pound Inn in Aller, Langport is a traditional village pub with a well-earned reputation for good honest food, drinks and rooms. We offer a family-friendly and dog-friendly service with regular events (quizzes, bingo, markets, live music nights) and special offers. Check out the website and/or follow us on Facebook for the latest news. Formerly known as the White Lion Public House, this 16th -century pub was re-christened the Old Pound Inn in 1980, named after the old village animal pound that occupied the site before it became a pub. The Old Pound Inn has a good selection of West Country beers that are pulled from the sprung stillage in our cellar. We have an open Dutch fire at the centre of the bar, a lounge area, a snug, and a 44-cover restaurant serving good honest food daily. We are of course a dog-friendly place - ask your server if they have any dog snacks available!
tagline: The Old Pound Inn is a traditional village pub in Langport

title: Feltham's Farm
subtitle: Feltham’s Farm is 22 acres of organic land in the north of Somerset’s beautiful Blackmore Vale. It is run by Marcus Fergusson and Penny Nagle, who moved here six years ago. There are always people around, as our cheese business employs between two and four people while living on site there are up to four international volunteers at any time. This is a community of people interested in good food, sourced both locally and organically. The farm is great for children – Marcus and Penny have three of
bodyContent: the farm Feltham’s Farm is now certified organic with The Soil Association . We have always farmed using organic principles, so that means no chemicals on the land and no antibiotics or restricted treatments for our animals, which are all free range and fed organic food. We do not use chemicals, pesticides, or GM modified seeds, we try to avoid single use plastics (difficult with PPE these days), and where possible we use biodynamic principles too .. the cheese Our cheese business came about almost by accident, after Marcus was made redundant from a corporate job in London (much to his relief). We wanted to do something on the farm but at 22 acres it was too small to farm conventionally while making enough money to live on. Marcus has always been obsessed with cheese and after a one-day course at River Cottage , there was no turning back. We’re just a few years in to this adventure but we have won numerous awards and the order book keeps getting fatter. In many ways, it seems that this is a mid-life crisis that seems to be panning out OK. the cottage & cheese experience room As well as going through organic conversion, we have been looking closely at the way we use our buildings. Feltham’s Cottage and the Cheese Experience Room will be 100% sustainable, powered by solar panels for electricity and ground source heat pumps for heating and hot water. As with any busy working farm there are sometimes piles of stone in yards, tractors blocking views, and compost that needs moving. However, you can relax safe in the knowledge that everything we and you are doing is sitting lightly on the planet. Please do help us recycle where possible. Our two double-bedroomed cottage is modern, warm and cosy, with Wi-Fi, a wood burning stove (fire wood is provided free), local produce in a hamper, and crisp white sheets. The Cheese Experience Room will be completed by July 2021 and is directly opposite the cottage, with underfloor heating, a wet room and sunny porch. It will have a table-tennis table, table football and more – as well as offering an additional kitchen/eating area and rooms.
tagline: Feltham’s Farm is 22 acres of organic land in the north of Somerset’s beautiful Blackmore Vale.

title: Giant Tortoise Encounter at Noah's Ark Zoo Farm
subtitle: Spend 20 minutes behind the scenes with the keepers and the Giant Tortoises, learning about their personalities! This is your chance to feed a giant and find out about how they live in the wild. You can even get the chance to give them a scratch! Encounters are at 2.30pm daily and must be prebooked.

title: Barrington Court, National Trust
subtitle: Barrington Court, located in the stunning south Somerset countryside, is a charming Tudor manor house complimented beautifully with Gertrude Jekyll-inspired gardens, apple orchards and a working kitchen garden.
bodyContent: Barrington Court Somerset National Trust - Discover the haunting echoes of the past at Barrington Court, a Tudor manor house free from collections and furniture. Explore using your imagination and your senses to discover a house full of memories, where light fills the rooms and you feel you can almost touch the past. The property was saved from ruin and restored by the Lyle family in 1920s, when the Court House resembled a barn rather than the proud manor house that it is. Close your eyes and you’ll almost be able to hear the sounds and see the sights of the glamorous parties held in the great hall during Barrington’s heyday. On the first floor listen out for the voices resonating from the past, of the young evacuees who called Barrington home during the Second World War. Stroll through the Gertrude Jekyll inspired gardens, which with their focus on plant varieties and colours are a delight for all the senses. Be spurred on in your own garden or allotment by the stone-walled kitchen garden that produces a variety of delicious fruit and vegetables. Don’t just take our word for it, why not stop off in the Strode House Restaurant to taste these home-grown delights. Barrington Court predominantly featured in BBC’s highly acclaimed recent production of Hilary Mantel’s Wolf Hall.
tagline: Barrington Court, located in the stunning south Somerset countryside.

title: Fleet Air Arm Museum
subtitle: The all-weather attraction is the perfect place for all the family. With immersive experiences like the Search and Rescue Sea King Helicopter walk through and a walkthrough of the iconic Concorde 002.
bodyContent: This year make sure to set your sights on the Fleet Air Arm Museum in Ilchester and see where time flies. This must-see attraction has four large exhibition halls each containing dozens of incredible aircraft which tell the rich history of naval aviation. Grab your wingman and step inside the first British Concorde, experience the thrills of a working flight deck, and get up close to a wide range of rare and historical aircraft.
tagline: The all-weather attraction is the perfect place for all the family.

title: The Hollies
subtitle: The Hollies was built in 1851 in a meadow beside the old Bath – Wells turnpike.
bodyContent: The Hollies was built in 1851 in a meadow beside the old Bath – Wells turnpike. This was also the Fosse Way, built by the Roman Legions some 2000 years ago. The house, with its late Georgian facade, was once the home of the curate of St. Lukes Church, which is next door. It is now a gracious guest house with three individually designed rooms overlooking the award-winning garden. Every room has its own bath or shower room and is complete with television, radio alarm clock, hairdryer, bath robes and tea and coffee tray. Our comfortable Library with over 2000 books is available for guests.
tagline: The Hollies was built in 1851 in a meadow beside the old Bath – Wells turnpike.

title: Three Abbey Green
subtitle: A Grade II listed city centre Georgian building, parts of which date back to 1689, Three Abbey Green (including the Jane Austen Wing next door) is a Four Star Gold Award bed and breakfast.
bodyContent: A Grade II listed city centre Georgian building, parts of which date back to 1689, Three Abbey Green (including the Jane Austen Wing next door) is a Four Star Gold Award bed and breakfast, hidden away in a quiet cobbled square in the heart of central Bath. A stone’s throw from Bath Abbey and the Roman Baths, everything you could wish to see is on your doorstep. We think Three Abbey Green is one of the most beautiful buildings in Bath, a city overflowing with Georgian grandeur and astonishing architecture. We never cease to be excited about running our family business in Abbey Green. It is rare to find such a beautiful, almost pedestrian-only square in the heart of a city. It should be remembered, however, that we are in the centre of a vibrant city and pedestrians are not always as quiet as we might like them to be! The main house has seven rooms (including two large suites ideal for families or groups) and the associated Jane Austen Wing in Four Abbey Green, adjacent to the main house, has three rooms, each with its own character and unique charm. Three Abbey Green is a family business started in 2002 by Derek and Sue. From the beginning, the ethos of the business has always been to provide the highest standard of accommodation combined with excellent customer service, reflecting our own expectations. Nici took over the reins in 2010 with her husband Alan. They also have a child, Finlay, and a dog called Bear, but they still aim to balance provision of excellent service with a normal, busy family life. It is a point of pride for us to maintain our high standards without compromising the personal touch that brings guests back to stay with us again and again.
tagline: A Grade II listed city centre Georgian building, parts of which date back to 1689

title: Horseshoe Cottage, Lime Kiln Farm
subtitle: Horseshoe is the largest of our three beautiful luxury self catering holiday cottages set in stunning Somerset countryside just 15 minutes drive from Bath.
bodyContent: Horseshoe is the largest of our three beautiful luxury self catering holiday cottages set in stunning Somerset countryside just 15 minutes drive from Bath. The views are wonderful and there is a large private garden, perfect for family parties or BBQs. This converted stable building has two large ensuite bedrooms, sleeping up to 6 and is renovated to a very high standard, complete with all modern conveniences including free WIFI . The cottage is all on one level and suitable for wheelchair users. With easy access to the Bath Park & Ride, we are also perfectly located for exploring the many tourist attractions including local pubs and Lavender Farm, Cheddar Gorge, Wookey Hole Caves, Wells, Stourhead House & Gardens and the nearby Longleat Safari Park.
tagline: Horseshoe is the largest of our three beautiful luxury self catering holiday cottages

title: Spacious Double Room in West Bath
subtitle: Spacious Double bedroom in Victorian terraced house to the west of the city of Bath.
bodyContent: Property has good transport links to city centre, as well as being close to all local amenities you should need for a pleasant stay with us. The house is situated to the west side of the beautiful city of Bath. Furnished with a mix of modern and vintage furniture, the property has all you need for a relaxing stay. There are good transport links to the town centre, with services stopping less than two minutes from us. There is also ample free street parking outside our door. The breakfast room/lounge has a very homely feel and contains books, games and suggestions on where to go in Bath. Guests also have use of our ultra fast fibre broadband. We’ve equipped the kitchen to make cooking easy with a host of ingredients and basic utensils. You’ll have your own private double bedroom with large comfortable double bed and ample storage space. You can also benefit from shared use of the modern and well equipped kitchen, comfortable living room and bathroom. I like to give guests their own space during their stay, however I am always available to offer recommendations and help, both before and during their stay. I am never far away or am in the house, and am always on hand should you need me. I usually arrange for a self check in but can always be on hand if a guest would like me to help them check in. We are a five minute walk from the high street where you’ll find a supermarket, takeaways and a few local shops. There are a number of good pubs and bars in the area all walking distance from us. Alternatively, its less than ten minutes into town by taxi and shouldn’t cost you more than £6-£7. The property is less than two minutes from the bus stop where you can catch regular services into the town centre. There is plenty of on street parking outside the house. We are about ten to fifteen minutes walk from Oldfield Park train station where you can access services to London and Bristol. Check-In: 3PM-9PM Not suitable for children (2-12 years) Not suitable for infants (under 2 years) Not suitable for pets No smoking No parties or events
tagline: Spacious Double bedroom in Victorian terraced house to the west of the city of Bath.

bodyContent: This detached barn is 3/4 of a mile from Church Farm along a country lane. It has its own landscaped garden and private driveway with plenty of parking. title: Brocks Guest House
subtitle: Come and stay in our elegant Georgian home built by John Wood the younger in 1765. Ideally situated in our unique location between the World heritage Royal Crescent and The Circus.
bodyContent: ⭐ Book Direct for Reward Card Offers Come and stay in our elegant Georgian home built by John Wood the younger in 1765. Ideally situated in our unique location between the World heritage Royal Crescent and The Circus. We are just a gentle walk from the centre of this beautiful Heritage City. All rooms have Freeview Television, Hair Dryers, Radio Alarm Clocks and Refreshment Tray. A free car parking permit is available as is complementary Wi-Fi in all rooms. Brocks Guest House has been awarded Four Stars in connection with AA Quality Standards. The summary report received from the AA Hotel Services Inspector stated the following: “Brocks has much to commend, not least attentively maintained accommodation. Bedrooms offer a good level of comfort, lighting in rooms is very effective with good ceiling and task lighting. When assessed for a grading under the new AA Quality Standards for Guest Accommodation, Brocks achieves Four Stars with a recommended Guest Accommodation designator”.

title: Bath View Four Apartment
subtitle: Two luxury apartments situated in the residential, conservation area of Oldfield Park.
bodyContent: Two luxury apartments situated in the residential, conservation area of Oldfield Park, just 10 minutes walk from Bath city centre. Bath View Two sleeps 2 people . Bath View Four sleeps 5 people. Both apartments are decorated in a modern style with high quality fixtures and fittings. Both are equipped in full for a self catering break. There are amazing views over the whole of Bath from Bath View Four. Parking and WIFI are free. This apartment has two bedrooms, two bathrooms and a spacious lounge with lots of seating and amazing views over the city of Bath. There is a fully fitted kitchen with dining table seating 6. Local Bars, restaurants, shops are just 5 minutes walk away. Bath’s many interesting tourist sites such as The Roman Baths and Thermae Bath Spa are within a 10-15 minute walk. Bath Spa Train Station and Coach station are just 10 minutes walk.
tagline: Two luxury apartments situated in the residential, conservation area of Oldfield Park.

title: Bath Townhouse 8
subtitle: Bath Townhouse is a beautiful Georgian townhouse situated in the centre of Bath.
bodyContent: This townhouse is split in to two apartments; Bath Townhouse 14 and Bath Townhouse 8. They can be combined to sleep 23 or rented separately. This is a perfect location for groups of all kinds: mixed, female, male, families, wedding groups and corporate groups. The property has been lovingly restored and decorated to the highest standards in a modern vintage style which makes the most of the many original features, including the cornicing, Georgian fireplaces, original shutters , beautifully restored Georgian windows and original vault area. Both apartments are fully equipped for a self catering holiday break, with fully fitted kitchens, wide screen TVS, free WIFI and top quality bedding and towels. Bath Townhouse 8 has 3 spacious bedrooms, 3 beautifully presented wet rooms/bathrooms, a comfortable lounge with modular, colourful seating, modern lighting, fully fitted kitchen with table and chairs for 9 people. The lower ground floor has a additional entertainment area in the vaults, a great area if the ‘kids’ want their own space! Bars, restaurants, shops, and all Bath’s many interesting tourist sites are right outside the front door! The Roman Baths and Thermae Bath Spa are just a stones throw away. Bath Spa Train Station and Coach station are 5 minutes walk. Whether you are in Bath to watch Bath Rugby play at home at the famous Recreation Ground, visit your son or daughter at Bath University, have a little retail therapy in the great independent shops or enjoy the many festivals that take place in Bath then this is the perfect property for you and your group!
tagline: Bath Townhouse is a beautiful Georgian townhouse

Bath Townhouse 8 has 3 spacious bedrooms, 3 beautifully presented wet rooms/bathrooms, a comfortable lounge with modular, colourful seating, modern lighting, fully fitted kitchen with table and chairs for 9 people. The lower ground floor has a additional entertainment area in the vaults, a great area if the ‘kids’ want their own space! Bars, restaurants, shops, and all Bath’s many interesting tourist sites are right outside the front door! The Roman Baths and Thermae Bath Spa are just a stones throw away. Bath Spa Train Station and Coach station are 5 minutes walk. Whether you are in Bath to watch Bath Rugby play at home at the famous Recreation Ground, visit your son or daughter at Bath University, have a little retail therapy in the great independent shops or enjoy the many festivals that take place in Bath then this is the perfect property for you and your group!

title: The Salt Path
subtitle: Locations: Minehead, Porlock Weir, Culvercliffe, North Hill, Bossington Hill. Release date: May 2025
bodyContent: The big screen adaptation of the best-selling book by Raynor Winn introduced the South West Coast Path to a new global audience. Starring Gillan Anderson (Raynor Winn) and Jason Issacs (Moth Winn), it charts the couple’s healing walk along the 630-mile path from Minehead to Poole Harbour in Dorset. Shot in the summer of 2023, although Somerset has only 35 miles of the path, the county gets more than its fair share of screen time as Raynor and Moth set off on their epic journey. Despite the controversary that followed, the film is a wonderful advert for the stunning Somerset coast and Exmoor. Several scenes were filmed in Minehead, notably along Quay Street at the landmark ‘hands and map’ sculpture that marks the beginning of the path, with the easily identifiable Butlin’s building in the distance. Culvercliffe Walk , North Hill and Bossington Hill all feature, and then Porlock Marsh and finally Porlock Weir , where Raynor and Moth eat at a café before heading into Devon. Every year around 9 million people use the South West Coast Path, many of them starting their journey in Minehead. There are options for exploring parts of the route by bus, and the West Somerset Railway means you can arrive in Minehead via a 20-mile heritage train ride through stunning Somerset countryside. title: Coates English Willow
subtitle: Discover an enormous range of willow baskets made by our team of skilled craftsmen and women using our own home-grown willow.
bodyContent: Discover authentic Somerset craftsmanship at Coates English Willow's unique Willow Basket shop, home to an enormous range of baskets handmade by skilled craftsmen and women using home-grown willow. From practical everyday designs to decorative treasures, find the perfect gift or souvenir while supporting this traditional industry. Can't find what you need? Our bespoke service creates tailor-made baskets, log baskets and willow hurdles to your exact specifications. Budding basket-makers will find willow, tools and books to get started, plus seasonal living willow kits for garden features. Explore the Basket Museum's rare willow artefacts dating from 1850, watch our film on willow cultivation and Coates Artists' Charcoal production, or enjoy a Willow Walk with three routes, including a popular Sculpture Trail for children with a free prize on completion. Shop online anytime, and prebook tours via our website.

title: Ancient Pathways uncovering 2000 years of lead mines
subtitle: Somerset Fascinating Facts Here are a number of fascinating historical walks around the remote Hamlet of Charterhouse, which has been the site of lead mining for over 2000 years
customFields:
[{"key":"NewsID","value":"239"},{"key":"NewsBody","value":"







In Charterhouse Somerset mining took place during the late Iron Age but it was the Romans who began serious extraction of the lead in AD 49. In the 17th and 18th centuries miners from Cornwall tried to exploit the ore they thought lay further underground but soon discovered the lead petered out as they delved deeper.

However, they found they could profitably re- smelt the slag left behind by the Romans and thus an industry was born. 

The remains of this operation can be discovered on the Velvet Bottom track walk where the black glassy slag and flues still remain.  

This long history of lead mining has created many valuable wildlife habitats, including rare plants that flourish in the toxic heavy metals of lead, zinc and cadmium.

For more on Somerset's incredible history and heritage go to our interactive E Book.

title: North Petherton
subtitle: Before it became a town, North Petherton was the largest village in England. It was an important settlement as far back as Saxon times and archaeologists have found plenty to interest them on the site of the current church, St Mary The Virgin, which has one of the tallest, most elaborate towers in the region.
bodyContent: North Petherton has a number of claims to fame including the fact that the poet and civil servant Geoffrey Chaucer was Deputy Forester at the royal estate of Petherton Park. A chance ‘find’ nearby centuries later brought the town more fame as it turned out to be one of the most important this country has unearthed. It was the Alfred Jewel – now in the Ashmolean Museum – which is thought to be the top of a ninth century pointing stick for reading, a skill King Alfred was keen to promote. Built in 1827, the Bridgwater and Taunton Canal runs through the Parish and offers tranquil walks along the tow path with a chance to see kingfishers, dragonfly and planets! The planets are part of a sculpture trail of the solar system graphically indicating the distance between them and the sun. Maunsel Lock Canal Centre and Tea Shop offers local food and boat trips. North Petherton is on the Macmillan Way West long distance footpath and close to North Moor, a nationally important grazing marsh and ditch system on the Somerset Levels and Moors .

title: Nunney
subtitle: Nunney is a beautiful village with much of historic interest.
bodyContent: Nunney is a beautiful village with much of historic interest. The centrepiece is the ruin of medieval Nunney Castle, inspired by French castles seen by Sir John de la Mare on campaign. The walls are largely intact and it is in perfect scale with its surroundings. A Village Trail, available from Frome Tourist Information, is the best way to explore the points of interest including the parish church and the George, an old character coaching inn. Once a year on the first Saturday in August the village streets are turned over to stalls of all kinds for a good old fashioned Street Fayre.
