title: The Apartment, Bath
subtitle: An exceptional two-bedroom luxury holiday home in central Bath, loved by guests for its perfect location, stylish decor, comfort, cleanliness and first class self-catering accommodation.
bodyContent: From Nespresso to Nintendo, The Apartment, Bath is an excellently-located two-bedroom apartment in central Bath. The first bedroom is a large, bright double bedroom with king size bed (or twin beds on request). The open fireplace and large sash windows are elegant original features and south-facing views take in the length of Ralph Allen Drive and Widcombe Hill. At the rear of the property, the second bedroom is a well-proportioned double bedroom, featuring a comfy double bed, original fireplace and built in wardrobe. The homely lounge is flooded with light from the large, original south-facing 16-pane sash window. The room hosts an extendable dining table and chairs, designer sofa (which can convert to a sofa bed) and a feature armchair. Brimming with technology, the lounge is equipped with satellite TV, blu-ray player, Nintendo Wii and wall-mounted 40” Samsung LCD TV. A well-equipped and cleverly designed galley kitchen features high-end integrated appliances to meet your every need, including a built-in double oven and sleek induction hob, full suite of cooking facilities and an integrated NEFF fridge with ice-box. A Nespresso machine and milk frother are provided for that much needed espresso or cappuccino to kick-start your day. And there is a washer dryer, so you can pack a little lighter! The newly renovated bathroom features a large walk-in rain shower with separate handheld spray. A chrome towel rail is complemented by a lit, motion-activated mirror cabinet featuring de-mist function and integrated razor/electric toothbrush socket. This gorgeous two-bedroom holiday home in central Bath is ranked in the ‘10 Best Holiday Homes in Bath’ by Booking.com and consistently rated positively by guests.
tagline: An exceptional two-bedroom luxury holiday home in central Bath

title: Caroline Quentin - Drawn to Nature
subtitle: Join Caroline Quentin as she celebrates Drawn to Nature, an uplifting exploration of the restorative power of the natural world. Through personal stories and reflections, she shares the people, places and gardens that have shaped her lifelong love of nature.

title: Priston
subtitle: Priston is a small village just five miles south of Bath, enveloped by fields which are vibrant with yellow rapeseed flowers in spring and golden with ripening crops in summer.
bodyContent: Priston is a small village just five miles south of Bath , enveloped by fields which are vibrant with yellow rapeseed flowers in spring and golden with ripening crops in summer. The traditional and friendly Ring o’Bells pub in the centre of the village is a meeting place for locals and visitors alike and serves interesting, quality food and drink. The rural 12th century church, topped with a golden cockerel, is worth a visit and this could be incorporated into a walk along one of the many public footpaths that that pass through Priston. These are clearly marked on an OS map of the area. Priston holds a traditional May Day fete on the first May Bank Holiday each year. This celebration of spring sees children dancing round the Maypole, musical entertainment, family games, food stalls and the famous egg-throwing competition. A popular music festival, now in its 11th year takes place in September and features music for various tastes, an art project and food stalls. The community café, run by volunteers, is open each Saturday morning in the village hall, serving tea, coffee, bacon butties and home-made cakes. A number of houses offer bed and breakfast in Priston for anyone looking for a rural idyll within close reach of Bath. Please see www.priston.org.uk for dates and times for all of the above and for more information about accommodation.

title: Dunster
subtitle: There are delights at every turn in Dunster, whether it be the castle on the hill with its magnificent stables or the packhorse bridge and working watermill. It is hardly surprising that in one of the most intact medieval villages in Britain there is so much to explore and hidden gems around every corner such as the Prior’s Dovecote, Tithe Barn and a church containing the longest Rood screen in the country. Set amid lush rolling fields that slope towards the sea, Dunster boasts picture-perfect h
bodyContent: Things to do in Dunster, Somerset. Dunster’s beautiful medieval village, in Somerset is incredibly preserved, with a rich history, hundreds of stunning listed buildings and dramatic views. The National Trust’s Dunster Castle proudly sits in the sweeping hills of nearby Exmoor National Park , where you’ll catch incredible views stretching over Exmoor and the Bristol Channel. This ancient feudal stronghold was developed into an opulent country home for the Luttrell family in the 19th century, and the castle grounds include the thoughtfully-designed subtropical gardens and the fully-restored Dunster Working Watermill , which sits alongside the River Avill. The castle overlooks the village below, where there’s a plethora of tea rooms, local gift shops, excellent restaurants and places to stay. On the high street you’ll find the 17th-century Yarn Market, which was essential for the village’s production and trade of wool and cloth. A short walk from the high street is the idyllic Gallox Bridge, originally used by packhorses to transport goods to the market. Nearby you’ll find the Grade II listed Dovecote, a nesting house for domestic pigeons. This ancient monument was a relic from the Benedictine Dunster Priory along with the Tithe Barn and the Priory Church of St George. One of the most atmospheric ways to experience the medieval village is at the Dunster by Candlelight Festival. Taking place on the first Friday and Saturday of December, lanterns are lit throughout the village replacing the electric street lamps whilst the cobbled streets come alive with choirs, bell ringers and street entertainers. Dunster beach is the perfect spot for a picnic and, much like the rest of the surrounding area, it remains totally unspoilt and natural. Admire the beach and village from the many different walking routes, or take in the Somerset countryside and coast as you ride on the West Somerset Railway , England’s longest heritage line, which leaves from the station just outside Dunster village.

title: Noah’s Ark Zoo Farm
subtitle: Noah’s Ark Zoo Farm is a conservation charity and the largest zoo in Somerset with over 100 species of animals. The multi award winning Zoo is open 7 days a week and aims to make Noah's Ark a place of joy, wonder, adventure and refreshment that supports the well-being of all visitors, staff and volunteers. Through education and fun, they aim to inspire and motivate this generation and the next to consider sustainable lifestyles and care for our planet.
bodyContent: Amazing Animals The home of the big Zoo animals! Visit Noah’s Ark and come face to face with a cheeky mob of meerkats, be awed by African elephants and dazzled by the zebra herd! Experience the majestic beauty and see the skies come alive during the daily birds of prey displays! The Wings of Wonder display showcases the owls, hawks, falcons and eagles in an unforgettably mesmerizing spectacle. Indoor and Outdoor Adventures Play and adventure never stops with our 10 play areas across the 100-acre site. Enjoy the huge indoor play barns including under 5’s soft play and a giant rainbow slide. The Zoo also has accessible play equipment including nest swings and a wheelchair accessible roundabout. Fancy an a-maze-ing adventure? Navigate through Britain’s longest hedge maze. The British wildlife themed maze has 3.4km of paths and wooden nest tower at the center. Keep the whole family smiling and active all day, whatever the weather! Accessibility Noah’s Ark Zoo Farm is proud to be an accessible attraction. Facilities include multiple accessible toilets, Changing Places facility, accessible play equipment, hearing loops and more. Please visit the website before your visit for up-to-date information and to view the Access guide. Prices Buy online and save! Noah’s Ark recommends that all tickets, including those for free essential carers and under 2’s are purchased online prior to your arrival. Prices are seasonal, please check the website for up-to-date ticket prices. Food and Drink With a range of delicious hot and cold food and drink options available in our Food Barn and convenient snack kiosks across the Zoo, there is something for everyone! Alternatively, visitors are very welcome to bring their own lunch and enjoy it in one of our many picnic spots. Mini Experiences Noah’s Ark offers incredible up-close mini experiences with Meerkats, Capybara, Andean Bears and Giant Tortoise. You will enjoy 20 minutes behind the scenes with the keeper, learn some interesting facts and get involved with their feeding and enrichment programme. Pre-book your experience online to ensure availability. Minimum age and terms and conditions apply. Animal Experiences Find out what it’s like to be a keeper for the day with our one-to-one keeper experiences before the zoo opens. Experiences include: African Elephants, Junior Keeper Experience, and Giraffe and Rhino experience.
tagline: You’ll be amazed at the variety of nature you’ll see with over 100 species of animals

title: Somerset Lavender
subtitle: Enjoy our family-run lavender farm, with spectacular views and wonderful gardens. Stop off for home made refreshments and shop for fragrant lavender products made with our own produce.
bodyContent: This family-run working lavender farm offers its visitors spectacular views across its lavender fields in a quiet and relaxing environment. Visitors are invited to stroll around the garden and take in the soothing scent of lavender or to sit and admire the scenery from the rose arbour. If you are interested in growing some lavender bushes of your own there is a selection of varieties on display in the lavender garden, indicating some of the differences in size and colour that are on offer when you consider your options. Plants are available for purchase and practical advice is on hand to help you with the care and maintenance of your lavender plant. For those interested in the farming element, tours of the distillery are run during the harvest where you can view the machinery and learn about how we plant, harvest and distil the lavender for the essential oil. Keep an eye on our website for updates on the times and dates of the harvest tours. Our willow run will entertain younger visitors and there is also a farm shop stocking lavender products and gifts as well as a small café serving tea, cake and light lunches. Key Features Specalist Farm Shop offering lavender products grown and made on the farm Cafe serving home made cake and light lunches Plant nursery with a wide range of name lavender plants Lavender Garden Healing Garden Flower and Vegetable Garden Lavender Fields Specialist Features In the cafe you can try Lavender tea, Lavender cake and shortbread. Fresh Herb Teas Travel and Trade Groups must book ahead

title: ⭐Shepton Mallet Prison
subtitle: Built in 1610 following on Act introduced by King James I, which stated that all counties had to have their own ‘House of Correction’; Shepton Mallet was the oldest working prison in the United Kingdom...
bodyContent: ⭐ Reward Card Discount Available Built in 1610 following on Act introduced by King James I, which stated that all counties had to have their own ‘House of Correction’, Shepton Mallet was the oldest working prison in the United Kingdom. Shepton Mallet Prison is a recently decommissioned (2013) Georgian jail where visitors can walk in the footsteps of our social history and hear officers shine a light on what life was like for both the incarcerated and those who guarded them through the ages. Before its closure, it was a category C lifer prison holding 189 prisoners. Opened in 1646, it was expanded in 1790, with further building work undertaken in the 1820s and 1830s, including the installation of a treadwheel for those sentenced to hard labour. In 1930, the inmate numbers fell and the prison was closed. During the Second World War, the prison was reopened and used as a military prison. It was initially used by the British Army and later by American forces, who constructed a new execution block for condemned prisoners. It was also used for the storage of important historical documents, including the Domesday Book. It returned to civilian use in 1966. Shepton Mallet prison is also known for its tales of paranormal activity. One of the most popular stories is that of the White Lady. She is frequently seen or sensed in various locations, especially A Wing. Staff and prisoners would often complain of an icy wind moving through the wing, the sweet smell of perfume and shadowy figures. She supposedly dates from the late 1700s, when she spent some time in the prison. During a lovers' tiff which escalated, she murdered her betrothed. Once found guilty and sentenced to death, she was housed in Shepton Mallet Prison. On the evening before her execution, she asked for her wedding dress to be brought to the prison, which they allowed. She wore it to bed that night, but in the morning the officers found that she had died during the night. No cause of death was ever found, so we are left to presume that she died of a broken heart. Perhaps this is why she still haunts the prison? In the early 1950s, the Kray Twins were also held here after deserting the British Army. Today, the prison is open as a tourist attraction offering Guided Tours, Self-Guided Tours, Escape Rooms, Night Behind Bars and Ghost Hunting Behind Bars. This is an immersive experience without gizmos or gimmicks – the jail is very much as it was when the last prisoners left in 2013. In 2025, Shepton Mallet Prison received the prestigious Trip Advisor Travellers’ Choice, for the 7th time running, placing it among the top 10% of attractions worldwide.

subtitle: Country cafe tea room near Wedmore & Glastonbury & Street, Somerset
bodyContent: A wonderfully deceptive yard leads you to one of Somerset's best kept secrets. Generous traditional food from pies to the best cakes & cream teas with a very warm welcome. Proper Somerset fayre that you won't find for miles around. Using quality local suppliers this is a little hideaway not to be missed. We are a regular cycling stop cafe and approved by the British Horse Society. In the Winter alongside the cosy cafe there is a woodburner in the cabin area. Perfect for dogs, walkers and cyclists. This is also the home of the Peat & Science Museum, a lifetime family collection of working the levels including WW1 bomber parts! title: The Royal Hotel Weston
subtitle: Weddings in an amazing venue on Weston's sea front.
bodyContent: Weddings As Weston’s Premier Hotel we hold a Civil Wedding and Civil Partnership Licence, enabling you to simplify the arrangements by holding all aspects of your special day in one venue. The Birnbeck Suite with its stunning bay windows boasts superb views of our extensive lawns, the Welsh Coast and Weston Bay. Our Wedding Coordinator will guide you discreetly through your day as Master of Ceremonies, to ensure your Wedding is as special as every Bride and Groom deserves creating those perfect memories for you, the Wedding Party and your Guests. You will be greeted with a Red Carpet Arrival and personal welcome from our Wedding Coordinator or a member of Senior Management. Once your photographs are completed, you and your guests may enjoy an arrival drink. After which the Bride and Groom will be invited to receive their guests prior to the Wedding Breakfast. Please contact our In House Wedding Coordinator or our Reception Team to arrange an appointment where all your requirements can be discussed. Here at the Royal Hotel we understand no Wedding Day is identical therefore, we endeavour to tailor your special day to your individual requirements. You can request our wedding brochure HERE . Conferences The Royal Hotel is able to offer a range of conference room facilities, The Birnbeck Suite, recently refurbished, is the hotels largest function room, with its extensive bay windows overlooking Weston bay and our lawn, it offers natural light and boasts spectacular views. It has the capacity to hold up to 200 delegates for your conference and catering requirements, (subject to room set up). The Regent Room, an Edwardian style conference room, Most suited for smaller meetings, interviews and training can hold up to six delegates (Boardroom Style).

title: Thatchers Cider
subtitle: For more than a hundred years, family-run Thatchers Cider has been quietly perfecting the magic that turns apples into cider.
bodyContent: For more than a hundred years, family-run Thatchers Cider has been quietly perfecting the magic that turns apples into cider. Here at Myrtle Farm in Sandford, each generation has passed on cider-making secrets, like encouraging bees to pollinate the apple blossom, or looking after the 150 year old oak vats where the cider matures. We lovingly craft a range of ciders but whichever you choose, they have all been made with the same care and attention, and with the same hands-on experience – we wouldn’t have it any other way. Nestled at the foot of the Mendip Hills , the Thatchers orchards are our pride and joy. With apples such as Dabinett, Somerset Redstreak and Porters Perfection, as well as some newer varieties such as Angela, Lizzie and Prince William, it’s here that the journey starts, inspired by the heritage and values of our company. Our flagship brand Thatchers Gold is a full flavoured, medium dry Somerset cider, with a wonderfully rich, golden colour. Thatchers Vintage is well balanced and mature, with a distinctive depth of character, while Thatchers Haze is a premium cloudy cider that has a crisp, sweet finish. We have recently introduced a new cider to our range, the gloriously pink Rosé, bursting with fruity apple flavours. Our other ciders include Thatchers Katy, Old Rascal and Green Goblin, together with our Stan’s Range of traditional ciders, such as Cheddar Valley, Trad. and Big Apple. Available on line and in our Cider Shop, Finally, holding down the fort at home, we have our award-winning Cider Barn range that’s exclusive to Myrtle Farm.that includes very special ciders such as Thatchers 458, Vilberie and Redstreak. You can buy all our ciders online at www.thatcherscider.co.uk Or visit our Cider Shop at Myrtle Farm. Here the shelves are packed with our ciders, alongside produce such as local cheeses and chutneys, and gifts including books and clothing. Our draught ciders are available straight from the barrel, so you can try before you buy. Why not book onto a tour of Myrtle Farm and see how we make our ciders. Visit www.thatcherscider.co.uk/visitus for more information. To book a tour of Myrtle Farm, please visit www.thatcherscider.co.uk
tagline: For more than a hundred years, family-run Thatchers Cider has been quietly perfecting cider.

title: Ferne Animal Sanctuary
subtitle: Ferne Animal Sanctuary is set within 72 acres of beautiful & protected countryside in the Blackdown Hills on the Devon/Somerset border. This charitable sanctuary takes in unwanted, abandoned and neglected animals and gives them a fantastic life either at the sanctuary or by finding them a special forever home.
bodyContent: Ferne Animal Sanctuary is set within 72 acres of beautiful & protected countryside in the Blackdown Hills on the Devon/Somerset border. This charitable sanctuary takes in unwanted, abandoned and neglected animals and gives them a fantastic life either at the sanctuary or by finding them a special forever home. Ferne Animal Sanctuary, located near Chard in Somerset, is a remarkable facility dedicated to the rehoming of dogs, cats, and horses. In addition to this, the sanctuary provides ongoing care and welfare for a wide variety of animals, including sheep, goats, cattle, pigs, geese, chickens, and an aviary housing birds from around the world. It is also home to smaller animals such as rabbits, guinea pigs, chinchillas and ferrets, ensuring they all receive the care and attention they need. Founded in 1939, at the onset of World War II, the charity was established to care for pets whose owners were going to war, or who had been displaced by the conflict. Over the years, it has forged strong connections with HM Armed Forces and the Royal Family. A typical visit to Ferne lasts between 90 to 150 minutes, during which visitors can enjoy observing the animals in their natural habitats. The experience includes a sensory garden designed to calm the senses with a variety of sounds, sights and smells. Visitors can explore the Willow Walk, which offers insights into animal care, as well as informative displays about our water voles, dragonflies, birds, and fungi. There's also a machinery wall showcasing equipment used throughout the years, along with a small play area for our younger visitors. Take the time to enjoy the stunning natural landscape of the Blackdown Hills from our viewing platform. Relax, gaze across the hills, and marvel at the beauty of nature at its finest. During the school holidays, Creative Corner offers a range of animal-themed activities and arts and crafts. We also host special events and workshops throughout the year, with full details available on our website. The Visitor Centre is open from 10 AM to 4 PM from Easter to October half term, though the shop and sanctuary are open every day, except Christmas Day, Boxing Day, and New Year's Day. Our well-stocked pet supplies and gift shop has everything you need for your animals, as well as delightful treats to tempt you. Dog friendly (dogs must be kept on leads) and accessible, Ferne has a good network of tarmac paths. However, due to the number of gates, we recommend that wheelchair users are accompanied. We have designated parking spaces for wheelchair users and visitors with special needs next to our Visitor Centre as well as in the main car park. All money raised goes to support our animal care and welfare. Unleash the Party Fun at Ferne Animal Sanctuary! title: Wellington Monument
subtitle: A striking landmark recently restored, on the edge of the Blackdown Hills.
bodyContent: The Wellington Monument stands as a tribute to the Duke of Wellington and his victory at the Battle of Waterloo. Its prominent location on top of Wellington Hill, on the edge of the Blackdown Hills, has led it to become a symbolic marker on a journey within the local area and to the wider South West. In contrast to other memorials to the Duke, the Wellington Monument has a more informal countryside setting. It can be approached along a path lined with beech hedgerows and is surrounded by a wildlife rich meadow. This is an ideal place for a picnic or to fly a kite. A one mile walk taking in the surrounding area is a rewarding way to see the beautiful Blackdown views. Standing high on the Blackdown Hills, the Wellington Monument, at 175ft, is the tallest three-sided obelisk in the world. An ambitious construction, it commemorates a modern yet classical hero. The story of its origins, and shambolic construction, repeats itself in the story of its conservation and repair up to the present day. The £3.1m project to repair Wellington Monument has now finished, thank you to everyone who supported the project. Find out more about the journey to repair the worlds tallest three-sided obelisk here. How to get there by road Exit M5 at J26 and follow the signs for Wellington. At the roundabout take the first exit onto A38. After approx 1 mile (3.2km) turn left onto Monument Road. Follow this road and at the top of a steep hill you'll come to a crossroads, turn right. Entrance to the car park is approx 218yds (200m) on the right. Facilities and access Our Wellington Monument car park is open from 13 May. Please follow social distancing measures The Monument is around 500m from the car park There are no toilet facilities on site. The nearest accessible Changing Places toilet is at the Iron Duke pub, Wellington, less than 3 miles from the Monument.
tagline: A nature reserve and visitor centre under the guardianship of the National Trust

title: TEALS
subtitle: TEALS is a brand new eco farm store offering locals - as well as holiday makers - a surprising and very special destination to stop off at. It comprises a colourful food market, bakery, bottle shop and gift store and is set next to a spacious apple orchard.
bodyContent: Stop for lunch, a coffee break and to stretch the legs, or to stock up on fresh and tasty groceries. Remaining loyal to local and celebrating the region’s best producers, TEALS is packed with sustainably sourced products from fantastic local suppliers. Discover fresh meats from nearby hills and locally churned cheeses, delicately flavoured gelato and locally ground coffee. A bakery and bottle store sell wine and local cider, while the healthy kitchen serves up tasty and nutritious plates from across the region. There’s also a nature-inspired kids play area and a gift store. With a strong sustainability ethos and powered by renewable energy, TEALS is an agricultural build on a greenfield site. It uses reclaimed timber, minimises waste and trees were planted to help offset the build - it is also pending B Corp status. It’s the mission of local co-founders Ash and Nick Sinfield to make a positive contribution to the region, connecting communities to producers, as well as travellers to the area. Situated halfway between London and Cornwall - at the North/South Cadbury junction - TEALS is the ideal stop off for those travelling between the two regions, as well as the local community. With eight electric car charging points, TEALS is the first low plastic, fuel-free services on the A303. Bringing life, vibrancy and a welcoming atmosphere, as well as original experiences, TEALS promises to enrich each journey with a powerful sense of local.
tagline: TEALS is a brand new eco farm store for locals - as well as holiday makers

title: West Somerset Railway, The Gauge Museum
subtitle: The Gauge Museum can be found at Bishops Lydeard, one end of Britain’s longest independent heritage railway. The newly re-furbished Gauge Museum combines a wide collection of original objects from the railway’s past, with a range of interactive exhibits to help visitors experience and explore some of the fascinating history of our line.
bodyContent: Housed in a historic goods shed built in 1876, the Gauge Museum tells the complete story of the West Somerset Railway, from its original design, at the hands of Isambard Kingdom Brunel, to its near demise under the Beeching axe and subsequent rescue and re-birth as a heritage line. Discover Somerset’s Engineering Past Our newly refurbished gallery offers a bright and welcoming space for visitors; with a range of interactive exhibits and working models designed to help you get ‘hands on’ with our history. Why not come and take on the role of signalman in our working signal box – do you have what it takes to set the points? Step aboard our beautiful Victorian sleeping car, take a seat, and experience for yourself the height of luxury travel from the lost age of steam. Discover the history of the goods shed building with our new interactive goods exhibit. Find out more about the people who built and worked on the railway with our new interactive touch screen, giving access to never-before seen pictures from our railway’s past. And do not forget to visit our model railway upstairs to watch our skilled operators in action. Education and Learning A range of museum trails are available for young visitors and we regularly host family STEM events (Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics) as well as offering learning sessions, resource packs and loans boxes for schools. For more information, please visit our website http://www.wsrht.co.uk/
tagline: The Gauge Museum can be found at Bishops Lydeard

title: Babbling Brook
subtitle: Our Restaurant is well known for consistently good food and our Chef Dave has done an amazing job since starting with us over 3 years ago.
bodyContent: We have been winning awards for our kitchen and pub since 2015. We have a passion for locally sourced food and drinks and are lucky enough to have a host of wonderful local suppliers to choose from. You can find a list of our suppliers here. We only have a maximum of 2 chef's in the kitchen at one time. We are small but very good at what we do. We are able to change most menu options to suit any allergies, intolerances or lifestyle choices. We follow the same philosophy of local sourced when it comes to our bar and we use local suppliers for the majority of our drinks.​ We have a substantial West Country collection of Gins and our Wines are supplied by Regency Wines a small West Country based company. You can find more suppliers here Sustainability is very important to us with our waste managed through a contract with a specialist waste recycling company to recycle our glass, tin, cardboard, plastics, cooked food waste and kitchen oil. Other measures include careful monitoring of our water use and reuse of water for our plants. We have also switched to low energy LED light bulbs throughout the premises. With sensor timers in places to save energy. We prioritise local suppliers and producers in our food and drink sourcing to help miles travelled to supply us as well as sourcing fairtrade products for hot beverages. We offer 4 ensuite rooms, 2 Doubles and 2 Singles all with their own garden access from our cottage gardens. Why not stay away for the night? Enjoy a wonderful meal and the odd tipple and just stumble back to the bed for the night?

title: Spot birds and wildlife at scenic
subtitle: A man-made lake in North Somerset is now a beautiful nature reserve with an abundance of wildlife and habitats.
bodyContent: Walk information Distance: about 1 mile Difficulty: easy – a level, fully-accessible gravel path runs around Backwell Lake Duration: 30 mins at a very leisurely pace to enjoy the scenery. Lots of public rights of way run around Backwell so it will be easy to make a longer route if you want to, such as walking up Backwell Hill, to the southeast of Backwell, to see the Jubilee Stone. Map: OS Explorer 154 A man-made lake in North Somerset is now a beautiful nature reserve with an abundance of wildlife and habitats. Take a short stroll around Backwell Lake to enjoy the scenic views. Backwell Lake was constructed in the 1970s as a balancing pond, to store surface water running from housing estates in Nailsea during times of heavy rainfall. Since its construction it has developed into an important wildlife habitat and is now a designated local nature reserve. The site is managed by Wessex Water, which works with local volunteers to conserve and enhance the wildlife. This has included changing how the grass is managed to help wildflowers grow. Backwell Lake supports more than 10 species of birds and the lake is important for wildfowl, especially during winter. On your way round, also look out for coot, moorhen, swift, cormorant, mute swan, tufted duck and grey heron among others. Click HERE for full details and FREE PDF copy

bodyContent: Nowhere else does fun and entertainment quite like Butlin’s. title: Dunkery Beacon Country House
subtitle: Welcome to Dunkery Beacon Country House near Dunster – a truly unique and special place to stay in the heart of Exmoor National Park.
bodyContent: Dunkery Beacon Hotel near Minehead offers luxury accommodation and provide the perfect place to escape the rigours of day-to-day life and relax and unwind in a truly tranquil, rural location where breath-taking scenery abounds. Dining & Drinks Relaxed, friendly and sophisticated award-winning dining with a seasonally changing menu and a focus on locally-sourced produce. Our extensive wine list is supplied by top London wine merchant Berry Bros. & Rudd and West Country merchant Christopher Piper Wines. Experience Exmoor in all its glory from our idyllic rural location, with spectacular views across the countryside and moor. There’s wild moorland, lush, deep, wooded, river valleys, pretty thatched cottages and acres of woodland. Sit back, relax…and let nature take over!
tagline: Welcome to Dunkery Beacon Country House near Dunster

title: Ferne Animal Sanctuary
subtitle: Ferne Animal Sanctuary is set within 72 acres of beautiful & protected countryside in the Blackdown Hills on the Devon/Somerset border. This charitable sanctuary takes in unwanted, abandoned and neglected animals and gives them a fantastic life either at the sanctuary or by finding them a special forever home.
bodyContent: Ferne Animal Sanctuary is set within 72 acres of beautiful & protected countryside in the Blackdown Hills on the Devon/Somerset border. This charitable sanctuary takes in unwanted, abandoned and neglected animals and gives them a fantastic life either at the sanctuary or by finding them a special forever home. Ferne Animal Sanctuary, located near Chard in Somerset, is a remarkable facility dedicated to the rehoming of dogs, cats, and horses. In addition to this, the sanctuary provides ongoing care and welfare for a wide variety of animals, including sheep, goats, cattle, pigs, geese, chickens, and an aviary housing birds from around the world. It is also home to smaller animals such as rabbits, guinea pigs, chinchillas and ferrets, ensuring they all receive the care and attention they need. Founded in 1939, at the onset of World War II, the charity was established to care for pets whose owners were going to war, or who had been displaced by the conflict. Over the years, it has forged strong connections with HM Armed Forces and the Royal Family. A typical visit to Ferne lasts between 90 to 150 minutes, during which visitors can enjoy observing the animals in their natural habitats. The experience includes a sensory garden designed to calm the senses with a variety of sounds, sights and smells. Visitors can explore the Willow Walk, which offers insights into animal care, as well as informative displays about our water voles, dragonflies, birds, and fungi. There's also a machinery wall showcasing equipment used throughout the years, along with a small play area for our younger visitors. Take the time to enjoy the stunning natural landscape of the Blackdown Hills from our viewing platform. Relax, gaze across the hills, and marvel at the beauty of nature at its finest. During the school holidays, Creative Corner offers a range of animal-themed activities and arts and crafts. We also host special events and workshops throughout the year, with full details available on our website. The Visitor Centre is open from 10 AM to 4 PM from Easter to October half term, though the shop and sanctuary are open every day, except Christmas Day, Boxing Day, and New Year's Day. Our well-stocked pet supplies and gift shop has everything you need for your animals, as well as delightful treats to tempt you. Dog friendly (dogs must be kept on leads) and accessible, Ferne has a good network of tarmac paths. However, due to the number of gates, we recommend that wheelchair users are accompanied. We have designated parking spaces for wheelchair users and visitors with special needs next to our Visitor Centre as well as in the main car park. All money raised goes to support our animal care and welfare. Unleash the Party Fun at Ferne Animal Sanctuary! PARKING & TRANSPORT · All major credit cards accepted · Coach parking · On site parking · Parking (free) PET INFORMATION · Dogs Accepted SPECIALIST FEATURES · In countryside TRAVEL & TRADE · Groups accepted
tagline: Ferne Animal Sanctuary is set within 72 acres of beautiful & protected countryside.

title: Oldfields
subtitle: Oldfields is a large, elegant and traditional Victorian bed & breakfast with panoramic views of Bath.
bodyContent: Oldfields is a large, elegant and traditional Victorian bed & breakfast with panoramic views of Bath. It is superbly positioned, only 10 minutes walk to the city centre and is built from the honey-coloured stone for which Bath is famous. Although the house is equipped with every modern feature to ensure that visitors experience maximum comfort and convenience, it retains many of the elaborate cornices and artistry of its original character. The bedrooms are beautifully furnished with rich fabrics and antiques and offer a full range of amenities. You are assured of a warm welcome from the resident Managers.
tagline: Oldfields is a large, elegant and traditional Victorian bed & breakfast

title: The Paragon Townhouse
subtitle: The Paragon is a wondrously quirky Georgian Townhouse located in the bustling heart of historic Bath.
bodyContent: Arching over the ancient steps that lead from Roman Road down to Bath’s Artisan Quarter and Walcot Street, this listed building has been described as “like a Landmark Trust house but more beautiful.” Packed full of original features the house sleeps 8 in four double bedrooms and is spread over a total of 6 floors. Up to 2 extras sleep in comfortable day beds in the larger rooms. Awarded a special Gold by VisitBritain for 2018 / 19 and with the kitchen in the original vaults below street level you could not find a more original or characterful property for your special stay in Bath.
tagline: The Paragon is a wondrously quirky Georgian Townhouse

title: Brooks’ View
subtitle: Brooks’ View is the epitome of the favoured cottage for those seeking a special place to stay.
bodyContent: Unashamedly a luxury romantic self-catering cottage 12 minutes from Bath city centre, the cottage is ideal for weekends away, mini moons, honey moons or just a few days’ escape in the delightful countryside. Many walks for walkers and splendid for cyclists being on Sustrans Two Tunnels Route 24. Sleeping 2 in the master bedroom, recently converted Brooks’ View not only has a luxury 1400 pocket sprung bed but also a decadent bathroom with a large walk in shower and a Victorian roll top claw bath. The cosy living room has a comfortable sofa and a snuggle sofabed for that extra guest. In the winter the traditional wood burning stove provides a lovely focal point and also extra heat. There is a small dining area with a traditional pine table and 4 chairs. The kitchen is fully equipped and has both a dishwasher and a clothes washer. On those halcyon days you can easily breakfast on the patio just outside the cottage. Built in the early 1800s, Brooks’ View is one of 4 artisan cottages built for the Somerset Coal Canal workers in the tiny hamlet of Tucking Mill, in the Midford Valley, an Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty. An area of total peace and calm yet so close to the City. An ornithologist’s delight too..with the bird feeders attracting gold finches, coal finches, blue tits, herons and nuthatches to mention a few. Down by the brooks there is a summerhouse with a patio and a lovely stone barbecue. Ideal for enjoying that glass of cool crisp wine. Flyfishing can be arranged if you fancy a breakfast trout. AROUND AND ABOUT Lying in the historic hamlet of Tucking Mill there is plenty to interest our guests. The wildlife lovers will adore the birds and the geologists the delights of exploring the basis of the structure of the UK. this is the home of William Smith and many of his original surveys were done around this area. Bath is the most obvious attraction with the historic Abbey where Edgar the first King of England was crowned, the Roman Baths and the Thermae Spa together with the most wonderful Georgian architecture much loved by Jane Austen and her fans today. At only 20 minutes distance there is Longleat, the Saxon town of Bradford on Avon, the National Trust village of Lacock used in Jane Austen and Harry Potter films and 45 minutes drive takes you to . And there are many more…Cheddar Gorge, Wookey Hole, Bristol with the Science Museum and famous zoo. MEDIA FACILITIES There is free Wifi throughout the cottage and there is a small TV in the bedroom as well as a larger flat screen in the sitting room. An iPod Docking station is also provided. There is a selection of DVDs, a variety of books as well as some board games. PARKING Free private parking space for one car is provided and a second by arrangement REWARD CARD The benefits of the Reward Card with special discounts and extras like 3 hours for 2 in the Thermae Spa are available in this cottage. Full details in the cottage and on this website. ABOUT TUCKING MILL SELF CATERING Brooks’ View is one of the five 4 Star Luxury Gold properties in Tucking Mill Self Catering owned by Michael and Ann. There are two apartments in the city centre, The Old Smithy Loft and No 2 Hedgemead Court, and three cottages just 12 minutes drive away at Tucking Mill, Midford, a historic hamlet just outside the city boundaries in an Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty. THOSE LOOKING AFTER YOU The property is managed by the Family Team..With Ann who has a background in hospitality and much travelling, Michael who built the barbecues and is in charge of the logs,birdfeeding and Head Housekeeper Nikki the team will do its utmost to ensure you enjoy your stay. You will also probably see Rob our invaluable man of all trades around… Short and long breaks available
tagline: Brooks’ View is the epitome of the favoured cottage for those seeking a special place to stay.

title: Jungle Book Sculpture Trail
subtitle: Looking for an outdoor family adventure in the Taunton area? Step into the wild this season with the Jungle Book Sculpture Trail
bodyContent: a { text-decoration: none; color: #464feb; } tr th, tr td { border: 1px solid #e6e6e6; } tr th { background-color: #f5f5f5; } Looking for an outdoor family adventure in the Taunton area? Step into the wild this season with the Jungle Book Sculpture Trail , running from 3rd April to 10th October at Coates English Willow , Stoke St Gregory. This enchanting trail invites visitors to wander through lush greenery in search of 12 beautifully crafted Jungle Book characters , each waiting to be discovered among the trees and foliage. Children can enjoy a fun wordsearch along the way — and there’s a prize at the end to celebrate their efforts! At just £4.75 per person , it’s an affordable and magical day out for families, nature lovers, or anyone looking to explore one of Somerset’s most charming rural attractions. Whether you're local to Taunton or visiting for the holidays, the trail offers a wonderful combination of creativity, outdoor fun, and a touch of classic storybook adventure. Make it part of your spring or summer plans and enjoy a wild day out right on Taunton’s doorstep.
tagline: Follow the Jungle Book Sculpture Trail This Spring & Summer!

title: Julian Hight - Ancient Tree Explorer
subtitle: Join author, photographer and ancient tree specialist Julian Hight for an exploration of Britain's remarkable ancient trees, their history, ecology and folklore. Drawing on more than 20 years of research, this event celebrates some of the country's most enduring natural landmarks.
bodyContent: a { text-decoration: none; color: #464feb; } tr th, tr td { border: 1px solid #e6e6e6; } tr th { background-color: #f5f5f5; } a { text-decoration: none; color: #464feb; } tr th, tr td { border: 1px solid #e6e6e6; } tr th { background-color: #f5f5f5; } Join Julian Hight as he discusses Ancient Tree Explorer , a comprehensive guide to some of Britain's most remarkable ancient trees and woodlands. Featuring more than 300 places to visit, the book explores everything from millennial oaks and ancient yews to remnants of historic hunting forests, Celtic rainforests and the great wood of Caledonia. Alongside practical guidance and photography, it examines the ecology, folklore and history that surround these living landmarks. An author, designer, photographer and musician, Julian Hight has spent more than two decades documenting Britain's ancient trees. He is the author of four books and chairs the Wessex Ancient Tree Forum. This event offers nature lovers, history enthusiasts and walkers the opportunity to learn more about Britain's ancient treescape and the stories these remarkable trees continue to tell. Tickets Available on the Website
tagline: Discover Britain's ancient trees with author and explorer Julian Hight.

title: Timsbury
subtitle: Timsbury is an attractive village to visit in north east Somerset, surrounded by lovely rolling hills and valleys.
bodyContent: Timsbury is an attractive village to visit in north east Somerset, surrounded by lovely rolling hills and valleys. It is close to Bath (18mins.), Bristol, Frome, Wells and also to Midsomer Norton which Midsomer Murders is named after (not Midsummer Murders). By car it is on the B3115 and is 30 mins. from Bristol airport - set your Satnav to BA2 0HY. It is easy to park and there are bus services. It has a good village pub, The Seven Stars, and other eating places such as Connies Tea Rooms & Bistro, accommodation and shops. It has many buildings of both architectural and historical interest. (photos of 7 stars Connies and High Street). It is a good base to discover the Somerset countryside with lovely interesting walks including along the Cam river valley, and its wildlife and history with old buildings. (photo the square and the church) There are lovely walks in the area which you can follow in our book. You can discover remains of early coal mining blended into the landscape, such as the Somersetshire Coal Canal. It was home to the world famous Father of Geology, William Smith who lived in nearby Rugbourne Farm while he was surveying for the canal. For more information: timsbury.org.uk .

title: Watchet
subtitle: Watchet, Somerset, maritime history colours every part of the town while the wild beauty of its coastline is untouched with ancient ammonite fossils lying on the shore, just waiting to be found.
bodyContent: Watchet port, in Somerset was highly valued by Alfred the Great, as he attempted to fend off the Vikings, and it even had its own mint, producing coins. Before that there was an Iron Age fort that has fragments still evident today. The port came into its own once again in the 19th century when iron ore from the nearby Brendon Hills was exported to Wales. In 2000, the harbour was converted into a modern Marina. Watched over on one side by the 150 year old lighthouse and on another by a statue of Coleridge’s Ancient Mariner, the quay makes for an interesting stroll with views across the Bristol Channel. Several boats offer fishing trips. There are plenty of other walks around Watchet, from day long rambles along parts of the Coleridge Way, The Mineral Line or the West Somerset Coastal Path, to shorter circular saunters in the surrounding countryside. For details on walks visit the Tourist Information Centre. The West Somerset Railway , brought here by Brunel, stops at the picturesque station in Watchet, next to the Marina and town centre. Passengers can spend time in one of the many bars and cafes or visit one of the Museums before resuming their journeys. The Market House Museum covers the fascinating history of a town where kings, queens, murderous knights, pirates, saints and even a famous singing sailor have their stories to tell. The Boat Museum houses an intriguing collection of local flat bottomed boats. The town is packed with independent shops full of antiques, vintage, craft and gifts. There are various art shops and galleries throughout the town as well as East Quay , a gallery and artist studios with restaurant and places to stay on the harbourside. Watchet is lucky enough to have not one but two beaches. To the east of the harbour you’ll find Helwell Bay, rich in fossils - ammonites, bi-valves and ‘Devil’s Toe Nails’. West Street beach has a wonderful old boating lake, extraordinary rock formations with quartz and alabaster running through them, as well as plenty of rock pools to explore. If you’re lucky, you might even spot the resident Peregrine Falcons along with Oyster Catchers and Egret.

title: RSPB Nature Reserve Ham Wall
subtitle: Enjoy the sights and sounds of this magical wetland, created by the RSPB when peat extraction ended on this site.
bodyContent: Enjoy the sights and sounds of this magical wetland, created by the RSPB when peat extraction ended on this site. Ham Wall is a special place that teems with wildlife. You might be lucky enough to see or hear secretive bitterns, otters, water voles, marsh frogs and great crested newts which all call this place home. Enjoy the stunning views across the marshes to Glastonbury Tor and follow secluded paths through the mystical landscape. In winter, make sure you hang around until dusk to see the starlings and their spectacular displays as they gather to roost in the reed beds. Discover the wetland and its amazing wildlife by coming along to a range of regular events including special canoe safaris and spooky Halloween skull trails! Pay and display car park £3 per car for the day. RSPB members park for free when displaying membership card on the dashboard. Blue badge holders park for free. There are on site toilet facilities including disabled access and baby changing facilities. Toilets are open during car park opening hours. The opening hours for the car park are: 1st October - 31st January – 06.00 to 18.30 1st February - 31st March -06.00 to 20.00 1st April - 30th September- 06.00 to 22.00 All the birds, animals and this amazing landscape is here because the RSPB and its partners are giving nature a home in this special place. The RSPB is a charity and we rely on support from people like you. Small Welcome Building open 10am - 4pm every weekend and some weekdays. Hot drinks and flapjacks available along with information about the reserve and the RSPB. If you have any questions email the reserve office ham.wall@rspb.org.uk or phone on 01458 860494
tagline: Enjoy the sights and sounds of this magical wetland, created by the RSPB.

title: Kilve
subtitle: Lying at the northern end of the Quantocks, Kilve is a picturesque village consisting of 3 settlements.
bodyContent: Things to do in Kilve, Somerset. Kilve lying at the northern end of the Quantocks , Kilve is a picturesque village consisting of 3 settlements. Here you will find the ruins of the old Chantry, founded in 1329 and once used for storing barrels of spirits smuggled in to Kilve Pill. The beach is a Site of Special Scientific Interest and a favourite haunt of geologists with its spectacular rock formations and fossils, including ammonites and reptile remains. The only parking for Kilve beach is at the Pay and Display Car Park.

title: The Bishop's Palace
subtitle: The Bishop’s Palace and Gardens in Wells has been home to the Bishops of Bath and Wells for over 800 years and this stunning medieval palace is now open for all to enjoy. It’s a great family day out in Somerset with a full programme of year-round events, free guided walks, open-air music and theatre, garden workshops and more and a slice of cake with afternoon tea at the ever-popular Bishop’s Table café is always welcome!
bodyContent: ⭐ Reward Card Discount Available Visit Highlights: There are 14 acres of outstanding RHS Partner gardens to explore (including the beautiful well pools from which the city takes its name), Dragon’s Lair play area, guided tours, children’s trails and workshops and a café with the best views in Wells! Multi media tours of the Palace building are also included with admission with the choice of an adult version or one tailored for a more family audience including quizzes, treasure hunts and talking Bishops from years gone by! Visitors are guided around the Palace buildings through five narrative themes using stories, music, imagery, quizzes and talking Bishops bringing stories of their tenure and legacy at the Palace to life in an interactive and engaging way. A year-round programme of themed family events is also included with admission including a Civil War Weekend; Archery, Vikings and more! Other events are ticketed separately including summer outdoor theatre; the Palace’s Garden Fair and History Live. The Bishop’s Palace dates from the early-thirteenth century when Bishop Jocelin Trotman received a crown licence to build a residence and deer park on land to the south of the Cathedral of St Andrew. Although home to the Bishop and other families, visitors can walk in the footsteps of past bishops through a number of rooms within the Palace. Visitors are also welcome to look around the Bishop’s private Chapel and explore the ruined Great Hall. The moat has been home to mute swans since the 1800s. The tradition of swans on the moat at The Bishop’s Palace in Wells is thought to go back to the 1850’s when it is likely that a Bishop’s daughter first taught the swans to ring a bell at the Gatehouse for food. We now have two swan bells – one just beneath the window on the left of the Gatehouse, the other to the right – both with a rope hanging down for the swans to pull. The Palace Gardens are open daily from 10am until 4pm in winter and 9.30am - 5.30pm in summer although there may be restricted access due to events and activities taking place (check the website for details). There are toilets on site. Guided tours are also included with Admission – check available times at the Ticket Office on arrival. Families: There’s so much for families to do at The Bishop’s Palace, whatever the weather. Little ones love to explore the gardens, trying to spot the swans and their cygnets; there are waterfalls and springs to see, trees to climb and places to hide. Children also love to explore the magical discovery area that is the Dragon’s Lair in a far corner of the Gardens! And throughout the school holidays, there are always plenty of events to keep families busy including crafting, outdoor gardening, family trails, storytelling and more. Refreshments: The Bishop’s Table café is open daily serving delicious, locally-sourced homemade food and some of the best coffee and cake you'll find in Wells. It’s the perfect place to meet friends for breakfast, lunch and afternoon teas or Sunday Lunches are now being served! Accessibility: From the main entrance of the Palace to the Palace building, around the gardens and to the café's dining area, there is level access. We have one lift to all floors of the Palace building. The outer gardens are accessible via a bridge which is 810mm wide. There are fully accessible toilets with level access within the Stableyard area and the Palace building. There are three spaces available on site for accessible parking, however, it is necessary to book these at least 48 hours before arrival via info@bishopspalace.org.uk or call 01749 988111.
tagline: The Bishop's Palace and Gardens, Wells, Somerset is a great family day out in Somerset.

title: Oake Manor Golf Club
subtitle: Oake Manor Golf Club is superb 6149 yard golf course with stunning rural views and featuring water hazards on 10 of the 18 holes
bodyContent: Oake Manor Golf Club is located in some of Somerset’s most beautiful countryside nestling between the Quantock, Brendon and Blackdown hills, yet only a few minutes’ drive from junction 26 of the M5. A superb 6149 yard golf course with stunning rural views and featuring water hazards on 10 of the 18 holes. Oake Manor Golf Course is one of those special places that offers high standards of service and facilities, combined with a friendly, relaxed atmosphere that welcomes all golfers, members or visitors, seven days a week. The facilities are first-rate, with an 11 bay covered driving range, 9 hole par 3 course, short game practice area and putting green. A warm welcome is guaranteed by our PGA Professionals in the golf shop which is an approved Titleist custom fitting centre. Non-members welcome.
tagline: A superb 6149 yard golf course with stunning rural views

title: Yeo Valley
subtitle: We’re a family farm and dairy business that’s grown into Britain’s largest organic brand. Somerset is our home, our workplace and the backdrop and inspiration for everything we do. We’ve been farming and making dairy products in Blagdon since 1961. Our business has grown with farms across the Mendips and production sites across Somerset employing over 1,700 people.
bodyContent: We make organic yogurts that are naturally tasty and healthy. At the heart of Yeo Valley Organic is our incredible British Friesian cows who happily graze outside on our organic lush pastures. We farm organically because that’s how to get the best tasting ingredients. This inspires all the incredible products we make from our popular Natural yogurt to our organic fruit compotes and ice cream. We firmly believe that organic is the way forward for our own health, and for the health of wildlife and the planet. It’s about brilliant nutritious dairy, created by nature. We love nothing more than to open up our doors (and farm gates) so that people can come and see it all for themselves. We offer farm tours, cooking demos, garden open days and even a summer music festival. More information
tagline: We’re a family farm and dairy business that’s grown into Britain’s largest organic brand.

title: Wells & Mendip Museum
subtitle: We aim to give you a stimulating and enjoyable experience, and our volunteers will provide you with a warm welcome. Find us in the Cathedral Close, in the former home of the Cathedral Chancellors.
bodyContent: Our museum tells the stories of Wells and the Mendip Hills. Our displays include a Jurassic sea dragon, and unique archaeology collections from the Mendip caves, featuring the bones of ancient animals who roamed here thousands of years ago. Find out about the incredible array of rocks and minerals to be found on the Mendip Hills, and how people have explored its caves. We have a wonderful collection of embroidery samplers, and tell the story of the early Cathedral stonemasons through a collection of sculpture and statues on loan from the cathedral. Our temporary exhibitions feature the work of local and well-known artists. We also have a library and are home to the Wells City Archives (both open to researchers by appointment). The museum shop stocks an array of attractive gifts, cards and books.
tagline: We aim to give you a stimulating and enjoyable experience

title: Woodborough Inn
subtitle: A warm welcome, great food & drink and a cracking pub atmosphere is what makes The Woodborough Inn so special
bodyContent: Sat in the heart of the village of Winscombe and surrounded by the beautiful Mendip hills, The Woodborough Inn is the perfect place to relax and explore the local area which includes the beautiful Cheddar Gorge, the cathedral city of Wells and Glastonbury Tor. The Mendips providing a great space to enjoy the great outdoors. Whether a gentle walk or some extreme mountain biking; The Mendips has it all. Our guest accommodation consists of 7 cosy en-suite rooms, ideal for visitors to the West Country, business people and families alike, and come at competitive rates. Open daily from 11am, lunch from 12-2.00pm and our dinner service runs from 5.30pm. Sunday food hours are 12-3 and 5.30-7.30pm. Our chefs serve up some fabulous food. Hearty pub classics, an exciting range of specials, plus pizza and lighter dishes; all food cooked fresh using locally sourced ingredients. Our Sunday roasts are also not to be missed! Local real ales are always on tap along with crisp lagers, craft beers and local ciders. We have a wonderful wine list and our popular new “Gin List” heads up our selection of premium spirits. We also offer a great range of soft drinks, coffee, tea and cake! This is a popular spot for walkers and naturally, well-behaved dogs are welcome.
tagline: A warm welcome, great food & drink and a cracking pub atmosphere

title: Dig deep into Shipham’s mines
subtitle: This circular walk features in the new book Miles More Mendip, by Sue Gearing and Les Davies. From the car park, head towards the village hall entrance.
bodyContent: Walk information Distance: 4.75 miles Difficulty: easy with some stiles, ups and downs, and one steep-ish short hill Duration: About 2-3 hours Map: OS Explorer 141 This circular walk features in the new book Miles More Mendip, by Sue Gearing and Les Davies. From the car park, head towards the village hall entrance. Immediately turn right on a footpath which goes down under trees. The path comes out onto the open playing field. Continue on, cross a stile, and descend through the bumpy land, the remains of former lead mining. Go to the right of a closed reservoir and head down to the wall below. Turn left on the path alongside the wall. Cross right over a pipe stile and go through the field and onto the main road. Cross to the Star Inn (#1 on map). Take the No Through Road to the right. At the top, reach a bridleway track (#2) going left, with a Bristol Water installation on the corner. The pure Mendip water is thanks to filtration through many layers of limestone. subtitle: A Victorian home, tastefully decorated with very comfortable antique French beds. Central Bath location. Excellent breakfast choices.
bodyContent: A well appointed, stylish late Victorian home. We offer you: Immaculate ensuite accommodation Affordable rates Central city location Superb breakfasts Free adjacent street parking Great insider information on Bath Whether you are visiting Bath on business or taking a break, we aim to make your visit memorable for quality rooms at reasonable rates, high service levels and an aura of relaxed ease and comfort. We offer sound advice on Bath's shopping, sight seeing and eating out. And then there's breakfast to look forward to...

title: Beautiful loft room with views over Bath
subtitle: A bright and comfortable loft bedroom situated in a newly decorated and well equipped house just a fifteen minute walk away from the centre of Bath.
bodyContent: A bright and comfortable loft bedroom situated in a newly decorated and well equipped house just a fifteen minute walk away from the centre of Bath. This is one of four private rooms within the house. Situated in Oldfield Park and very close to Oldfield Park Train Station and local buses, this is a perfect base for exploring Bath. There is a free car park just fifty metres from the house which is a truly rare find in Bath! Four bedroom Victorian house retaining many period features. With an eclectic mix of individually furnished, quirky bedrooms and modern kitchen and bathroom. Stripped wooden floors in communal areas and 3 of the bedrooms with carpeted, snug attic room. Bright and airy and set over 3 floors. Easy off street parking. 200mb fibre optic broadband. Flat walk in to town (15 minutes walk/ 5 minutes taxi). 2 minutes walk to Oldfield Park Train Station (2 minutes to Bath Spa; 12 minutes to Bristol Temple Meads). The private double room benefits from use of a shared kitchen with breakfast bar. A comfortable living space in the centre of the house, with an extensive library of books for both the avid and casual reader. The property also boasts a garden at the rear; a great spot for relaxing during the summer months. I like to give guests their own space during their stay, however I am always available to offer recommendations and help, both before and during their stay. I am never far away or am in the house, and am always on hand should you need me. I usually arrange for a self check in but can always be on hand if a guest would like me to help them check in.
tagline: A bright and comfortable loft bedroom situated in a newly decorated

title: Burys Cottage
subtitle: Burys Cottage has a cosy and romantic feel to it. The location is at the end of a row of other cottages.
bodyContent: The open-plan kitchen and living room is perfect for quiet nights in, after a day out exploring the area. The kitchen is equipped with everything you should need to make some delicious meals. The bedroom has a 4-poster bed. It is made up with fresh, white linen ready for your arrival. We provide a hand towel and bath towel per person. There is plenty of storage and hanging space. There is an en-suite bathroom, with a shower-head over the bath. On the other side of the patio is the Indoor Heated Pool and Games Room, which is available for our guests to use during their stay. Burys Cottage is locate on the edge of the village ‘Winsley’, 5 miles from Bath and 2 miles from Bradford on Avon. There are plenty of walks right from the doorstep, a Farm Shop, village shop and village pub all within 1 mile.
tagline: Come and stay in our elegant Georgian home built by John Wood

title: Old Stables: rural retreat, sleeps 6
subtitle: The Old Stables is created from a stone built-stable block dating from the 1840’s.
bodyContent: It is located in the beautiful Georgian village of Freshford which lies at the junction of the Frome and Avon valleys in the southern Cotswolds. There are some wonderful walks to local pubs following the riverside and canals. All just 15 minutes from Bath by car but the secret of this location is the 9 minute train journey to Bath from the village station, just a short stroll from the cottages. A three bedroom cottage (two king and one twin-bed) with a fully equipped kitchen opening onto a dining room There is a separate living room with TV/DVD and two large leather couches . The living room has large patio doors that open up onto the courtyard area. The Old Stables can accommodate 6 people. This cottage has: Three bedrooms (two king size and one with twin beds) One family bathroom , a Living room with Freeview TV/DVD two large leather couches and a dining room with a table seating 6.The Kitchen is equipped with all the cookware you might need dishwasher along washing machine/dryer and Iron/Ironing board. Hairdryers , bed linen and towels are all provided in the bedrooms.We provide a “Welcome pack” of tea, coffee, sugar, milk, bread, butter, eggs and bacon. The cottage has Free WiFi. Neighbourhood overview: Freshford is a beautiful ancient village with a wonderful pub just a few minutes walk from the cottage( The Inn at Freshford) that serves restaurant quality food and all the local beers and ciders.The village has an excellent fully stocked( from wine to organic humus!)community shop that also has a great cafe that serves lunch. There is also a local doctors surgery. The village is nestled at the junction of the Frome and Avon valleys . The Kennet and Avon canal is a 15 minute walk from the cottage. Getting around: You don’t need a car to stay in the cottage. The village station is a few minutes walk away. Trains are hourly off peak and thrice hourly at peak times. Bath 9 mins, Bristol 22 mins. London Padington to Bath Spa 1.5 hours Bath Spa to Freshford 9 minutes Bath Spa to Freshford “ https://www.thetrainline.com/train-times/bath-spa-to-freshford ” Freshford to Bath Spa “ https://www.thetrainline.com/train-times/freshford-to-bath-spa ” There is also a local bus service to all the adjacent villages and Bath. The cottage has two parking spaces suitable for one medium and one small car or a single large SUV. Other things to note If you are a runner or keep fit enthusiast the owner is a qualified Personal Trainer (Bath Uni) with much Marathon and half marathon experience. She specialises in Ladies training. Please let us know if you would like guided running or some Personal Fitness training
tagline: The Old Stables is created from a stone built-stable block dating from the 1840’s.

title: Broad Street House
subtitle: This listed property is spread across two floors, the open plan living and dining space works well for groups
bodyContent: Sleeps: Broad Street House is a bright and spacious maisonette in Bath’s historic centre, providing character accommodation for 12 people in four bedrooms. Bedrooms: There are four bedrooms, each with three beds. Two of the bedrooms have adult bunk beds. Bathrooms: There are two shower rooms. One on each floor next to the bedrooms. Kitchen: An open plan kitchen and dining area leads into the sitting room. General Points: This listed property is spread across two floors, the open plan living and dining space works well for groups and the location is one of the best in Bath for being in the thick of the city centre action. Parking: A parking permit for 1 vehicle (this is all we are allowed by The Council!) will be waiting at the property when you arrive. This enables you to park for free in the central area parking zone in the marked, on street parking bays. Additional long stay, Pay and Display parking is available at Manvers St and Charlotte St car parks in the city centre.
tagline: Property is spread across two floors, the open plan living and dining space works well for groups

title: Yeovil Train Station

bodyContent: The station is 2 miles outside the town, in the village of Stoford. Although Yeovil is in Somerset, the station was in Dorset until 1991.

title: Wookey Hole Caves & Attractions
subtitle: Wookey Hole Caves is a magical place of caves, legends, and adventure for all ages. It’s an experience millions of years in the making with plenty to do inside and out. Enjoy vintage penny arcades, museums, adventure golf, and soft play zones, and of course the famous, beautiful caves.
bodyContent: ⭐ Reward Card Discount Available Wookey Hole Caves and attractions lies In the heart of Somerset. A magical place of caves, legends, and adventure for the young and young at heart. When you visit Wookey Hole, you’ll enjoy an experience millions of years in the making. There is plenty to do inside and out, from vintage penny arcades to museums, adventure golf, and soft play zones, to name but a few of the attractions. Not forgetting the breathtakingly beautiful caves, for which Wookey Hole is renowned. Your visit will take you through 8 chambers. Each with a unique beauty and story. You’ll also pass our cheese tunnel, home to the delicious Wookey Hole cheese. The cheese is not the only resident of the caves. Over the years, Wookey Hole has been home to giant hyenas, bears, Neanderthals, and many local people. It has even been a site of pagan and Roman worship. You’ll find Wookey Hole holds a surprise around every corner. You might even get to meet our most famous resident, the Witch of Wookey Hole. We have found she most likes to visit during school holidays! The world-famous Wookey Hole Circus School performs at Wookey Hole at weekends and in School Holidays. Every year over 250,000 people visit Wookey Hole and take-home cherished memories of a great day out. Whether it is your first time or your fiftieth, there is always something new to discover. We can’t wait to welcome you.
tagline: At Wookey Hole Caves and Attractions, Somerset, there’s always fun and adventure to be had.

title: East Quay Kitchen
subtitle: East Quay Kitchen is East Quay’s in-house restaurant. Offering Mediterranean and Middle Eastern inspired dishes, served from 9am to 8pm every day in season (check our website at other times). Sit inside in the restaurant or out in the courtyard, soaking up the atmosphere from the artist studios and watching the boats in the marina.
bodyContent: East Quay Kitchen is in the heart of the arts centre and spills out into the sunny courtyard. Serving breakfast, lunch, afternoon bar snacks with an evening menu every day. The menu is inspired by Mediterranean and Middle Eastern cuisine and is mainly vegetarian and vegan with some meat and fish. The menu changes seasonally, but favourites include a breakfast of Turkish Eggs, two poached eggs, whipped yoghurt, chili butter, dill and focaccia (£7) or for lunch a Middle Eastern Flatbread, beetroot falafel, chickpeas, shirazi salad, hummus, pickles, fried potatoes, amba & tahini sauce (£12). During the summer months the summer kitchen is also open, which serves lighter meals such as salad bowls and wraps. Go to the website for an up to date menu. In the evenings you can also get bar snacks and an evening menu which serves sharing platters and light evening meals. Head Chef Richard Pettitt, previously owned Anise in Taunton and worked at The Ritz London and The Ledbury in London, dishes have been inspired by his travels and love of world cuisine. East Quay Kitchen aims to be sustainable as possible. This includes reducing the meat and fish options, choosing suppliers carefully. We consider the whole life-cycle of products and seek to have a positive benefit wherever possible.
tagline: East Quay Kitchen is East Quay’s in-house restaurant. Offering Mediterranean and Middle Eastern

title: Mendip Basecamp
subtitle: Basecamp is an award-winning, off-grid family adventure campsite in the Mendip Hills...
bodyContent: Basecamp is an award-winning, off-grid family adventure camp in the Mendip Hills National Landscape - just minutes from the M5 and Weston-super-Mare. Surrounded by ancient woodland you can pitch where you like, park right by your tent and enjoy evenings around the campfire. Well-behaved dogs are welcome! With no check-out time, you can leave whenever you are ready. Mendip Basecamp is camping how it should be: rural, laid-back and relaxed but with essential luxuries. Usually reserved for schools and private groups, in 2020, Mendip opened Basecamp up to families for the very first time- and hasn’t looked back since. Public bookings are available throughout the summer holidays and summer weekends. Bring your own tent or campervan, book bell tents, glamphouses or stay in Mendip Lodge (with free breakfast). Facilities include hot showers, clean flushing toilets, a camp shop, a country Lodge with a cider garden (and live music), an onsite activity centre, USB charging and WIFI. Free activities throughout the summer include live music, orienteering, circus skills, treasure hunts, free climbing tower and nature craft. The campsite is less than a 5-minute woodland walk from Mendip Activity Centre, home to over 20 different adventurous, outdoor activities including rock climbing, kayaking, archery, frisbee golf and air rifle. New for 2026, Mendip Basecamp is launching Mendip Mini Fests - six family-friendly festivals running throughout the summer holiday weekends. Great entertainment, headline bands, local talent competition, and more! Included at no extra cost, exclusively for campsite guests.
tagline: Mendip Basecamp was delighted to be awarded the Gold campsite at the 2023-2024

bodyContent: This year make sure to set your sights on the Fleet Air Arm Museum in Ilchester and see where time flies. This must-see attraction has four large exhibition halls each containing dozens of incredible aircraft which tell the rich history of naval aviation. Grab your wingman and step inside the first British Concorde, experience the thrills of a working flight deck, and get up close to a wide range of rare and historical aircraft.
